The '''Black Russian''' is a [[cocktail]] of [[vodka]] and [[coffee liqueur]]. It contains 50 ml vodka and 20 ml coffee liqueur, per [[IBA Official Cocktail|IBA]] specified ingredients.<ref name="IBA">{{Cite web|title=Black Russian|url=https://iba-world.com/black-russian/|url-status=live|access-date=December 6, 2021|website=IBA World|date=29 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210609011406/https://iba-world.com/black-russian/|archive-date=2021-06-09}}</ref>

The drink is made by pouring the vodka and coffee liqueur over [[ice cube]]s or cracked ice in an [[old-fashioned glass]] and stirring.<ref name="SpiritDrinks">{{Cite web | title = SpiritDrinks.com - Black Russian | publisher = SpiritDrinks | url = http://www.spiritdrinks.com/cocktails/Black_Russian.asp | access-date = July 12, 2010}}</ref> The Black Russian is often garnished with a lemon slice and a Luxardo maraschino cherry on a stick.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Black Russian|url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/236/black-russian|access-date=January 24, 2022|website=Difford's Guide for Discerning Drinkers}}</ref>

== History ==
The Black Russian cocktail first appeared in 1949 and is ascribed to Gustave Tops, a [[Belgians|Belgian]] [[Bartender|barman]], who created it at the [[Hotel Metropole, Brussels|Hotel Metropole]] in [[Brussels]] in honor of [[Perle Mesta]], then [[United States Ambassador to Luxembourg]].<ref name="sicard">{{Cite web | last = Regan| first = Gary | title = Behind The Drink: Black Russian | publisher = Liquor.com | date = 8 September 2008 | url = https://www.liquor.com/articles/behind-the-drink-the-black-russian/ | access-date = 6 September 2019}}</ref> The cocktail owes its name to the use of vodka, a typical Russian spirit, and the blackness of the coffee liqueur.

==Variations==
* Dirty Black Russian, Tall Black Russian, Australian Black Russian or Colorado Bulldog: served in a [[highball]] glass and topped up with [[cola]].<ref>{{Cite web | title = Tall Black Russian | publisher = Fluid Trade | url = http://www.fluidtrade.co.uk/cocktailview.aspx?CocktailID=303&x=0 | access-date = June 8, 2010 | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20091103184824/http://www.fluidtrade.co.uk/cocktailview.aspx?CocktailID=303&x=0 | archive-date = November 3, 2009 }}</ref>
* Black Magic: served with a dash of [[lemon]] juice and a [[lemon twist]] to garnish.<ref>{{Cite web | title = Black Magic | publisher = in-the-spirit.co.uk | url = http://www.in-the-spirit.co.uk/cocktails/view_cocktail.php?id=35 | access-date = June 8, 2010 | archive-date = November 5, 2016 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20161105062645/http://www.in-the-spirit.co.uk/cocktails/view_cocktail.php?id=35 | url-status = dead }}</ref>
* Irish Russian or Smooth Black Russian: served with a head of [[Guinness]].<ref name="sicard"/><ref>{{Cite web| title = Smooth Black Russian recipe| publisher = DrinksMixer.com| url = http://www.drinksmixer.com/drink2057.html| access-date = June 8, 2010| archive-date = May 17, 2020| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200517021531/http://www.drinksmixer.com/drink2057.html| url-status = dead}}</ref>
* Brown Russian: served in a [[highball glass]] and topped with [[ginger ale]].<ref>{{Cite web | title = Brown Russian | publisher = SpiritDrinks | url = http://spiritdrinks.com/cocktails/BrownRussian.asp | access-date = July 23, 2010}}</ref>
* Belarusian or [[White Russian (cocktail)|white Russian]]: served with [[milk]] or [[cream]].<ref name="IBA"/>
* Mudslide: served with Irish cream, either fresh cream or ice cream, with or without chocolate sauce rim.<ref>{{Cite web | title = Mudslide | publisher = Difford's Guide | url = https://www.diffordsguide.com/en-au/cocktails/recipe/1374/mudslide | access-date = 26 July 2021}}</ref>
* Mind Eraser: topped up with sparkling water.<ref name="minderaser">{{Cite web|title=The Mind Eraser: Vodka Drinks We Love|url=https://www.liquor.com/recipes/mind-eraser/|access-date=2021-06-13|website=Liquor.com|language=en}}</ref>
* Paralyzer: Made with [[cola]] and [[milk]] in addition to vodka and coffee liqueur.<ref>{{Cite web | title = Vodka Paralyzer| publisher = All Recipes | url = https://www.allrecipes.com/recipe/152922/vodka-paralyzer/ | access-date = 11 March 2023}}</ref>

'''French 75''' is a [[cocktail]] made from [[gin]], champagne, lemon juice, and sugar. It is also called a '''75 cocktail''', or in French simply a {{Lang|fr|soixante quinze}} ('seventy five').

The drink was popular during [[World War I]] in a [[brandy]]-based form.<ref name="MacElhone1">{{citation|author1-last=MacElhone|author1-first=Harry|author1-link=Harry MacElhone|title="Harry" of Ciro's A B C of Mixing Cocktails|date=1923|publisher=[[Dean & Son]]|publication-place=London, United Kingdom|url=https://archive.org/details/vintage-cocktail-books-euvs/1923%20Harry%20of%20Ciro's%20ABC%20of%20mixing%20cocktails%20(second%20impression).pdf}}</ref>{{rp|p=65}} Barman [[Harry MacElhone]] said it was named after [[Canon de 75 modèle 1897|a French light field gun]] of {{convert|75|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} calibre.<ref name="MacElhone1" />{{rp|p=65}}

==History==
The drink with its current name and recipe developed over the 1920s, though similar drinks date to the 19th century. In the 19th century, the ''champagne cup'' was a popular cocktail, consisting of champagne, lemon juice, sugar, and ice. Gin was sometimes added, yielding a drink much like the French 75.<ref>"[http://liquor.com/articles/behind-the-drink-the-french-75/ Behind the Drink: The French 75]", David Wondrich, July 09, 2012</ref>

The drink was first recorded as the "75" in ''Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails'', 1922 edition, by [[Harry MacElhone]], and in the same year in Robert Vermeire's ''Cocktails: How to Mix Them'', which credits the drink to MacElhone.<ref name="ford">"[http://cold-glass.com/2012/10/28/the-french-75-cocktail/ The French 75 Cocktail—Tom Collins in a Tuxedo]", by Doug Ford, October 28, 2012</ref> However, the recipes differed from the current form – MacElhone's version consisted of [[Calvados]], gin, grenadine, and absinthe, while Vermeire added lemon juice.<ref name="ford"/>

The recipe took its now-classic form and "French 75" name in ''Here’s How'', by Judge Jr. (1927), consisting of gin, sugar, lemon juice, and champagne.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1927-Here-s-How-2nd-impression/28|title=1927 Here's How by Judge Jr ( 2nd impression)|website=euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz}}</ref> This recipe was republished with the name "French 75" in ''[[The Savoy Cocktail Book]]'' (1930), which helped popularize the drink. Some later cocktail books use [[cognac]] instead of gin, such as ''[[The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks]]'' by [[David A. Embury]].

The French 75 was popularized in America at the [[Stork Club]] in New York. It appears in the movie ''[[Casablanca (movie)|Casablanca]]'' (1942) and is referenced twice in the [[John Wayne]] films ''[[A Man Betrayed (1941 film)|A Man Betrayed]]'' (1941) and ''[[Jet Pilot (film)|Jet Pilot]]'' (1957). In 2016, it appears in the ITV series ''[[Mr. Selfridge]]'', which is set in London in the 1910s and 1920s.

A fanciful alternative story of the invention of the French 75 was related by humorist [[Jean Shepherd]] on November 17, 1969, wherein he credits [[Gervais Raoul Lufbery]] as the inventor. The mixture, as related by Shepherd, is champagne and cognac on ice with perhaps a twist of lemon.<ref>[http://podbay.fm/show/129951381/e/1185336300 Podcast] 27:00</ref> This version is not credible, given the documented earlier version.{{opinion|reason=The more certain you are of your opinion that it's not credible, the easier it ought to be to find a credible source who shares your opinion.|date=November 2025}}

==Similar drinks==
The recipe of the French 75 is very similar to one of the most popular cocktails, the [[Tom Collins]], with champagne replacing [[carbonated water]]. According to the recipe in Harry MacElhone's book ''Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails'', a French 75 is supposed to be served in a [[highball glass]]. The highball glass, which the Tom Collins cocktail is also served in, supports the theory of the French 75 being a variation of the Tom Collins.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://jeffreymorgenthaler.com/french-75/|title=French 75|date=January 26, 2019|website=Jeffrey Morgenthaler}}</ref>

A "French 125" replaces the gin with cognac.<ref>{{cite web |title=French 125 (French '75' with cognac) |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/3642/french-125-french-75-with-cognac |website=Difford's Guide |access-date=8 March 2025}}</ref>  A "French 95" replaces the gin with bourbon.<ref>{{cite web |title=French 95 (a French '75' with bourbon) |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/4238/french-95-a-french-75-with-bourbon |website=Difford's Guide |access-date=8 March 2025}}</ref>

A '''Brandy Alexander''' is a [[brandy]]-based dessert cocktail,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Experience the Taste of Classic Style With 20 Timeless Cocktails |url=https://www.thespruceeats.com/classic-cocktails-you-must-try-759886 |website=The Spruce Eats}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=17 Delicious Cocktails That Let You Drink Dessert |url=https://www.thespruceeats.com/delicious-dessert-cocktail-recipes-4153407 |website=The Spruce Eats}}</ref> consisting of [[Cognac (drink)|cognac]], [[crème de cacao]], and cream, that became popular during the early 20th century.<ref>''Imbibe Magazine'', May/June 2010, p. 38</ref> It is a variation of an earlier, gin-based cocktail called simply an [[Alexander (cocktail)|Alexander]]. The cocktail known as Alexander today may contain [[gin]] or [[brandy]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Unforgettables | International Bartenders Association |url=https://iba-world.com/iba-cocktails/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20170309093042/http://iba-world.com/iba-cocktails/ |archive-date=9 March 2017 |access-date=26 February 2021}}</ref> Ice cream can be added for a "frozen Brandy Alexander".<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1IPdtz40iXUC&dq=frozen+brandy+alexander&pg=PT38 |title=Buller's Professional Course in Bartending For Home Study |date=16 September 1983 |publisher=Harvard Common Press|isbn=9780916782337 }}</ref>

== History ==
There are many rumours about the origins of the cocktail. Some sources say it was created at the time of the London wedding of [[Mary, Princess Royal and Countess of Harewood|Princess Mary]] and [[Henry Lascelles, 6th Earl of Harewood|Viscount Lascelles]] in 1922.<ref>Classic Cocktail Club, Milan, Italy.</ref> Drama critic and [[Algonquin Round Table]] member [[Alexander Woollcott]] said it was named after him. Other sources say it was named after the Russian tsar [[Alexander II of Russia|Alexander II]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=National Brandy Alexander day |url=http://eatocracy.cnn.com/2013/01/31/national-brandy-alexander-day/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141020183229/http://eatocracy.cnn.com/2013/01/31/national-brandy-alexander-day/ |archive-date=20 October 2014 |access-date=20 October 2014 |publisher=eatocracy}}</ref>

The drink was possibly named after Troy Alexander, a bartender at [[George Rector|Rector's]], a New York City restaurant, who created the drink in order to serve a white drink at a dinner celebrating [[Phoebe Snow (character)|Phoebe Snow]], a character in a popular advertising campaign in the early 20th century.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Behind the Drink: The Brandy Alexander |url=http://liquor.com/articles/behind-the-drink-the-brandy-alexander/# |access-date=20 October 2014 |publisher=Liquor.com}}</ref>

[[John Lennon]] was introduced to it on March 12, 1974, by [[Harry Nilsson]], on Lennon's so-called "lost weekend". The pair began heckling the [[Smothers Brothers]], and whilst being ejected Lennon allegedly assaulted a waitress.<ref>{{Cite web |title=When John Lennon and Harry Nilsson Got Tossed From the Troubadour for Heckling |url=http://ultimateclassicrock.com/john-lennon-harry-nilsson-troubadour/ |access-date=29 July 2018 |website=Ultimate Classic Rock |date=12 March 2015 |language=en}}</ref> Lennon later said the drinks "tasted like [[milkshake]]s".<ref>{{Cite news |title=The John Lennon we did not know |language=en-US |work=TODAY.com |url=https://www.today.com/popculture/john-lennon-we-did-not-know-wbna19418319 |access-date=29 July 2018}}</ref>

==In film and television==
[[File:Brandy_Alexander_on_the_Rocks.jpg|thumb|A Brandy Alexander served on the rocks]]
In the 1962 film ''[[Days of Wine and Roses (film)|Days of Wine and Roses]]'', alcoholic Joe Clay, played by [[Jack Lemmon]], takes Kirsten Arnesen, played by [[Lee Remick]], out on a date. When she explains that she dislikes liquor but likes chocolate, he orders her a Brandy Alexander, thus beginning Kirsten's descent into alcoholism.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Aftab |first=Kaleem |date=20 March 2009 |title=The movie cocktail – what's your poison tonight? |language=en-GB |work=The Independent |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/films/features/the-movie-cocktail-whats-your-poison-tonight-1649249.html |access-date=29 July 2018}}</ref>

In the 1970 [[Television pilot|pilot]] of the television series, ''[[The Mary Tyler Moore Show]]'', the namesake character adds to a running gag by asking for a Brandy Alexander during a job interview.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lee |first=Lanee |date=2020-07-29 |title=Drink in History: The Brandy Alexander |url=https://chilledmagazine.com/drink-in-history-the-brandy-alexander/ |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=Chilled Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref>

In the 1981 film ''[[Tattoo (1981 film)|Tattoo]]'', [[Bruce Dern]] takes [[Maud Adams]] out for dinner and orders a Brandy Alexander. When she comments that he does not look the Brandy Alexander type, he replies, "I like the foam...it reminds me of the ocean."<ref>{{Citation |title=Tattoo (1981) – Quotes |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0083178/quotes/qt4069005 |access-date=29 July 2018}}</ref>

In the 1981 television adaptation of ''Brideshead Revisited'' ([[Brandy Alexander#In print|discussed below]]), Anthony Blanche ([[Nickolas Grace]]) takes Charles Ryder ([[Jeremy Irons]]) out for drinks, ordering four Brandy Alexanders for the two of them: "I expect you would prefer sherry, but my dear Charles, you're not going to have sherry tonight. You're going to try this delicious concoction instead." When Charles reacts hesitantly to his first sip, Anthony proceeds to drink all four cocktails in rapid succession.<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?si=FYiUxP1S87xfdnx0&v=aj6XAFMWPYE&feature=youtu.be |title=Brideshead Revisited - Brandy Alexanders |date=2011-12-03 |last=MundusVultDecipi0000 |access-date=2025-01-20 |via=YouTube}}</ref>

In “Indian Summer”, the eleventh episode of the [[Mad Men season 1|first series]] of [[Mad Men]] (2007), [[Peggy Olson]] is seen drinking a Brandy Alexander on a date.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mad Men “Indian Summer” (2007), IMDb |url=https://m.imdb.com/title/tt1108366/}}</ref> Peggy says [[Joan Harris|Joan Holloway]] often orders the drink for her, but that it is usually sweeter. 

In the 2008 [[James Gray (film director)|James Gray]] movie ''[[Two Lovers (2008 film)|Two Lovers]]'', Michelle ([[Gwyneth Paltrow]]) tells Leonard ([[Joaquin Phoenix]]) she drinks Brandy Alexanders with her boyfriend Ronald, a rich lawyer. Leonard orders one at a restaurant to impress her, but ruins the effect by mistaking the stirrer for a straw.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mason |first=Ian Garrick |date=27 April 2009 |title=Magnetic Suns and Moth Balls: An essay on James Gray's Two Lovers |url=https://www.iangarrickmason.com/film-two-lovers |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170430030251/https://www.iangarrickmason.com/film-two-lovers |archive-date=30 April 2017 |access-date=29 July 2018 |publisher=iangarrickmason.com}}</ref>

==In print==
The character Brandy Alexander in the novel ''[[Invisible Monsters]]'' by [[Chuck Palahniuk]] is named after the drink.<ref>{{Cite web |date=27 March 1974 |title=The Rockford Files |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0071042/ |via=IMDb}}</ref>

[[Anthony Blanche]] orders four "Alexandra cocktails" in [[Evelyn Waugh]]'s novel ''[[Brideshead Revisited]]''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Waugh |first=Evelyn |title=Brideshead Revisited |year=1962 |isbn=9780140008210 |page=48 |chapter=2 |orig-year=1945 |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/bridesheadrevisi0000waug_y3b8/page/48/mode/1up}}</ref> [[Christian Kracht]] repeats the four Brandy Alexanders motif in his 1995 novel ''[[Faserland]]''.<ref>''[[Faserland]]'' (1995) chapter 7</ref>
 
In Kurt Vonnegut's book, ''[[Mother Night]]'', the protagonist suspects that an overly flattering article in the ''[[New York Herald Tribune|Herald Tribune]]'' about his neighbor was "written by a pansy full of Brandy Alexanders."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Vonnegut |first=Kurt |title=Mother Night |page=50}}</ref>

'''Caipirinha''' ({{IPAc-en|ˌ|k|aɪ|p|ɪ|ˈ|r|iː|n|j|ə}} {{respell|KY|pi|REEN|yə}}; {{IPA|pt-BR|kajpiˈɾĩɲɐ}}) is a Brazilian cocktail made with [[cachaça]], sugar, lime, and ice.<ref name="law">{{cite web |title=Lista de Publicações |trans-title=List of Publications |url=http://www6.senado.gov.br/legislacao/ListaPublicacoes.action?id=237488 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120224052558/http://www6.senado.gov.br/legislacao/ListaPublicacoes.action?id=237488 |archive-date=2012-02-24 |access-date=2015-06-15 |website=senado.gov.br |publisher=[[Federal Senate (Brazil)|Federal Senate of Brazil]] |language=pt-BR}}</ref> The drink is prepared by mixing the fruit and the sugar together, then adding the liquor. Known and consumed nationally and internationally, caipirinha is one of the most famous components of [[Brazilian cuisine]], being the most popular national recipe worldwide<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-12-18 |title=Segredos da caipirinha perfeita |url=https://www1.folha.uol.com.br/webstories/comida/2022/12/segredos-da-caipirinha-perfeita/ |access-date=2024-07-27 |website=[[Folha de S.Paulo]] |language=pt-BR |archive-date=2024-07-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240726225302/https://www1.folha.uol.com.br/webstories/comida/2022/12/segredos-da-caipirinha-perfeita/ |url-status=live }}</ref> and often considered the best drink in the country<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-06-30 |title=Caipirinha é o melhor drink brasileiro, elege TasteAtlas; veja os outros |url=https://www.sonoticiaboa.com.br/2024/06/30/caipirinha-melhor-drink-brasileiro-tasteatlas-veja-outros |access-date=2024-07-27 |website=Só Notícia Boa |language=pt-BR |archive-date=2024-07-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240726075143/https://www.sonoticiaboa.com.br/2024/06/30/caipirinha-melhor-drink-brasileiro-tasteatlas-veja-outros |url-status=live }}</ref> and one of the best cocktails/drinks in the world, having reached third place in 2024, according to the specialized website ''[[TasteAtlas]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=72 Best Alcoholic Beverage Recipes |url=https://www.tasteatlas.com/best-rated-alcoholic-beverages-recipes-in-the-world |access-date=2024-07-27 |website=[[TasteAtlas]] |archive-date=2024-07-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240727194536/https://www.tasteatlas.com/best-rated-alcoholic-beverages-recipes-in-the-world |url-status=live }}</ref>

Due to its importance and popularity, the caipirinha was declared [[Cultural heritage|Brazilian Cultural Heritage]] in 2003;<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ferri |first=Marcelo |date=2023-10-04 |title=Caipirinha: Patrimônio Cultural do Brasil |url=https://hi-mundim.com.br/gastronomia/caipirinha-patrimonio-cultural-do-brasil/ |access-date=2024-07-27 |website=Hi-Mundim |language=pt-BR |archive-date=2024-07-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240726160421/https://hi-mundim.com.br/gastronomia/caipirinha-patrimonio-cultural-do-brasil/ |url-status=live }}</ref> in 2019, it was considered Intangible Heritage of [[Rio de Janeiro]], despite its origins in [[Piracicaba, São Paulo]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Diniz |first=Márcio |title=De origem paulista, caipirinha é declarada patrimônio imaterial do Rio |url=https://catracalivre.com.br/viagem-livre/de-origem-paulista-caipirinha-e-declarada-patrimonio-imaterial-do-rio/ |access-date=2024-07-27 |website=Catraca Livre |date=24 October 2019 |language=pt-BR |archive-date=2024-07-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240726075143/https://catracalivre.com.br/viagem-livre/de-origem-paulista-caipirinha-e-declarada-patrimonio-imaterial-do-rio/ |url-status=live }}</ref> It is part of the [[List of IBA official cocktails|list of official cocktails]] of the [[International Bartenders Association]] (IBA).<ref name="IBA" />

==History==

Although the origin of the drink is unknown, there is a consensus in the academic community that Caipirinha was invented in the [[interior of São Paulo]], Brazil, in 1918.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Garcia |first=Roosevelt |date=2022-01-20 |title=A caipirinha faz 100 anos |trans-title=The caipirinha turns 100 years old |url=https://vejasp.abril.com.br/coluna/memoria/a-caipirinha-faz-100-anos/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220201165804/https://vejasp.abril.com.br/coluna/memoria/a-caipirinha-faz-100-anos/ |archive-date=2022-02-01 |access-date=2023-01-01 |website=vejasp.abril.com.br |language=pt-BR}}</ref> Some accounts say it came about around 1918 in the region of [[Alentejo]] in Portugal, with a popular recipe made with [[lemon]], [[garlic]], and [[honey]], indicated for patients with the [[Spanish flu]]. Another account is that Caipirinha is based on [[Poncha]], an alcoholic drink from [[Madeira]], [[Portugal]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Ehrlich |first=Richard |date=2002-10-20 |title=My Round: Madeira mixes things with the best |url=http://www.independent.co.uk/life-style/food-and-drink/features/my-round-madeira-mixes-things-with-the-best-614638.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141221080721/https://www.independent.co.uk/life-style/food-and-drink/features/my-round-madeira-mixes-things-with-the-best-614638.html |archive-date=2014-12-21 |access-date=2012-08-22 |website=[[Independent.co.uk]] |language=en-UK}}</ref> The main ingredient is ''[[aguardente]] de cana'', which is made from sugar cane. Sugar cane production was switched from Madeira to Brazil by the Portuguese as they needed more land to plant it on. Before this people in Madeira had already created ''aguardente de cana'', which was the ancestor to [[cachaça]].<ref>{{cite web| url = http://www.madeira-edu.pt/LinkClick.aspx?fileticket=vm2ZzgKck9g%3D&tabid=1454&language=pt-PT| title = SUGAR´S ROUTE IN MADEIRA| access-date = 2012-12-02}}{{Dead link|date=June 2021 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

Today, it is still used as a tonic for the common cold. Commonly, practitioners add some [[distilled spirits]] to home remedies to expedite the therapeutic effect. Aguardente was commonly used. "Until one day, someone decided to remove the garlic and honey. Then added a few tablespoons of sugar to reduce the acidity of the lime. The ice came next, to ward off the heat," explains Carlos Lima, executive director of IBRAC (Brazilian Institute of Cachaça).<ref>{{cite web |last=Ferrareze |first=Ana |title=A história da caipirinha |trans-title=The history of caipirinha |url=http://revistacasaejardim.globo.com/Revista/Common/0%2c%2cEMI278045-16940%2c00-A+HISTORIA+DA+CAIPIRINHA.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111117035757/http://revistacasaejardim.globo.com/Revista/Common/0%2C%2CEMI278045-16940%2C00-A%2BHISTORIA%2BDA%2BCAIPIRINHA.html |archive-date=2011-11-17 |access-date=2012-12-02 |website=revistacasaejardim.globo.com |language=pt-BR |quote=Até que um dia alguém resolveu tirar o alho e o mel. Depois, acrescentaram umas colheres de açúcar para reduzir a acidez do limão. O gelo veio em seguida, para espantar o calor |trans-quote=Until one day, someone decided to remove the garlic and honey. Then added a few tablespoons of sugar to reduce the acidity of the lime. The ice came next, to ward off the heat}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Rodrigues |first=Rafael |title=CAIPIRINHA |url=http://www.drinquepedia.com/drinques/historia?drinque=146 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130927030512/http://www.drinquepedia.com/drinques/historia?drinque=146 |archive-date=2013-09-27 |website=drinquepedia.com |language=pt-BR}}</ref>

According to historians, the caipirinha was invented by landowning farmers in the region of [[Piracicaba]], the interior of the [[State of São Paulo]] during the 19th century as a local drink for 'high standard' events and parties (parties at Barão de [[Serra Negra]] palace), a reflection of the strong sugarcane culture in the region.<ref>(in Portuguese) Cascudo, Luis da Camara (2006). "Prelúdio da cachaça" - Global Editora</ref> Original recipes use a kind of lemon called "galeguinho", a small yellow/green lemon very common in São Paulo countryside houses' backyards. Currently, it is made with a bigger green lemon called a Tahiti lemon, a species of lemon more widespread in country markets.{{Citation needed|date=December 2024}}   
    
The caipirinha is the strongest national cocktail of Brazil,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Mackay |first=Jordan |date=2006-08-10 |title=Made in Brazil |url=http://7x7.com/content/made-brazil |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090214193457/http://7x7.com/content/made-brazil |archive-date=2009-02-14 |work=[[7x7 (magazine)|7x7]]}}</ref> and is imbibed in restaurants, bars, and many households throughout the country. Once almost unknown outside Brazil, the drink became more popular and more widely available in recent years, in large part due to the rising availability of first-rate brands of cachaça outside Brazil.<ref name="Everyday with Rachael Ray">{{cite web|last=Willey|first=Rob|url=http://www.belezabrazil.com/pages/pres_03.asp?id=70|publisher=Cane and Able|date=February 2006|title=Everyday with Rachael Ray|access-date=2007-01-14|quote=The caipirinha—a sour-sweet combination of crushed limes, sugar, and cachaça— become the darling of American bartenders, and first-rate cachaça is, at last, finding a place on American liquor-store shelves.|archive-date=2007-12-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071224184353/http://www.belezabrazil.com/pages/pres_03.asp?id=70|url-status=live}}</ref> The [[International Bartenders Association]] designated it as one of its [[IBA Official Cocktail|Official Cocktails]], as a Contemporary Classic.<ref name="IBA" />

==Name==
The word ''caipirinha'' is the [[diminutive]] of the word [[Caipiras|Caipira]], which refers to a people from the state of São Paulo. "Caipira" is a [[Grammatical gender#Gender shifts|two-gender noun]]. The diminutive mostly refers to the drink, in which case it is a feminine noun.

Caipifruta is a variant of caipirinha, consisting of cachaça, crushed fresh fruits (either singly or in combination), and crushed ice.  Fresh fruits used to create caipifrutas include [[tangerine]], [[Lime (fruit)|lime]], [[kiwifruit]], [[passion fruit]], [[pineapple]], [[lemon]], [[grapes]], [[mango]], [[Spondias mombin|cajá (Spondias mombin fruit)]], and [[cashew|caju (cashew fruit)]].

=== Around the world ===
[[File:Caipirinha, Highgate, N6 (7285728440).jpg|thumb|Bar in [[London]] with the sign "Caipirinha"]]
Many variations of the drink are known. In some regions, [[brown sugar]] is used instead of [[White sugar|refined sugar]]. Even in Brazil, variants with artificial sweeteners or a wide variety of fruits can be found. Furthermore, cachaça is sometimes replaced by [[vodka]] ([[caipiroska]], trademark registered by [[Smirnoff]]), [[Licor Beirão]] (known as caipirão), [[rum]] (caipiríssima, trademark registered by [[Bacardi]]), sake "Caipirinhas" (saquerinha) or wine (caipivinho) are also made.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cinco receitas de caipirinhas e caipiroskas |url=https://bomgourmet.com/bomgourmet/bebidas/e-para-beber-caipira-caipirinha-caipiroska-ou-caipirissima/ |access-date=2024-07-27 |website=Bom Gourmet |archive-date=2024-07-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240727194536/https://bomgourmet.com/bomgourmet/bebidas/e-para-beber-caipira-caipirinha-caipiroska-ou-caipirissima/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In [[Cape Verde]], caipirinha is also prepared with [[grog]], a strong local rum.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |date=2017-06-19 |title=Top-5 special drinks Cape Verde |url=https://www.capeverdeislands.org/special-drinks-cape-verde/ |access-date=2024-07-27 |website=CapeVerdeIslands.org |language=en-GB |archive-date=2024-07-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240727194536/https://www.capeverdeislands.org/special-drinks-cape-verde/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Corinthians na África? The '''daiquiri'''  ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|d|aɪ|k|ər|i|,_|ˈ|d|æ|k|-}}; {{langx|es|daiquirí}} {{IPA|es|dajkiˈɾi|}}) is a [[cocktails|cocktail]] whose main ingredients are [[rum]], citrus juice (typically [[lime juice]]), and [[sugar]] or other sweetener.

The daiquiri is one of the [[The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks#Six basic drinks|six basic drinks]] listed in [[David A. Embury]]'s classic ''[[The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks]]'', which also lists some variations.

== Origins ==
''[[Daiquirí, Cuba|Daiquirí]]'' is also the name of a beach and an [[mining|iron mine]] near [[Santiago de Cuba]] in eastern Cuba, and is a word of [[Taíno people|Taíno]] origin.<ref name=taino>{{Cite web |last=The United Confederation of Taíno People |title=Taíno Dictionary |url=http://www.uctp.org/VocesIndigena.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071016055722/http://www.uctp.org/VocesIndigena.html <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archive-date=2007-10-16 |access-date=2007-10-18 |language=Spanish}}</ref>

Historians widely agree that the cocktail was invented by an American mining engineer named [[Jennings Cox]], who was in Cuba (then at the tail-end of the [[Captaincy General of Cuba|Spanish Captaincy-General government]]) at the time of the [[Spanish–American War]] of 1898. It is also possible that [[William A. Chanler]], a [[United States House of Representatives|US congressman]] who purchased the Santiago iron mines in 1902, introduced the daiquiri to clubs in [[New York City|New York]] in that year.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Lately |first=Thomas |title=A pride of lions: the Astor orphans; the Chanler chronicle |publisher=W. Morrow |year=1971}}</ref>{{rp|168}}<ref>{{Cite web |title=Daiquiri cocktail story |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/g/1083/daiquiri-cocktail/story |access-date=2025-07-13 |website=www.diffordsguide.com |language=en}}</ref>

Originally the drink was served in a [[tall glass]] packed with cracked ice. A teaspoon of sugar was poured over the ice, and the juice of one or two limes was squeezed over the sugar. Two or three ounces of white [[rum]] completed the mixture. The glass was then frosted with a long-handled [[spoon]]. Later the daiquiri evolved to be mixed in a [[cocktail shaker|shaker]] with the same ingredients but with shaved ice. After a thorough shaking, it was poured into a chilled [[coupe glass]].

The Daiquiri was subsequently refined and popularized by Emelio “Maragato” Gonzalez and Constantino “Constante” Ribalaigua Vert in Havana.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Daiquiri |url=https://library.cocktailkingdom.com/exh.essential-drinks.html |access-date=2025-07-13 |website=Cocktail Kingdom Library}}</ref> 

The basic recipe for a daiquiri is also similar to the [[grog]] British sailors drank aboard ships from the 1780s. By 1795 the [[Royal Navy]] daily grog ration contained rum, water, ¾ ounce of lemon or lime juice, and 2 ounces of sugar.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Stephen R. Bown |url=https://archive.org/details/scurvyhowsurgeon00bown_0/page/181 |title=Scurvy |publisher=Thomas Dunne Books |year=2003 |isbn=0-312-31391-8 |page=[https://archive.org/details/scurvyhowsurgeon00bown_0/page/181 181] |url-access=registration}}</ref> This was a common drink across the Caribbean, and as soon as ice became available this was included instead of the water.

Consumption of the drink remained localized until 1909, when [[Rear Admiral]] Lucius W. Johnson, a [[United States Navy|U.S. Navy]] medical officer, tried Cox's drink. Johnson subsequently introduced it to the [[Army and Navy Club (Washington, D.C.)|Army and Navy Club]] in [[Washington, D.C.]], and drinkers of the daiquiri increased over the space of a few decades. It was one of the favorite drinks of the writer [[Ernest Hemingway]] and U.S. President [[John F. Kennedy]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Salvatore Calabrese |url=https://archive.org/details/completehomebart0000cala |title=Complete Home Bartender's Guide |publisher=Sterling Publishing Company, Inc. |year=2002 |page=[https://archive.org/details/completehomebart0000cala/page/76 76] |quote=daiquiri John F Kennedy. |url-access=registration}}</ref>

The drink became popular in the 1940s. [[World War II]] rationing made [[whiskey]] and [[vodka]] hard to come by, yet rum was easily obtainable owing to U.S. President [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]]'s [[Good Neighbor policy]], which opened up trade and travel relations with Latin America, Cuba, and the Caribbean. The Good Neighbor policy, also known as the Pan-American program, helped make Latin America fashionable.{{according to whom|date=July 2022}} Consequently, rum-based drinks (once frowned upon as the choice of sailors and down-and-outs) also became fashionable, and the daiquiri saw tremendous popularity in the US.

== Frozen daiquiri ==
A wide variety of alcoholic mixed drinks made with finely pulverized ice are often called '''frozen daiquirí'''. These drinks can also be combined and poured from a [[blender]], eliminating the need for manual [[pulverisation]] and producing a texture similar to a [[smoothie]]. On larger scales, such drinks are often commercially made in larger machines and come in various flavors with various alcohol or liquors.<ref name="commercial_frozen">{{Cite web |title=Frozen Cocktail Market Size, Share, & Industry Analysis, By Type (Margarita, Mojito, Pina Colada, and Others), By Distribution Channel (On-Trade and Off-Trade), and Regional Forecast, 2024 – 2032 |url=https://www.fortunebusinessinsights.com/frozen-cocktails-market-103816 |website=Fortune Business Insights |access-date=2024-07-23 |archive-date=2021-11-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211127053817/https://www.fortunebusinessinsights.com/frozen-cocktails-market-103816 |url-status=live }}</ref> Another way to create a frozen daiquiri (mostly fruit-flavored variants) is by using frozen [[limeade]], providing the required texture, sweetness and sourness all at once.<ref name="strawberry_recipe">{{Cite web |title=Strawberry Daiquiri |url=http://mybestcocktails.com/recipe-80-Strawberry-Daiquiri.html |website=MyBestCocktails}}</ref>

{{short description|Cocktail made with vodka}} {{Infobox drink | name = Cosmopolitan | image = Cosmopolitan (5076906532).jpg | caption = A cosmopolitan garnished with a lemon twist | type = [[List of cocktails|Cocktail]] | ingredients ={{plainlist|* 40 mL [[Vodka]] Citron * 15 mL [[Cointreau]] * 15 mL Fresh [[lime juice]] * 30 mL [[cranberry juice]]}} | served = [[Straight up]]: chilled, without ice | garnish = Lime slice | prep = Shake all ingredients in [[cocktail shaker]] filled with ice. Strain into a large [[cocktail glass]]. Garnish with lime slice. | drinkware = Cosmopolitan or [[cocktail glass]] }} [[File:Cosmopolitan.jpg|thumb|upright|A cosmopolitan]] A '''cosmopolitan''', or, informally, a '''cosmo''', is a [[cocktail]] made with [[vodka]], [[Cointreau]], [[cranberry juice]], and freshly squeezed or sweetened [[lime juice]]. The traditional garnish is a lime slice but a [[Twist (cocktail garnish)|twist]] or wedge can be used instead. Other variations substitute [[lemon]] or [[orange (fruit)|orange]]. The cosmopolitan is a member of the [[Gimlet (cocktail)|Gimlet]] family of cocktails. Though often presented far differently, the cosmopolitan also bears a likeness in composition to the [[kamikaze (cocktail)|kamikaze]] shooter. ==Preparation and serving== The [[International Bartenders Association]] recipe is based on vodka citron, a lemon-[[flavored vodka]]. {{cite web |url=http://iba-world.com/cocktails/cosmopolitan/ |title=Official Cocktail recipe: Cosmopolitan |publisher=International Bartenders Association |access-date=2017-08-13 }} The use of citrus-flavored vodka as the basis for this cocktail appears to have been widely popularized in the mid-1990s by cocktail expert [[Dale DeGroff]]{{cite web|url=http://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/473/cosmopolitan-2-degroffs-formula |title=Cosmopolitan #2 (DeGroff's formula) Cocktail Recipe – How To Make Cocktail Recipes |publisher=diffordsguide |access-date=2014-03-15}} and is used in the IBA-approved recipe. Many bartenders, however, continue to use a standard unflavored vodka — this alternative would undoubtedly be historically consistent with any of the supposed predecessors of this drink that were popular in [[Ohio]], [[Provincetown, Massachusetts|Provincetown]], or [[Minneapolis]] during the 1970s, or in [[San Francisco]] during the 1980s.{{cite book|last=Calabrese|first=Salvatore|title=Classic Cocktails|year=1997|publisher=Prion Books|location=London|isbn=1-85375-240-1|page=103}}{{cite magazine|last=Kammerling|first=Alex|title=All You Need to Know About The Cosmopolitan|magazine=Class, the magazine of bar culture|date=June 2003}}{{cite book|title=150 Classic Cocktails|year=2003|publisher=Hamlyn|location=London|isbn=0-600-60992-8|page=38}}{{cite book|title=Cocktails: The Complete Book of Cocktail Recipes for the Bartender|year=2007|publisher=[[Octopus Publishing Group]]|location=London|isbn=978-0-600-61671-9}} A lemon twist is sometimes used to [[Cocktail garnish|garnish]]. The cosmopolitan is usually served in a large [[cocktail glass]], also called a ''martini glass''. For this reason, the drink is sometimes mistakenly categorized as a type of [[martini (cocktail)|martini]]. ==Origins and mixology== The origin of the cosmopolitan is disputed,{{cite web|title=The Definitive History of the Cosmopolitan: Quibbling over who invented it is only half the tale. Here's how the pink drink went from a Cleveland gay bar to Madonna's call drink to SATC, according to the people responsible for it|date=Sep 11, 2019 |first=PRIYA |last=KRISHNA|url=https://punchdrink.com/articles/definitive-history-cosmopolitan-cosmo-vodka-cranberry-cocktail/|work=[[Punch (website)|Punch]]}} with some histories tracing it from the gay community in 1970s [[Provincetown, Massachusetts]], moving west to [[Cleveland]] and [[Minneapolis]], and landing in [[San Francisco]]. From there, it moved back east, with the contemporary recipe being mixed in 1989 in [[New York City]]. Another claim to the cosmo's origin is [[South Beach, Florida]], in the mid-1980s. === Various creation claims === ==== The 1930s ==== While the cocktail is widely perceived to be a more modern creation, there is a recipe for a "Cosmopolitan Daisy" which appears in ''Pioneers of Mixing at Elite Bars 1903–1933'', published in 1934: {{blockquote|Jigger of Gordon's Gin ({{cvt|1+1/2|USoz|mL|disp=sqbr}} Beefeater)
2 dash Cointreau ({{cvt|1/2|USoz|mL|disp=sqbr}} Cointreau)
Juice of 1 Lemon ({{cvt|1|USoz|mL|disp=sqbr}} Lemon Juice)
{{tspUS|1|disp=sqbr}} Raspberry Syrup (homemade)
Shake with ice and strain into a cocktail glass.{{cite book|title=Pioneers of Mixing at Elite Bars: 1903-1933|first=Charles Christopher |last=Mueller|date=1934|location=New York|publisher=Trinity Press|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yjTvtAEACAAJ}} }} Made with ingredients that would have been readily available during the period, this identically named cocktail aims for the same effect. If this drink is, in fact, the source of the modern cosmopolitan, then it would be an adaptation of a [[Brandy daisy|Daisy]] rather than a Kamikaze.{{cite web|title=Cosmopolitan Cocktail|work=THE COCKTAIL SPIRIT |first= ROBERT |last=HESS|url=http://www.smallscreennetwork.com/video/41/cosmopolitan/|publisher=Small Screen Network|access-date=2013-11-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171223220129/http://smallscreennetwork.com/video/41/cosmopolitan|archive-date=2017-12-23|url-status=dead}}{{cite web|url=http://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/595/cosmopolitan-3-1934-recipe |title=Cosmopolitan #3 (1934 recipe) Cocktail Recipe – How To Make Cocktail Recipes |publisher=diffordsguide |access-date=2014-03-15}} ==== {{circa}} 1970s: Provincetown ==== One version of the creation of this popular drink credits the accomplishment to the [[gay community]] in Provincetown, Massachusetts.{{Cite book |last1=Harrington |first1=Paul |last2=Moorhead |first2=Laura |year=1998 |title=Cocktail: The Drinks for the 21st Century |location=New York |publisher=Viking (Penguin Putnam Inc.) |page=76 }}{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170713194957/http://www.barrypopik.com/index.php/new_york_city/entry/cosmopolitan_cocktail/|archive-date=July 13, 2017|url=http://www.barrypopik.com/index.php/new_york_city/entry/cosmopolitan_cocktail|website=The Big Apple|first= Barry |last=Popik|date=January 10, 2005|title=Cosmopolitan (cocktail)}} ==== 1970s: John Caine ==== John Caine is the owner of several popular bars in San Francisco and a cosmopolitan expert. He partially credits the upsurge in cocktails during the 1970s to the Cosmo being served at [[fern bar]]s. Caine is credited with bringing the Cosmo west from Cleveland.{{cite web |url=http://eastbaymonthly.com/kilduff-07-06.html |title=Belly Up to the Bar: John Caine brought the cosmo to Frisco |access-date=2008-05-20 |last=Kilduff |first=Paul |work=The Kilduff Archive |publisher=The Monthly: The East Bay's Premier Magazine of Culture and Commerce |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101005015818/http://eastbaymonthly.com/kilduff-07-06.html |archive-date=2010-10-05 |url-status=dead }} ==== 1975: Neal Murray ==== Bartender Neal Murray says he created the cosmopolitan in 1975 at the Cork & Cleaver steak house in Minneapolis, Minnesota.{{cite web |url=http://www.citypages.com/bestof2006/sexdrugsrocknroll/bestof2828.asp |title=Best Locally Created Cocktail |work=Best of the Twin Cities 2006 |publisher=CityPages.com |access-date=2018-08-22 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070109064707/http://citypages.com/bestof2006/sexdrugsrocknroll/bestof2828.asp |archive-date=2007-01-09 }} According to Murray, he added a splash of cranberry juice to a Kamikaze and the first taster declared, "How cosmopolitan." Murray's Cosmopolitan used 1.5 oz Gordon's vodka, .75 oz Rose's Lime, .75 oz Leroux triple sec, and .5 oz cranberry juice.{{Cite book |last=Charming |first=Cheryl |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Bartender_s_Ultimate_Guide_to_Cockta/nI_uEAAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&printsec=frontcover&bsq=%22Neal%20Murray's%20Cosmopolitan%22 |title=The Bartender's Ultimate Guide to Cocktails: A Guide to Cocktail History, Culture, Trivia and Favorite Drinks|year=2022 |publisher=Mango Media |isbn=978-1-64250-793-5 |page=124 |language=en |author-link=Cheryl Charming |quote=1.5 ounces Gordon's vodka }} a 1972 product ! ==== {{circa}} 1985: Cheryl Cook ==== There are several other claims made as to the origin of the cosmopolitan. Cocktail historian [[Gary Regan]] credits bartender Cheryl Cook of the Strand Restaurant in South Beach, Florida, with the original creation. {{Cite book |last=Grimes |first=William |date=November 2001 |title=Straight Up Or On the Rocks: The Story of the American Cocktail |url=https://archive.org/details/straightuporonro00will |url-access=registration |publisher=North Point Press |page=[https://archive.org/details/straightuporonro00will/page/119 119] |isbn=9780865476011 }}. In a letter to Regan, Cook related the story of how she created the drink in 1985 or 1986: {{blockquote|What overwhelmed me was the number of people who ordered Martinis just to be seen with a Martini glass in their hand. It was on this realization that gave me the idea to create a drink that everyone could palate and was visually stunning in that classic glass. Vol. 7, Issue 6 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070707072947/http://www.ardentspirits.com/ardentspirits/Newsletter/vol7Issue06.html#cosmo |archive-date=2007-07-07 |url-status=dead }} }} Cook's original recipes called for "[[Absolut]] Citron, a splash of [[Triple sec]], a drop of [[Rose's lime]] and just enough cranberry to make it oh so pretty in pink." Although Absolut Citron was not introduced anywhere officially until 1988, it was test-marketed in Miami. ==== 1987: Patrick "Paddy" Mitten ==== [[Cheryl Charming]]'s ''The Cocktail Companion'' credits a bartender named Patrick "Paddy" Mitten with bringing the drink to New York City from San Francisco in October 1987.{{Cite book |last=Charming |first=Cheryl |author-link=Cheryl Charming|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LJYREAAAQBAJ |title=The Cocktail Companion: A Guide to Cocktail History, Culture, Trivia and Favorite Drinks |date=2018 |publisher=Mango Media Inc. |isbn=978-1-63353-924-2 |page=113 |language=en}} ==== 1989: Toby Cecchini & Melissa Huffsmith-Roth ==== Bartender Gaz Regan says that the internationally recognized version of the cocktail was created by Toby Cecchini and Melissa Huffsmith-Roth in 1989 at [[The Odeon]], a restaurant in Manhattan, based on a poorly described version of Cheryl Cook's creation. Cecchini and Huffsmith-Roth's Cosmopolitan includes 2 oz Absolut Citron vodka, 1 oz Cointreau, 1 oz lime juice, and .5 oz cranberry juice. A '''Bellini''' is a [[cocktail]] made with [[Prosecco]] and [[peach]] [[purée]] or [[nectar (drink)|nectar]]. It originated in [[Venice]], Italy.

==History==
The Bellini was invented sometime between 1934 and 1948<ref name="3000 Cocktails">{{cite web | url = http://www.thatsthespirit.com/en/drinks/articles/Bellini.asp | title = 3000 Drinks > Bellini | date= n.d.| publisher=ThatsTheSpirit.com | access-date= February 5, 2007 | archive-date= July 23, 2012 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120723052350/http://www.thatsthespirit.com/en/drinks/articles/Bellini.asp}}</ref><ref name="BBC Recipe">Jo' Pratt. [https://www.bbc.co.uk/food/recipes/bellinicocktail_67941 Food – Recipes – Bellini cocktail]. Undated. bbc.co.uk. Retrieved February 5, 2007.</ref> by [[Giuseppe Cipriani (chef)|Giuseppe Cipriani]], founder of [[Harry's Bar (Venice)|Harry's Bar]] in Venice, Italy. He named the drink the Bellini because its unique pink color reminded him of a painting by [[15th century|15th-century]] Venetian artist [[Giovanni Bellini]].<ref name="Fabulous Foods">Sicard, Cheri. [http://www.fabulousfoods.com/features/cocktails/bellinis.html Featured Cocktail – Bellini] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070218102512/http://www.fabulousfoods.com/features/cocktails/bellinis.html |date=February 18, 2007 }}. Undated. Fabulous Foods. Retrieved February 5, 2007.</ref>

The drink started as a seasonal specialty at Harry's Bar.<ref name="Fabulous Foods" /> Later, it also became popular at the bar's New York counterpart. After an entrepreneurial Frenchman set up a business to ship fresh white peach purée to both locations, it became a year-round favorite.<ref name="3000 Cocktails" />

The Bellini is an [[IBA Official Cocktail]]. They also suggest a Puccini, replacing the peach purée with an equal amount of [[mandarin orange|mandarin]] or tangerine juice; a [[Rossini (cocktail)|Rossini]], which uses [[strawberry]] purée; or a Tintoretto, which is made with [[pomegranate]] juice; or a Cipriani Bellini, named after the owner of the bar where the Bellini was invented (Harry’s Bar in Venice), this version emphasizes the use of fresh white peach purée and Prosecco.

==Preparation and serving==
The Bellini consists of puréed white peaches and [[Prosecco]], an Italian [[sparkling wine]]. Marinating fresh peaches in wine is an Italian tradition.<ref name="3000 Cocktails" />

==Similar cocktails==
The [[Cuba]]n Adalor cocktail is a drink calling for fresh peach smashed with a fork and topped with Champagne. It was published in a Cuban drink guide book in 1927.<ref>{{cite web |title=Cuba's Overlooked Role in Cocktail History |url=https://punchdrink.com/articles/cuban-cocktails-history-and-recipes-little-known-contributions-to-cocktail-culture/ |website=punchdrink.com |access-date=4 March 2019}}</ref>

A '''grasshopper''' is a sweet, mint-flavored, after-dinner alcoholic drink named for its green color, which comes from [[crème de menthe]]. Tujague's, a bar in the [[French Quarter]] of [[New Orleans]], [[Louisiana]], claims its owner Philip Guichet invented the drink in 1918.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.thebollard.com/bollard/?p=2119 |title= The Land of Forgotten Cocktails |date= August 1, 2008 |access-date=2009-03-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091207002514/http://www.thebollard.com/bollard/?p=2119 |archive-date=2009-12-07 }}</ref> The drink gained popularity during the 1950s and 1960s throughout the [[Southern United States|American South]].

==Composition==
A typical grasshopper cocktail is equal parts green [[crème de menthe]], white [[crème de cacao]], and cream shaken with ice and strained into a chilled cocktail glass.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.alcomixer.com/recipe/grasshopper |title= Flying Grasshopper recipe |access-date= September 12, 2011 |archive-date= May 14, 2014 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20140514001200/http://www.alcomixer.com/recipe/grasshopper |url-status= dead }}</ref>

===Variations===
A "vodka" or "flying" grasshopper replaces the cream with [[vodka]].<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.drinksmixer.com/drink6742.html |title= Flying Grasshopper recipe |access-date= 2017-11-08 }}</ref>

A "frozen" grasshopper adds mint ice cream to create a more dessert-like drink.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.drinksmixer.com/drink3644.html |title= Frozen Grasshopper recipe |access-date= 2017-11-08 |archive-date= June 30, 2022 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20220630104035/http://www.drinksmixer.com/drink3644.html |url-status= dead }}</ref>

An "after eight" adds a layer of dark chocolate liqueur to the crème de menthe, crème de cacao and cream.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.passionforcocktails.com/en/vodka/after-eight |title= After Eight |access-date= 2017-11-08 |archive-date= July 27, 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170727195249/http://www.passionforcocktails.com/en/vodka/after-eight |url-status= dead }}</ref>

In the North Central United States, especially Wisconsin, grasshoppers are blended drinks, with ice cream substituted for cream.<ref>{{cite web |publisher=Punch |url=https://punchdrink.com/recipes/blended-grasshopper/ |title=PUNCH | Blended Grasshopper |access-date=2018-01-12}}</ref>  A related variation is the "grasshopper milkshake", which contains [[mint chocolate chip]] [[ice cream]], [[milk]], and crème de menthe. This is blended and served in a tall glass decorated with a miniature or broken cream-filled chocolate [[sandwich cookie]].<ref name="Sunset">{{cite web |url= http://food.sunset.com/sunset/recipefinder.dyn?action=displayRecipe&recipe_id=659259 |title= Grasshopper Milkshake |access-date= 2017-11-08 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100519001941/http://find.myrecipes.com/recipes/recipefinder.dyn?action=displayRecipe&recipe_id=659259 |archive-date= 2010-05-19 |url-status= dead }}</ref>

A "[[Girl Scout]] Cookie" substitutes [[peppermint schnapps]] for crème de menthe.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.chowhound.com/recipes/girl-scout-cookie-10267 |title= Girl Scout Cookie Recipe |publisher= [[Chowhound]] |access-date= 2017-11-08 }}</ref>

In celebrating the 85th anniversary of the snack food, [[Hostess Brands|Hostess]] released a cooking book of recipes using [[Twinkie|Twinkies.]] One of the recipes is called a "Twinkie grasshopper"<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/recipe-twinkie-grasshopper-1442446433|title=Recipe: Twinkie Grasshopper|website=WSJ|date=September 16, 2015 |language=en-US|access-date=2019-08-12}}</ref> which is akin to a [[milkshake]].

{{otheruses|Fizz (disambiguation)}}

A "'''fizz'''" is a [[mixed drink]] variation on the older [[Sour (cocktail)|sour]]s family of [[cocktail]]. Its defining features are an acidic juice (such as lemon or lime) and [[carbonated water]]. It typically includes [[gin]] or [[rum]] as its alcoholic ingredient.

==History==
The fizz became widely popular in America between 1900 and the 1940s.  Known as a hometown specialty of New Orleans, the gin fizz was so popular that bars would employ teams of bartenders that would take turns shaking the drinks. Demand for fizzes went international at least as early as 1950, as evidenced by its inclusion in the French cookbook ''[[L'Art Culinaire Francais]]'' published that year.<ref>How's Your Drink? by Eric Felten published by Surrey Books November 29, 2007, page 80</ref>

==Gin fizz==<!-- This section is linked from [[Gin Fizz]] -->
{{Infobox drink
| name        = Gin fizz
| image       = File:15-09-26-RalfR-WLC-0032.jpg   
| type        = [[List of cocktails|Cocktail]]
| base        = [[Gin]]
| ingredients ={{plainlist|* 5 cl [[gin]]
* 3 cl fresh [[lemon juice]]
* 1 cl [[Syrup#Simple_syrup|simple syrup]]
* Splash of [[Carbonated water|soda water]]}}
| served      = [[Straight up]]: chilled, without ice
| garnish     = [[lemon]] slice
| prep        = Shake all ingredients with ice cubes, except soda water. Pour into glass. Top with soda water.
| drinkware   = [[Old fashioned glass]]
}}

A gin fizz is the best-known cocktail in the fizz family.  A gin fizz contains gin, lemon juice, and sugar, which are shaken with ice, poured into a tumbler and topped with carbonated water.<ref>[http://www.iba-world.com/index.php?option=com_content&id=196&tmpl=component&task=preview&Itemid=532 Gin Fizz<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> The drink is similar to a [[Tom Collins]], with a possible distinction being a Tom Collins historically used "[[Old Tom gin]]" (a slightly sweeter precursor to [[London Dry Gin]]), whereas the kind of gin historically used in a gin fizz is unknown.<ref name="Great">{{cite news|last=Sinclair|first=George|date=March 26, 2007|work=[[Scribd]]|title=The Great Tom Collins Hoax|access-date=25 November 2008|url=https://www.scribd.com/doc/18790/Tom-Collins-Article|archive-date=2 December 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081202024918/http://www.scribd.com/doc/18790/Tom-Collins-Article|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Simple variations on the gin fizz are 
* Silver fizz – addition of [[egg white]]
* Golden fizz – addition of [[Yolk|egg yolk]]
* Royal fizz – addition of whole egg
* Diamond fizz – [[sparkling wine]] instead of carbonated water, more commonly known as a "[[French 75 (cocktail)|French 75]]".
* Green fizz – addition of a dash of green [[crème de menthe]]

==Ramos gin fizz==
{{Infobox drink
| name        = Ramos gin fizz
| image       = Ramos_Gin_Fizz.jpg  
| caption     = Ramos gin fizz at a bar in New Orleans 
| type        = [[List of cocktails|Cocktail]]
| base        = [[Gin]]
| ingredients ={{plainlist|*4.5 cl [[gin]]
* 1.5 cl fresh [[lime juice]]
* 1.5 cl fresh [[lemon juice]]
* 3 cl [[Syrup#Simple syrup|simple syrup]]
* 6 cl [[cream]]
* 1 [[egg white]]
* 3 dashes [[orange flower water]]
* 2 drops [[vanilla extract]]
* [[Carbonated water|soda water]]}}
| served      = [[Straight up]]: chilled, without ice
| prep        = All ingredients except the soda are poured in a mixing glass, dry shaken (no ice) for two minutes, then ice is added and shaken hard for another minute. Strain into a highball glass without ice and topped with soda.
| drinkware   = [[Collins glass]]
}}
A '''Ramos gin fizz''' (also known as a "Ramos fizz" or "New Orleans fizz") contains gin, lemon juice, lime juice, egg white, sugar, cream, [[orange flower water]], and [[soda water]].  It is served in a large non-tapered {{convert|12|to|14|usoz|ml|adj=on}} [[Collins glass]].<ref>[http://www.neworleansonline.com/neworleans/cuisine/drinks/ramosginfizz.html "Ramos Gin Fizz"], New Orleans Online. Retrieved January 2, 2016.</ref>

The orange flower water and egg significantly affect the flavor and texture of a Ramos, compared to a regular gin fizz.  The key to making this egg cocktail is dissolving the sugar before adding ice; the sugar acts as an emulsifier, and it and the alcohol "cook" the egg white.<ref>[http://www.cleveland.com/taste/index.ssf/2009/07/creative_cleveland_bartenders.html Creative Cleveland bartenders are the chefs of the cocktail scene]</ref>

Henry C. Ramos invented the Ramos gin fizz in 1888 at his bar, the Imperial Cabinet Saloon on Gravier Street, [[New Orleans, Louisiana]].  It was originally called a "New Orleans fizz", and is one of the city's most famous cocktails. Before [[Prohibition in the United States|Prohibition]], the drink's popularity and exceptionally long 12-minute mixing time<ref>[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Uj417erX2W8 New Orleans' best cocktails: The Ramos Gin Fizz - YouTube<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> had over 20 bartenders working at the Imperial at once making nothing but the Ramos gin fizz{{snd}} and still struggling to keep up with demand. During the carnival of 1915, 32 staff members were on at once, just to shake the drink.{{cn |date=December 2022}}

The [[The Roosevelt Hotel New Orleans|Roosevelt Hotel]] in New Orleans also popularized the drink, abetted by Governor [[Huey P. Long|Huey Long's]] fondness for it.  In July 1935, Long brought a bartender named Sam Guarino from the Roosevelt Hotel to the New Yorker Hotel in New York City to teach its staff how to make the drink so he could have it whenever he was there.  The [[Museum of the American Cocktail]] has newsreel footage of this event.  The Roosevelt Hotel group trademarked the drink name in 1935 and still makes it today.

==Sloe gin fizz (purple fizz)==<!-- This section is linked from [[Sloe Gin Fizz]] -->

* 8 cl [[Carbonated water|soda water]]

| served      = [[On the rocks]]: poured over ice

A traditional sloe gin fizz contains [[sloe gin]] (a [[blackthorn|blackthorn plum]] flavored spirit), grapefruit juice, [[Syrup#Simple syrup|simple syrup]], egg white, and carbonated water. 
A popular alternative eliminates the egg white.<ref name="sloeginfizz">[http://www.esquire.com/drinks/sloe-gin-fizz-drink-recipe Sloe Gin Fizz Recipe - Esquire - How to Make the Perfect Sloe Gin Fizz]</ref> 
Though the original recipe uses grapefruit juice, variants including lemon juice exist as well.

==Less common gin fizzes==
* Japanese gin fizz – a standard gin fizz with a shot of lychee liqueur added
* Meyer lemon fizz – uses the sweeter [[Meyer lemon]] instead of normal lemon, and adds orange juice
* New Orleans "fiss" – 75% dry gin, 25% [[Creme Yvette]], 1 egg white, 1/2 tsp. powdered sugar, 1 tsp. cream, juice each of 1/2 of an orange, lime, & lemon<ref>{{cite book |last1=Grohusko |first1=Jacob |title=Jack's Manual |url=https://archive.org/details/jacksmanualonvin00groh |date=1910 |publisher=McClunn & Co. |location=New York |page=[https://archive.org/details/jacksmanualonvin00groh/page/60 60]}}</ref>
* Sour melon fizz – gin, lime juice, midori and ginger ale
* Strawberry gin fizz – gin, [[St. Germain liqueur]], strawberries, club soda, mint;<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://realhousemoms.com/strawberry-gin-fizz/|title = Strawberry Gin Fizz|date = 6 June 2014}}</ref> or gin, lime juice, sparkling water, mint sprigs<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cookrepublic.com/strawberry-gin-fizz-cocktail/|title = Strawberry Gin Fizz|date = 8 November 2018}}</ref>
* Tillhammer – gin, Spezi, a frozen dill pickle

==Non-gin fizzes==
* Chicago fizz – [[rum]], [[port wine]], lemon juice, sugar, and egg white
* Manhattan cooler – whisky (Scotch), lemon juice, sugar, and lemon-lime soda
* [[Mimosa (cocktail)|Mimosa]] (or [[Buck's Fizz (cocktail)|Buck's fizz]]){{Wikipedia:WikiProject Cocktails/Templates/Badges/IBAOfficialMini}} – champagne, orange juice, sometimes grenadine
* Pink fizz (or May blossom fizz<ref>{{cite book |last=MacElhone |first=Harry |authorlink=Harry MacElhone |title=Harry of Ciro's ABC of Mixing Cocktails |date=1923 |publisher=Dean & Son Ltd |location=London |page=50}}</ref>) – Swedish [[punsch]], lemon juice, grenadine, soda water<ref>{{cite book |last1=Tarling |first1=W.J. |title=Cafe Royal Cocktail Book |date=1937 |publisher=Pall Mall Ltd. |location=London |page=FIZZ}}</ref>
* Morning glory fizz – whisky (Scotch), [[absinthe]], lemon juice, one egg white, sugar, soda water<ref>{{cite book |last=MacElhone |first=Harry |authorlink=Harry MacElhone |title=Harry of Ciro's ABC of Mixing Cocktails |date=1923 |publisher=Dean & Son Ltd |location=London |page=49}}</ref>
* Whiskey fizz – whiskey (American blend), lemon juice, sugar, and lemon-lime soda
* Vodka fizz - vodka (plain or flavored), fruit juice, and sparkling water or soda
* Mojito – white rum, sugar, lime juice, soda water, and mint.

{{Infobox drink

A '''dark 'n' stormy''' is a [[highball]] cocktail made with [[dark rum]] (the "dark") and [[ginger beer]] (the "stormy") served over [[ice]] and garnished with a slice of [[lime (fruit)|lime]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |url=http://iba-world.com/new-era-drinks/dark-n-stormy/ |title=Dark 'N' Stormy |website=iba-world.com |publisher=International Bartenders Association |access-date=2017-07-06}}</ref> Lime juice and simple syrup are also frequently added.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.insider.com/best-2-ingredient-cocktails-2019-4 |title=14 easy 2-ingredient cocktails you can make at home |last=Vanderberg |first=Madison |website=Insider}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/recipes/a3747/dark-and-stormy-drink-recipe/ |title=Dark and Stormy Drink Recipe |date=2015-02-01 |work=Esquire |access-date=2017-07-08 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":3" /> This drink is very similar to the [[Moscow mule]] except that the Dark 'n' Stormy has dark rum instead of [[vodka]]. The original Dark 'n' Stormy was made with [[Gosling Brothers|Gosling Black Seal]] rum and [[Barritt's Ginger Beer]],<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.allatsea.net/ginger-beer-matter-dark-n-stormy/ |title=Does the Ginger Beer Matter in a Dark 'n' Stormy? |date=24 June 2016 |website=drinks.seriouseats.com |language=en |access-date=2020-01-15}}</ref>{{better source needed|date=December 2025}} but after the partnership between the two failed and the companies parted ways, Gosling Brothers created its own ginger beer. 

[[Gosling Brothers]] claims that the drink was invented in [[Bermuda]] just after World War I.<ref name=":0" />

== Trademark and litigation ==
[[File:Gosling Brothers Ltd building -- Hamilton, Bermuda -- 2014-06-19.JPG|thumb|Gosling Brothers building in Bermuda.]]

Gosling Brothers has registered a version of the name that uses one apostrophe ('N), while the [[International Bartenders Association]] uses two apostrophes ('N').<ref name=":1" />

In the United States, "Dark 'n Stormy" has been a registered [[trademark]] of [[Gosling Brothers]] Ltd of Bermuda since 1991.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |url=http://www.thedailybeast.com/articles/2015/09/22/will-the-real-dark-n-stormy-please-stand-up|title=Will the Real Dark N' Stormy Please Stand Up?|last=Haglage|first=Abby|date=2015-09-22|newspaper=The Daily Beast |access-date=2017-07-08}}</ref><ref name="nytimes" /> Gosling Brothers uses this registration to prohibit US marketing of a drink under the name "Dark 'n Stormy", or a related, confusing name, unless it is made with Gosling Black Seal rum.<ref name="nytimes">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/07/05/fashion/05shaken.html |title=The Right Stuff (by Law)|first=Jonathan|date=5 July 2009|work=New York Times|last=Miles|access-date=August 1, 2014}}</ref> Gosling's has litigated or threatened litigation over the mark against [[Pernod Ricard]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.law360.com/articles/735000/a-toast-to-2015-wine-and-beer-trademark-disputes-part-2|title=A Toast To 2015 Wine And Beer Trademark Disputes: Part 2 - Law360|last=Kluft|first=David|date=2015-12-09|website=Law360|language=en|access-date=2017-07-06}}</ref> [[Proximo Spirits]],<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.law360.com/articles/703237/rum-maker-says-rival-infringed-dark-n-stormy-trademark|title=Rum Maker Says Rival Infringed Dark 'N Stormy Trademark|last=Sullivan|first=Gail|date=2015-09-16|website=Law360|language=en|access-date=2017-07-06|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Infinium Spirits' Zaya, and a cocktail blog.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.bevlaw.com/bevlog/alcohol-beverages-generally/a-courtroom-cocktail-gosling-brothers-and-a-dark-stormy-message|title=A Courtroom Cocktail: Gosling Brothers and a Dark, Stormy Message|last=Volz|first=Michael|date=2015-11-17|work=Bevlog|access-date=2017-07-06}}</ref>

Because of Gosling Brothers' threats of litigation, some sources use other variations on the name, such as "safe harbor", to offer similar drinks.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JftDBAAAQBAJ&pg=PT298|title=Shrubs: An Old Fashioned Drink for Modern Times|last=Dietsch|first=Michael|date=2014-10-06|publisher=The Countryman Press|isbn=9781581576511|language=en}}</ref>

==Variations==
A cider and stormy, or dark 'n' stormy cider,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.thebermudian.com/food-a-drink/recipes/dark-n-stormy-cider/|title=Dark 'n Stormy Cider|date=September 30, 2019|website=The Bermudian Magazine}}</ref> or dark and stormy orchard,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.foodiewithfamily.com/dark-stormy-orchard-spice-up-the-holidays-announcement/|title=Dark & Stormy Orchard | Spice Up the Holidays Announcement|date=November 23, 2012|website=Foodie With Family}}</ref> is a mix of dark rum, apple cider, and ginger beer.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.plated.com/morsel/dark-and-stormy-recipe-cider/|title=This Dark and Stormy Recipe Includes Apple Cider|date=November 10, 2017}}</ref> The fall dark 'n' stormy contains bourbon, apple cider, lemon juice, and ginger beer.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://thebeachhousekitchen.com/2017/11/16/the-fall-dark-n-stormy/|title=The Fall Dark 'N' Stormy|date=November 16, 2017}}</ref>
