guide|publisher=Odd Firm of Sin Ltd|access-date=November 9, 2017}}{{Failed verification|reason=Claim is not supported|date=March 2020}} He was working at the New York Bar in Paris at the time, which later became [[Harry's New York Bar]], a frequent Paris hangout for [[Ernest Hemingway]] and other American migrants.{{cite book|author=MacElhone, Andrew|author2= MacElhone, Duncan|name-list-style=amp |title=Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails| page=35|isbn= 0-285-63358-9|publisher= Souvenir Press|orig-year= 1986|year= 1996}} The cocktail is said to have been created on the spur of the moment, according to the bar's own traditions, consisting only of vodka and tomato juice.{{cite web|last1=Chazan|first1=David|title=A century of Harry's Bar in Paris|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-15887142|website=BBC News|publisher=BBC|access-date=November 9, 2017|date=November 25, 2011|quote="The story is that there were a few customers, a few friends, and the bartender, Pete [sic] Petiot, made a cocktail for them with tomato juice and vodka."}} It was originally referred to as a "Bucket of Blood."{{cite magazine |url= https://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/recipes/a27481/bloody-mary-origins-recipe/ |title= The Secret Origins of the Bloody Mary |author= John Mariani |author-link= John Mariani |magazine= Esquire |date= February 21, 2014 }} Harry's Bar also claims to have created numerous other classic cocktails, including the [[White Lady (cocktail)|White Lady]] and the [[Sidecar (cocktail)|Side Car]].The History of Harry's New York Bar – Book and Bar's Website article New York's [[21 Club]] has two claims associated with it. One is that it was invented in the 1930s by bartender Henry Zbikiewicz, who was charged with mixing Bloody Marys. Another attributes its invention to the comedian [[George Jessel (actor)|George Jessel]], who frequented the 21 Club.{{cite book|author=Smith, Andrew F. |date=2007|title=The Oxford Companion to American Food and Drink|page= 55|publisher= Oxford University Press, Inc.|location= New York}} In 1939, [[Lucius Beebe]] printed in his gossip column ''This New York'' one of the earliest U.S. references to this drink, along with the original recipe: "George Jessel's newest pick-me-up which is receiving attention from the town's paragraphers is called a Bloody Mary: half tomato juice, half vodka."{{cite news|work=[[New York Herald Tribune]]|title=George Jessel's newest pick-me-up which is receiving attention from the town's paragraphers is called Bloody Mary|author=Lucius Beebe| date= December 2, 1939|page=9}}{{verify source|date=March 2014}}{{Cite web |title=The History of the Bloody Mary |url=https://drinktoma.com/blogs/news/the-history-of-the-bloody-mary?srsltid=AfmBOopRKcolwkyoYXxTVGfI2amdl7mUlnHl389DsJ8Nhan7kARPj44t |access-date=November 4, 2024 |website=Toma Bloody Mary Mixers |language=en}} In a 1939 publication by [[El Floridita]] called ''Floridita Cocktails'' a recipe called "Mary Rose" lists the main ingredients of a modern Bloody Mary.[https://euvslibrary.com/?p=532 Floridita Cocktails] This booklet may be one of the earliest publications depicting the name Mary, while using the same ingredients in today's Bloody Mary.{{Cite book|url=https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1939-Floridita-Cock-tails/44|title=Floridita Cocktails|publisher=El Floridita|year=1939|pages=44}} Fernand Petiot claimed to have invented the modern Bloody Mary in 1934 as a refinement to George Jessel's drink, at the [[King Cole Bar|King Cole Room]] in New York's [[St. Regis Hotel]], according to the hotel's own history.{{cite web|title=King Cole Bar: The History Of The Red Snapper|url=http://www.stregisnewyork.com/king-cole-bar|website=The St. Regis New York|publisher=Marriott International, Inc.|access-date=November 9, 2017}} Petiot told ''[[The New Yorker]]'' in July 1964:
I initiated the Bloody Mary of today. Jessel said he created it, but it was really nothing but vodka and tomato juice when I took it over. I cover the bottom of the [[cocktail shaker|shaker]] with four large dashes of salt, two dashes of [[black pepper]], two dashes of [[cayenne pepper]], and a layer of [[Worcestershire sauce]]; I then add a dash of lemon juice and some cracked ice, put in two ounces of vodka and two ounces of thick tomato juice, shake, strain, and pour. We serve a hundred to a hundred and fifty Bloody Marys a day here in the King Cole Room and in the other restaurants and the banquet rooms."{{cite web|url=http://www.epicurious.com/articlesguides/blogs/editor/2008/12/happy-birthday.html|title=Happy Birthday, Bloody Mary!|last=Park|first=Michael Y.|date=1 December 2008|publisher=Epicurious|access-date=11 July 2011|archive-date=5 December 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081205054208/http://www.epicurious.com/articlesguides/blogs/editor/2008/12/happy-birthday.html|url-status=dead}}
The cocktail was claimed as a new cocktail under the name "red hammer" in ''[[Life (magazine)|Life]]'' magazine in 1942, consisting of tomato juice, vodka, and lemon juice.{{cite journal |author= |title=Hollywood goes Russian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fk4EAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA38 |journal=Life Magazine |year=1942 |page=38 |volume=13 |issue=8 |quote='Red Hammer' is a new Hollywood cocktail. Helene Reynolds mixes one for Bob Turner at her party. It is part tomato juice and part vodka, with a dash of lemon.}} Less than a month later, a ''Life'' advertisement for [[French's]] Worcestershire Sauce suggested that it be added to a [[Non-alcoholic beverage|virgin]] "Tomato Juice Cocktail" along with tomato juice, salt, and pepper.{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_UUAEAAAAMBAJ |page=[https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_UUAEAAAAMBAJ/page/n111 110] |title=LIFE|publisher=[[Time Inc]] |date=October 5, 1942 |access-date=April 15, 2014}} The addition of salt to the alcoholic beverage was suggested that same year in a story in ''[[Hearst's International Combined with Cosmopolitan]]''.{{Citation | last = Dodge | first = David | author-link = David F. Dodge | title = Shear the Black Sheep | newspaper = Hearst's international combined with Cosmopolitan | volume = 113 | issue = 1 | page = 144 | date = July 1942 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=cKJXAAAAMAAJ&q=Bloody+Marys | access-date = April 15, 2014 | quote = 'A couple of Bloody Marys.' The bartender shook his head. 'You got me, friend.' 'A glass of tomato juice, ice, a slug of vodka and some salt.'}} ===Origin of the name=== Some drink aficionados believe the inspiration for the name was Hollywood star [[Mary Pickford]].{{cite web |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2002/07/24/potent-pick-me-up-2/ |title=Potent pick-me-up |work=[[Chicago Tribune]] |date=July 24, 2002 |access-date=May 1, 2012}} Others trace the name to a waitress named Mary who worked at a Chicago bar called the Bucket of Blood.[http://in.reuters.com/article/entertainmentNews/idINIndia-36812420081201 Bloody Marys at 1933 prices just the tonic for NYC] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091225051904/http://in.reuters.com/article/entertainmentNews/idINIndia-36812420081201 |date=December 25, 2009 }} Reuters, December 2, 2008 The tradition at Harry's New York Bar in Paris, according to manager Alain Da Silva in a 2011 interview, is that one of the patrons for whom the cocktail was first mixed in 1920 or 1921 declared, "It looks like my girlfriend who I met in a cabaret"; the cabaret's name was the Bucket of Blood and the girlfriend's name was Mary, so the patrons and bartender Petiot agreed to call it a "Bloody Mary". Alternatively, the name may have arisen from "a failure to pronounce the [[Slavic languages|Slav syllables]] of a drink called [[Vladimir]]" in English.{{cite book |last=Leigh Fermor |first=Patrick |author-link=Patrick Leigh Fermor |editor-last=Joliffe |editor-first=John |title=Auberon Herbert: A Composite Portrait |publisher= Michael Russell |date=November 1, 1976 | chapter=[[Auberon Herbert]] |isbn=978-0859550482}} Cited in {{cite book |last=Leigh Fermor |first=Patrick |author-link=Patrick Leigh Fermor |editor-last=Cooper |editor-first=Artemis |title=Words of Mercury |publisher=John Murray |year=2003 |isbn=978-0719561061 |page=160}} This gains some credibility from the anecdotal observation that the customer at the New York Bar for whom Petiot prepared the drink in 1920/21 was [[Smirnoff#History|Vladimir Smirnov]], of the [[Smirnoff vodka]] family.{{cite web |last=Samuels |first=Brian |title=The History of the Bloody Mary |publisher=The Boys Club |date=March 18, 2013 |url=http://theboysclub.net/brian/the-history-of-the-bloody-mary/ |access-date=August 30, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141013104147/http://theboysclub.net/brian/the-history-of-the-bloody-mary/ |archive-date=October 13, 2014}} The name "Bloody Mary" is associated with a number of historical figures, particularly [[Queen Mary I of England]], who was nicknamed "Bloody Mary" due to the executions of [[Protestant]]s during her reign.{{Cite book |last=Waller |first=Maureen |title=Sovereign ladies: the six reigning queens of England |year=2006 |publisher=Murray |isbn=978-0-7195-6628-8 |location=London}} ==Preparation and serving== In the United States, the Bloody Mary is a common "[[hair of the dog]]" drink, reputed to cure [[hangover]]s with its combination of a heavy vegetable base (to settle the stomach), salt (to replenish lost electrolytes), and alcohol (to relieve head and body aches). Bloody Mary enthusiasts enjoy some relief from the numbing effects of the alcohol, as well as the [[placebo effect]].{{cite web|url=http://www.washingtonian.com/articles/restaurants/8837.html|title=Here's to the Bloody Mary|last=Shoffner|first=Robert|date=July 1, 2008|work=[[The Washingtonian (magazine)|The Washingtonian]]|access-date=June 9, 2009}}[http://women.webmd.com/features/9-myths-about-your-hangover "9 Myths About Your Hangover"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111225232328/http://women.webmd.com/features/9-myths-about-your-hangover |date=December 25, 2011 }} by Dana Dudepohl, ''[[Marie Claire]]'', at WebMD.com[http://www.cracked.com/funny-5644-bloody-marys/ But Does It Actually Cure Hangovers?] Cracked.com[https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2001-dec-30-mn-19052-story.html Mud in Your Eye; a Sheep's Eye in Your Drink] Los Angeles Times, December 30, 2001[http://www.huffingtonpost.com/zane-lamprey/why-i-love-the-bloody-mar_b_1118895.html Hangovers: There Is A Cure] Huffington Post, November 29, 2011 Its reputation as a restorative beverage contributes to the popularity of the Bloody Mary in the morning and early afternoon, especially at [[brunch]]es.{{cite news |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052748703421204576327380762930852 |title=The Bloody Mary Makeover |last=Garbarino |first=Steve |date=May 21, 2011 |journal=The Wall Street Journal|access-date=July 9, 2011}} The Bloody Mary is traditionally served over ice in a tall glass, such as a [[Highball glass|highball]], flared [[Pint glass|pint]] or [[hurricane glass]]. The two critical ingredients, vodka and tomato juice, are relatively simple; however, the drink almost never consists of these two ingredients alone. Among the more common additions to the juice base are salt or celery salt (either mixed in or as a salted rim), cracked pepper, hot sauce (such as [[Tabasco sauce|Tabasco]]), citrus juices (especially lemon or lime), [[Worcestershire sauce]], celery seed, horseradish, [[clam juice]] or olive brine, brown sugar or molasses, or [[bitters]]. Some or all of these ingredients can come pre-mixed with the tomato juice as a single "Bloody Mary mix" to which the vodka is added, or the drink may be hand-constructed by the bartender from raw ingredients according to the patron's preference. A common [[Cocktail garnish|garnish]] is a celery stalk when served in a tall glass; other common garnishes include olives, cheese cubes, a dill pickle spear, lemon wedges, dried [[sausage]], [[bacon]], and shrimp (as the taste of the drink is often reminiscent of [[shrimp cocktail]] sauce). In addition to the aforementioned more traditional ingredients, practically anything can be added to the drink itself or as a garnish according to the drinker's wishes or the bartender's or establishment's traditions. Some variations of the Bloody Mary served by restaurants are designed to be a meal as well as a drink, coming with massive "garnishes" on skewers inserted into the glass, including ribs, miniature hamburgers called "sliders", grilled or fried shrimp, kebabs, sandwich wedges, fruit slices, and even [[sashimi]]. The drink itself can be served in any of a variety of glasses, from wine glasses to schooners or beer steins, according to tradition or availability. It is a tradition in the upper Midwest, particularly in Wisconsin, to serve a Bloody Mary with a small beer chaser.{{Cite web|url=http://onmilwaukee.com/bars/articles/askomcbloodymarys.html|title=Ask OMC: Why do Bloodys come with beer chasers?|website=OnMilwaukee.com|date=August 18, 2009|access-date=May 1, 2016}} ===Variations=== There is a considerable amount of variation available in the drink's construction and presentation including the use of different base spirits like bourbon, rye, tequila, or gin. With tequila, it is often called a '''Bloody Maria'''. Similar variations exist: with [[absinthe]] the drink is called a '''Bloody Fairy''', with sake it's a '''Bloody Geisha''', with the anise-flavored [[Arak (drink)|Arak]] it's the '''Bloody Miriam''', and so forth.{{cite book |title= The 12 Bottle Bar: A Dozen Bottles. Hundreds of Cocktails. A New Way to Drink.|date = July 29, 2014|publisher = Workman|isbn = 9780761181385|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lfElAgAAQBAJ&dq=bloody+fairy+absinthe&pg=PA120}}{{cite web |title=The Bloody Miriam: A Classic Cocktail with a Jewish Twist |date=March 8, 2018|url=https://spoonuniversity.com/recipe/the-bloody-miriam-a-classic-cocktail-with-a-jewish-twist}} Another notable variation is the '''Bull Shot''', popular in the late '50s and '60s, which replaces tomato juice with beef bouillon or consommé.{{Cite web |last=Erickson |first=Nate |date=February 10, 2019 |title=I Urge You to Replace Your Bloody Mary with a Shot of Vodka and Beef Stock |url=https://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/a26243113/bullshot-cocktail-beef-broth-recipe/ |access-date=October 9, 2022 |website=Esquire |language=en-US}}{{Cite news |last=Wondrich |first=David |date=April 10, 2017 |title=Why the Bullshot Cocktail Is No Joke |language=en |work=The Daily Beast |url=https://www.thedailybeast.com/articles/2017/04/10/why-the-bullshot-cocktail-is-no-joke |access-date=October 9, 2022}} ====Bloody Margaret==== [[File:Bloody Margaret.jpg|thumb|A plain Bloody Margaret, served in a [[highball glass]] with a [[celery]] stick]] '''Bloody Margaret''' is a variation on the cocktail Bloody Mary, made with [[gin]] instead of [[vodka]]; it is also more often known as a '''Red Snapper''' or '''Bloody Gary''' in the [[United States]].{{cite web|url=https://www.socialandcocktail.co.uk/cocktails/bloody-margaret/|title=Bloody Margaret Cocktail Recipes - Gin Cocktails|publisher= Social + Cocktail Events Ltd|location=Glasgow|accessdate=May 17, 2018}}{{cite web|url=http://www.foodrepublic.com/recipes/red-snapper-cocktail-recipe/|title=Red Snapper Cocktail Recipe|publisher=foodrepublic.com|accessdate=May 25, 2018|date=May 29, 2011}} Ruddy Mary is an alternative name.{{cite web|last1=Cloake|first1=Felicity|title=How to make the perfect bloody mary|url=https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/wordofmouth/2013/may/02/how-to-make-perfect-bloody-mary|website=theguardian|date=May 2, 2013|publisher=The Guardian|access-date=November 9, 2017}}{{cite web|last1=Emen|first1=Jake|title=A Guide to the Bloody Mary and its Many Variations|url=https://www.eater.com/drinks/2016/2/16/10985162/bloody-mary-cocktail-guide|website=Eater|publisher=Vox Media|access-date=November 9, 2017|date=February 16, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190216122943/https://www.eater.com/drinks/2016/2/16/10985162/bloody-mary-cocktail-guide|archive-date=February 16, 2019|url-status=dead}} This article lists many variations. According to web site FoodRepublic.com, the Red Snapper originated in post-[[Prohibition]] New York City. A French barman named [[Fernand Petiot|Fernand “Pete” Petiot]] left [[Harry's New York Bar]] in Paris to work at the King Cole Room at the [[St. Regis New York|St. Regis Hotel]] in NYC. Petiot had been known in [[Paris]] for the tomato-juice-and-vodka cocktail, the Bloody Mary. Vodka was scarce then in New York, so Petiot swapped it for gin. The [[Astors]], owners of the St. Regis, didn't like the name Bloody Mary, and thus Red Snapper (originally a [[Lutjanus campechanus|fish]]) was chosen instead. ====Virgin Mary==== A "'''Virgin Mary'''", also known as a "'''Bloody Virgin'''", a "'''Virgin Bloody Mary'''", or "'''Bloody Shame'''", is a [[Non-alcoholic mixed drink|non-alcoholic cocktail]], generally using the same ingredients and garnish as a Bloody Mary (according to local custom), but with the spirits replaced by additional tomato juice or prepared mix.{{cite web|title=Bartending/Cocktails/Bloody Mary|url=https://en.wikibooks.org/w/index.php?title=Bartending/Cocktails/Bloody_Mary&stable=0#Variations_in_alcohol|website=WikiBooks|publisher=WikiMedia|access-date=November 9, 2017}} ==See also== {{Portal|Drink|Liquor}} * [[Caesar (cocktail)]] * [[List of cocktails]] * [[Michelada]] * [[Queen Mary (cocktail)]] * [[Tomato beer]] * [[Vampiro (cocktail)]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{Commons category-inline|Bloody Mary}} {{Alcoholic beverages}} {{IBACocktails}} {{Authority control}} [[Category:Cocktails]] [[Category:Cocktails with vodka]] [[Category:Spicy cocktails]] [[Category:Cocktails with tomato juice]] [[Category:Cocktails with lemon juice]] [[Category:Cocktails with lime juice]] [[Category:Citrus cocktails]] [[Category:Celery]] [[Category:Brunch]] [[Category:IBA official cocktails]]

The '''aviation''' is a [[cocktail]] made with [[gin]], [[maraschino]] [[liqueur]], [[crème de violette]] and [[lemon juice]]. Some recipes omit the crème de violette. It is served [[Bartending terminology#Straight, up, and straight up|straight up]], in a cocktail glass.

==History==
The aviation was created by Hugo Ensslin, head [[bartender]] at the Hotel Wallick in New York, in the early twentieth century.<ref>{{cite web|title=Aviation | url=http://www.drinkboy.com/Cocktails/Recipe.aspx?itemid=10 | last=Hess | first= Robert | publisher=Drinkboy.com | access-date=5 March 2011| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110121120104/http://drinkboy.com/Cocktails/Recipe.aspx?itemid=10| archive-date= 21 January 2011 | url-status= live}}</ref> The first published recipe appeared in Ensslin's 1916 ''Recipes for Mixed Drinks''. Ensslin's recipe called for two thirds El Bart gin, one third lemon juice, 2 dashes maraschino liqueur, and 2 dashes crème de violette.<ref>{{cite book | title=Recipes for Mixed Drinks | last=Ensslin | first=Hugo | publisher=Mud Puddle Books Inc | year=2009 |page=7 |orig-year=1917 | isbn=978-1-60311-190-4}}</ref>

[[Harry Craddock]]'s influential ''[[Savoy Cocktail Book]]'' (1930) omitted the crème de violette, calling for a mixture of two thirds dry gin, one third lemon juice and two dashes of maraschino.<ref name="Craddock25">{{cite book|first=Harry|last=Craddock|title=The Savoy Cocktail Book|publisher=Constable & Co.|location=London|year=1930|isbn=978-1-62654-0644|page=25}}</ref> Many later bartenders have followed Craddock's lead, leaving out the difficult-to-find violet liqueur.<ref name="Regan209">{{cite book |first=Gary |last=Regan |title=The Joy of Mixology |publisher=Clarkson Potter/Publishers |location=New York |year=2003 |page=209 |isbn=0-609-60884-3}}</ref>

[[Creme Yvette]], a violet liqueur made with additional spices, is sometimes substituted for crème de violette.<ref>{{cite news | url=http://voices.washingtonpost.com/all-we-can-eat/spirits/spirits-we-want-creme-yvette.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130202133026/http://voices.washingtonpost.com/all-we-can-eat/spirits/spirits-we-want-creme-yvette.html | url-status=dead | archive-date=2 February 2013 | title= Spirits: We Want Creme Yvette! |newspaper=The Washington Post| date=7 October 2009 | access-date=27 February 2013}}</ref>

==Related cocktails==
* The aviation can be considered a variation on the [[Sour (cocktail)|Gin sour]], using maraschino as its sweetener.<ref name="Craddock25" />
* The Blue Moon cocktail is made with gin, lemon juice, and crème de violette or Creme Yvette, without maraschino.<ref>{{cite news | url=http://projects.washingtonpost.com/recipes/2008/04/02/blue-moon-cocktail | title= Blue Moon Cocktail |newspaper=The Washington Post| date=2 April 2008 | access-date=8 October 2011}}</ref>
* The [[Water_Lily_(cocktail)|Water Lily]] substitutes an orange liqueur (such as [[triple sec]] or [[cointreau]]) for the maraschino.
* The Moonlight cocktail is made with gin, lime juice, [[Cointreau]], and crème de violette.<ref>{{cite web | title=The Cocktailian: Creme de violette lifts Aviation to the moon | url=https://www.sfgate.com/wine/article/the-cocktailian-creme-de-violette-lifts-aviation-2520581.php |work=San Francisco Chronicle | last=Regan | first=Gary | date=28 September 2007 | access-date=4 April 2011}}</ref>
* [[Takumi's aviation]] is made with gin, maraschino liqueur, [[parfait d'amour]], and lemon juice. The drink was created by the Japanese bartender [[Takumi Watanabe (bartender)|Takumi Watanabe]]. It was recorded in [[Gary Regan]]'s ''The Joy of Mixology'' (2017).<ref>{{cite web | title=Takumi's Aviation | url=https://www.liquor.com/recipes/takumis-aviation/ |work=Gary Regan  | date=26 April 2017 | access-date=9 February 2022}}</ref>
*The Beachcomber is a version based on rum sour.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Embury |first1=David A. |title=The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks |date=1963 |publisher=Faber and Faber Ltd |location=Russel Square London |page=135}}</ref>

A '''Clover Club cocktail''' is a shaken cocktail consisting of [[gin]], [[lemon juice]], raspberry syrup, and [[egg white]].  The egg white acts as an [[emulsifier]], forming the drink's characteristic foamy head.

== History and character ==
The Clover Club cocktail is a drink that pre-dates [[Prohibition in the United States|Prohibition]] in the United States, and is named for the [[Philadelphia]] men's club of the same name, which met in [[the Bellevue-Stratford Hotel]] at [[Broad Street (Philadelphia)|South Broad]] and Walnut Streets in [[Center City, Philadelphia|Center City]]. The Clover Club was chartered in 1882.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Deacon|first=Mary R.|url=http://archive.org/details/cloverclubofphil00deac|title=The Clover club of Philadelphia, by Mary R. Deacon|publisher=Avil Printing Company|others=State Library of Pennsylvania}}</ref>

Of the cocktail, Robert Hess claims<ref name="thespiritworld.net">Robert Hess, The Spirit World, "Clover Club Cocktail" April 2007.(http://thespiritworld.net/2007/04/09/the-clover-club-cocktail/)</ref>  "It has a long history [...] and was enjoyed by the captains of industry who were members of the famous club."<ref>Paystyle, Unimart, "Happy Hour: Clover Club Cocktail (The Remixes)" April 2009.(http://www.umamimart.com/2009/04/happy-hour-clover-club-cocktail-the-remixes/)</ref>

Published recipes for the cocktails, nearly identical to the modern "Clover Club cocktail" appear as early as 1908. and J. A. Grohusko's ''Jack's Manual'' features a drink called "A Clover Leaf." Grohusko writes that it "is said to be popular in the city of brotherly love. Certainly it is decorative for it has a soft orchid color, with a rim of white." The recipe itself features sugar, [[Gordon's Gin]], raspberry syrup, egg white and a sprig of mint.<ref>{{Cite web|title=1908 Jack's Manual by J A Grohusko|url=https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1908-Jack-s-Manual-by-J-A-Grohusko/14|access-date=2021-11-30|website=euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz}}</ref> Cocktail books such as ''Applegreen's Bar Book'', which published several editions and mentioned the Clover Club bar in its 1904 edition,<ref>{{Cite web|title=1904 Applegreen's Bar Book by John Applegreen|url=https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1904-Applegreen-s-Bar-Book-by-John-Applegreen/40|access-date=2021-11-30|website=euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz}}</ref> did not include the "Clover Leaf Cocktail" until 1909.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Applegreen|first=John|title=Applegreen's Bar Book or How to Mix Drinks|publisher=The Hotel Monthly|year=1909|location=Chicago|pages=9}}</ref>

Lifestyle and art sections of newspapers of the era included briefs about the cocktail describing it as "now new."<ref>{{Cite news|date=9 May 1909|title=Reign of the Cook is Passing|work=Pittsburgh Press|access-date=}}</ref>

Its earliest published appearance in a cocktail book as "The Clover Club Cocktail" was in 1910 in Raymond E. Sullivan's ''The Barkeeper's Manual''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=1910 The Barkeeper's Manual by Raymond E. Sullivan (second edition)|url=https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1910-The-Barkeeper-s-Manual-by-Raymond-E-Sullivan-second-edition/8/|access-date=2021-11-30|website=euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz}}</ref> His recipe included a mint sprig as garnish. The mint leaf would later fall of favor in the "Cocktail Club" and its inclusion would make the drink the "Clover Leaf."

In its heyday, the drink was described by Jack Townsend as being enjoyed by the pre-Prohibition gentleman who would have fit in with those of the club, and was a "Distinguished patron of the oak-paneled lounge."<ref name="cocktailchronicles.com">Paul Clarke, The Cocktail Chronicles, "A Change in Fortune." March 2006.(http://www.cocktailchronicles.com/2006/03/22/a-change-in-fortune/)</ref>  However, by the time that Townsend was writing about the drink it was becoming unpopular, and was eventually all but forgotten.<ref name="cocktailchronicles.com" /> 1931's ''Old Waldorf Astoria Bar Days'' by Albert Stevens Crockett describes the Clover Club's quick rise and fall. "That was before the 'Clover Club' had won in New York temples of thirst a wide but short-lived popularity."<ref>{{Cite web|title=1931 Old Waldorf Bar Days by Albert Stevens Crockett|url=https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1931-Ol-Waldorf-Astoria-Bar-Days-by-Albert-Stevens-Crockett/46|access-date=2021-11-30|website=euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz}}</ref>

The drink rapidly declined in popularity. In ''The Gun Club Drink Book'', by Charles Browne, published in 1939, he panned the once popular drink.  "A clover club cocktail is a Philadelphia concoction, maybe one of the jokes indulged in at the Clover Club. It's an awful mixture. [...] This will make three cocktails if there be found three people who want them."<ref>{{Cite book|last=Browne|first=Charles|title=The Gun Club Drink Book|publisher=Charles Scribner's Sons|year=1939|location=New York, NY}}</ref> It is unknown exactly which variation he was panning – by the late 1930s several variations of the "Clover Club" went under the name. Other ingredients included cream, nutmeg and vermouth.<ref>{{Cite web|title=1934 Cocktail Bill Boothby's World Drinks and how to mix them|url=https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1934-Cocktail-Bill-Boothby-s-World-Drinks-and-how-to-mix-them1|access-date=2021-11-30|website=euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz}}</ref>

Among the theories for its rapid decline is the use of raw egg in the cocktail, which many people shy away from, and partly due to the complexity of its preparation (see below).<ref name="agrandioseblog.com">A Grandiose Blog: Cocktails, Gadgets & More, "The Clover Club Cocktail Recipe Blog Love Mixology Mondays XVII" July 2007.(http://www.agrandioseblog.com/drink/mixology-mondays-xvii-blog-love-the-clover-club {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091123105538/http://www.agrandioseblog.com/drink/mixology-mondays-xvii-blog-love-the-clover-club |date=2009-11-23 }})</ref>  Despite the use of what some may consider to be strange ingredients the cocktail is enjoyable, and has been described as tart with the added syrup giving the drink complexity, and the egg white providing body as well as a foamy head.<ref name="thespiritworld.net" /><ref name="underhill-lounge.flannestad.com">Underhill-Lounge, "Clover Club Cocktail" July 2008.({{cite web |url=http://underhill-lounge.flannestad.com/2008/07/14/clover-club-cocktail/ |title=Underhill-Lounge » Clover Club Cocktail |accessdate=2009-11-27 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20080829134820/http://underhill-lounge.flannestad.com/2008/07/14/clover-club-cocktail/ |archivedate=2008-08-29 }})</ref>

Despite its origination in the fashionable Clover Club, the 1930s ''The Home Bartender's Guide'' recommended it for "Tuesday Afternoon Sewing Club" and "Crazy-Quilting Parties," suggesting a change in status that might have led to its decline.<ref>{{Cite web|title=1930 The Home Bartender's Guide and Song Book|url=https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1930-The-Home-Bartender-s-Guide-and-Song-Book|access-date=2021-11-30|website=euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz}}</ref>

== Preparation and variations ==
[[File:Clover Club.jpg|thumb|A Clover Club cocktail served at Rye in [[San Francisco]]]]
The drink can be a complex one to make due to the extra steps involved to get the head of foam on top of the drink.  Several sources recommend that the drink be "dry shaken" (shaken without ice) with one source suggesting this be done for at least a minute.<ref name="agrandioseblog.com"/><ref name="underhill-lounge.flannestad.com"/>  At this point ice should be added to the shaker to chill and dilute the drink. As of December 2014, Brooklyn's Clover Club restaurant used a traditional recipe of gin, dry vermouth, lemon, raspberry and egg white.<ref>[http://www.cloverclubny.com/cocktails/ Clover Club Restaurant, New York: Cocktails] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141227101222/http://www.cloverclubny.com/cocktails/ |date=2014-12-27 }}</ref>

There are several variations of this drink with the most common replacing the raspberry syrup with [[grenadine]] or [[Redcurrant sauce|red currant syrup]].<ref name="underhill-lounge.flannestad.com"/>

== Cultural impact ==
A [[Vocaloid]] producer by the name of {{Lang|ja|ゆうゆ}} (Yuuyu) has a song featuring [[初音ミク]] (Hatsune Miku) named after this cocktail, "{{Lang|ja|クローバー♣クラブ}}" (Clover♣Club) in which she describes the recipe.<ref>{{cite web |title=Clover♣Club 【Hatsune Miku】（Original）  |url=https://www.nicovideo.jp/watch/sm1937053 |website=Niconico |date=3 January 2008 |access-date=16 September 2021}}</ref>

"How long has it been since I’ve heard anyone order a Clover Club. They were quite wicked. Not as bad as a Martini, but much more deceptive." - from "The Late, Late Show," short story by John O’Hara, collected in his "Waiting for Winter," 1966, also in an O’Hara collection, "The New York Stories", 2013

Corpse reviver:
{{short description|Family of cocktails intended for curing hangovers}}

The '''corpse reviver''' family of named cocktails are sometimes drunk as alcoholic [[hangover]] tongue-in-cheek "cures", of potency or characteristics to be able to revive even a dead person. Some corpse reviver cocktail recipes have been lost to time,<ref>{{cite web |title=A short history of the corpse reviver |url=https://kindredcocktails.com/article/tis-pity-shes-corpse |website=kindredcocktails.com |access-date=1 February 2019 |archive-date=19 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210119181251/https://kindredcocktails.com/article/tis-pity-shes-corpse |url-status=dead }}</ref> but several variations commonly thought to be tied to the American Bar at the [[Savoy_Hotel#Bars|Savoy Hotel]] remain, especially those espoused by [[Harry Craddock]] that originally date back to at least 1930<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.smallscreennetwork.com/video/434 |title=Corpse Reviver – The Cocktail Spirit with Robert Hess -- Small Screen Network™ |access-date=2011-08-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716093248/http://www.smallscreennetwork.com/video/434 |archive-date=2011-07-16 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and are still being made.<ref>[http://ohgo.sh/archive/corpse-revivers/ The Corpse Reviver family of cocktails » Cocktail adventures at Oh Gosh!]</ref> Many "reviver" variations exist and the word is sometimes used as a generic moniker for any morning-after cocktail, also known as a "[[hair of the dog]]".

==History==
The use of the words "corpse reviver" to describe a mixed drink appears in literature as early as an issue of ''[[Punch (magazine)|Punch]]'' in 1861.<ref>{{cite journal|journal=Punch|date=21 Dec 1861|volume=41|page=247|title=A Smash for a Sensationist|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zpBIAAAAYAAJ&pg=RA1-PA247|last1=Lemon|first1=Mark|last2=Mayhew|first2=Henry|last3=Taylor|first3=Tom|last4=Brooks|first4=Shirley|last5=Burnand|first5=Francis Cowley|last6=Seaman|first6=Owen}}</ref> A recipe appeared in the ''Gentleman's Table Guide'' in 1871 that called for 1/2 a wine glass of brandy, 1/2 a wine glass of [[Maraschino]], and two dashes of [[Boker's Bitters]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Gentleman's Table Guide |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iD8CAAAAQAAJ |website=googlebooks.com |access-date=6 February 2019|last1 = Ricket|first1 = E.|last2 = Thomas|first2 = C.|year = 1871}}</ref> A recipe for a cocktail called the ''Criterion Reviver'' appeared in 1875 in Leo Engel's ''American and Other Drinks'' bar guide.<ref name=Engel>{{cite book |last1=Engel |first1=Leo |title=American & Other Drinks |date=1875 |publisher=Crerar & Smith |location=London |page=70}}</ref> Another recipe from 1903 for a ''Corpse Reviver'' made it as a fancy [[layered drink|pousse-café]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Whitehead|first1=Jessup Whitehead|title=The steward's handbook and guide to party catering|date=1903|page=305|publisher=J. Whitehead & Co.|url=https://archive.org/stream/stewardshandboo00whitgoog#page/n316/mode/2up}}</ref>

== Corpse reviver #1==
{{Infobox drink
| name        = Corpse reviver #1   
| type        = [[List of cocktails|Cocktail]]
| ingredients ={{plainlist|* 2 parts [[Cognac (brandy)|cognac]]
* 1 part [[apple brandy]] or [[Calvados (brandy)|Calvados]]
* 1 part sweet [[vermouth]]}}
| served      = [[Straight up]]: chilled, without ice
| prep        = Shake well and strain into cocktail glass.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Craddock |first1=Harry |title=The Savoy Cocktail Book |date=1930 |publisher=Constable & Company Ltd. |location=London |page=51}}</ref>
| drinkware   = [[Cocktail glass]]
}}

The first widely popularized corpse reviver cocktail is listed in ''[[The Savoy Cocktail Book]]'' and is a cognac-based cocktail that calls for two parts cognac, one part [[Calvados (brandy)|Calvados]] or apple brandy, and one part Italian vermouth. In bartender Craddock's notes he says "To be taken before 11AM, or whenever steam or energy is needed".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Craddock |first1=Harry |title=Savoy Cocktail Book |date=1934 |page=51}}</ref>

Bartender [[Trader_Vic's|Victor Bergeron]] (AKA Trader Vic) lists the corpse reviver #1 with the same ingredients and calls for twisting a lemon peel over the drink.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Vic |first1=Trader |title=Bartender's Guide |date=1947 |publisher=Garden City Books |location=New York |page=69}}</ref>

The 1956 edition of ''The Official Mixers Manual'' by Patrick Gavin Duffy lists the same ingredients.
{{clear|right}}

== Corpse reviver #2 and #2A==

{{Infobox drink
| name        = Corpse reviver #2
| image       = Corpse_Reviver_2.jpg  
| caption     = A corpse reviver #2 
| type        = [[List of cocktails|Cocktail]]
| ingredients ={{plainlist|*30 ml gin
*30 ml lemon juice
*30 ml [[Cointreau]]
*30 ml Lillet Blanc
*1 dash [[absinthe]]}}
| served      = [[Straight up]]: chilled, without ice
| prep        = Shake ingredients together in a [[cocktail shaker|mixer]] with ice. Strain into chilled glass. Garnish with orange zest.
| drinkware   = [[Cocktail glass]]
}}

The corpse reviver #2 as described in the ''Savoy Cocktail Book'' is the most commonly drunk of the corpse revivers, and consists of equal parts gin, lemon juice, [[Curaçao (liqueur)|curaçao]] (commonly [[Cointreau]]), [[Kina Lillet]] (now usually replaced with [[Cocchi Americano]], as a closer match to Kina Lillet than modern [[Lillet Blanc]]), and a dash of [[absinthe]]. The dash of absinthe can either be added to the mix before shaking, or added to the cocktail glass and moved around until the glass has been coated with a layer of absinthe to give a subtle absinthe aroma and flavor to the drink.<ref>[http://nashville.metromix.com/bars-and-clubs/article/absinthe-is-back-at/1796593/content Absinthe is back at the bar | Metromix Nashville]</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.smallscreennetwork.com/video/434 |title=Corpse Reviver – The Cocktail Spirit with Robert Hess -- Small Screen Network™ |access-date=2011-08-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716093248/http://www.smallscreennetwork.com/video/434 |archive-date=2011-07-16 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The Savoy №2 recipe noted that "Four of these taken in swift succession will unrevive the corpse again."<ref>{{cite web |title=In Search of the Ultimate Corpse Reviver |url=https://punchdrink.com/articles/ultimate-best-corpse-reviver-no-2-chartreuse-cocktail-recipe/ |website=punchdrink.com |access-date=2 February 2019}}</ref>

Both the original and the revised ''[[Trader Vic|Trader Vic's Bartenders Guide]]'' list the corpse reviver #2 the same as the Savoy, but substitutes [[punsch|Swedish Punsch]] for the Kina Lillet.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Vic |first1=Trader |title=Bartender's Guide |date=1947 |publisher=Garden City Books |location=New York |page=116}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Vic |first1=Trader |title=Trader Vic's Bartenders Guide, Revised |date=1972 |publisher=[[Doubleday_(publisher)]] |location=Garden City, NY |edition=revised}}</ref> In his notes he indicates that Kina Lillet may be substituted for the Swedish punsch, so he was likely aware of the Savoy version in both of his editions. In Patrick Duffy's 1956 ''Official Mixers Manual'' he lists the corpse reviver #2 as employing punsch and does not mention Lillet.<ref> Duffy, Gavin: ''Official Mixer’s Manual''. Garden City Books, revised and enlarged by James A. Beard, New York (1956), Page 40.</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Corpse Reviver Cocktails – Recipes and History |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/1172/cocktails/corpse-reviver-cocktails-recipes-and-history |website=diffordsguide.com |access-date=1 February 2019}}</ref> The use of punsch can also be found in Crosby Gaige's ''Cocktail Guide and Ladies Companion''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gaige |first1=Crosby |title=Cocktail Guide and Ladies Companion |date=1941 |publisher=Fireside Pres |location=New York |page=98}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Corpse Reviver |url=http://cocktailvirgin.blogspot.com/2016/01/corpse-reviver.html |website=cocktailvirgin.blogspot.com |date=21 January 2016 |access-date=1 February 2019}}</ref>

In the 21st century punsch is less likely to be stocked in most bars, and so a corpse reviver #2 made with punsch is sometimes differentiated by referencing it as a corpse reviver #2A,<ref>{{cite web |title=Ode To Corpse Reviver: Corpse Reviver 2A |url=http://cocktailquest.blogspot.com/2011/06/ode-to-corpse-reviver-no-2-version-2a.html |website=cocktailquest.blogspot.com |date=2 June 2011 |access-date=1 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Corpse Reviver 2a |url=http://www.twoatthemost.com/bluecoat-gin-and-the-corpse-reviver-no-2a/ |website=twoatthemost.com |access-date=1 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Corpse Reviver #2A |url=http://www.barnotes.co/recipes/corpse-reviver-2a |website=barnotes.co |access-date=1 February 2019 |archive-date=16 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210716192441/http://www.barnotes.co/recipes/corpse-reviver-2a |url-status=dead }}</ref> even though it will remain listed in some historical cocktail books as only the №2 or as a №2 with annotations.<ref>{{cite web |title=Corpse Reviver #2 (Duffy) |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2617/corpse-reviver-no2-duffys-recipe |website=diffordsguide.com |access-date=1 February 2019}}</ref> 

A corpse reviver with punsch is also sometimes referenced as a corpse reviver #3,<ref>{{cite web |title=Corpse Reviver #3 |url=https://www.absolutdrinks.com/en/drinks/corpse-reviver-no-3/ |website=absolut.com |access-date=1 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Corpse Reviver |url=http://www.drinkoftheweek.com/drink_recipes/corpse-reviver-3/#axzz5eHvvVVxR |website=drinkoftheweek.com |access-date=1 February 2019 |archive-date=16 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210716202459/http://www.drinkoftheweek.com/drink_recipes/corpse-reviver-3/#axzz5eHvvVVxR |url-status=dead }}</ref> but other guides use the №3 to instead mean a later Savoy version<ref>{{cite book |last1=Calabrese |first1=Salvator |title=Classic Cocktails |url=https://archive.org/details/classiccocktails0000cala |url-access=registration |date=1997 |publisher=Sterling |location=New York |page=[https://archive.org/details/classiccocktails0000cala/page/102 102]|isbn=9780806905075 }}</ref> that uses [[Fernet-Branca]]. When differentiated, the №2A nomenclature is more frequently used.

{{clear|right}}

==Savoy corpse reviver (Fernet)==
{{Infobox drink
| name        = Savoy corpse reviver   
| type        = [[List of cocktails|Cocktail]]
| ingredients ={{plainlist|*1 part [[brandy]]
*1 part [[Fernet Branca]]
*1 part white [[crème de menthe]]}}
| served      = [[Straight up]]: chilled, without ice
| prep        = Shake ingredients together with ice, and strain into a glass.
| drinkware   = [[Cocktail glass]]
}}
This recipe was a new variation at the Savoy's [[Savoy_Hotel#Bars|American Bar]] that employed Fernet-Branca as an ingredient, coming almost two decades after the corpse reviver appeared in the ''Savoy Cocktail Book'' with its #1 and #2 variations. Salvatore Calabrese states in his book ''Classic Cocktails'' that it was created by Johnny Johnson of the Savoy circa 1948, and lists it as a corpse reviver #3. Others believe it was invented later in 1954 by [[Joe Gilmore]], also of the Savoy.<ref>{{cite web |title=Savoy Corpse Reviver |url=http://www.lostsaloon.com/mixology/savoy-corpse-reviver-yet-another-corpse-reviver-recipe/ |website=lostsaloon.com |date=18 May 2016 |access-date=1 February 2019}}</ref>

Besides Calabrese, the Fernet version is sometimes categorized by others as the corpse reviver #3,<ref>{{cite web |title=The Corpse Revier Number 3 |url=http://thruthemixingglass.blogspot.com/2013/02/the-corpse-reviver-3.html |website=thruthemixingglass.com |date=9 February 2013 |access-date=1 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Corpse reviver #3 recipe |url=http://www.drinksmixer.com/drink6918.html |website=drinksmixer.com |access-date=1 February 2019 |archive-date=2 February 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190202042058/http://www.drinksmixer.com/drink6918.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> but it is not standardized and it is sometimes referenced as the №4.<ref>{{cite web |title=Corpse Reviver |url=https://www.thespruceeats.com/corpse-reviver-no-2-recipe-760015 |website=spruceeats.com |access-date=1 February 2019}}</ref>
{{clear|right}}

==Criterion reviver==

Leo Engel's 1875 reviver cocktail, the ''criterion reviver'', used an early version of bottled mineral water and carbonic acid to make a medicinal "encore" cocktail that included the directions to "drink while effervescing".<ref name=Engel/> Engel served the reviver cocktail while a bartender at the [[Criterion_Restaurant|Criterion Hotel's]] ''American Bar'', which some view as the first American-style cocktail bar in London.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Tarling |first1=W.J. |title=Cafe Royal Cocktail Book |publisher=Pall Mall Ltd. |location=London |page=preface |edition=Coronation}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The Return of the Cocktail |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/life-style/food-and-drink/features/cooler-shakers-the-return-of-the-cocktail-2142704.html |website=www.independent.co.uk |date=23 October 2011 |access-date=5 February 2019}}</ref> The drink called for:
*a bottle of Taunus water (naturally sparkling mineral water from the Grosskarben springs near [[Frankfurt]])
*glass and a half of Encore Whiskey (defunct brand)
*dash of brandy bitters

==Cafe Royal revivers==

The 1937 ''Cafe Royal Cocktail Book'', by W.J. Tarling, listed four different reviver cocktails.  These included a ''corpse reviver'' that called for a glass filled with brandy, orange juice, and lemon juice, topped off with champagne, as well as recipes for a ''new corpse reviver'', a ''stomach reviver'', and ''Godfrey's corpse reviver'' (attributed to Godfrey Baldini). The index indicated that the book did not have enough space for two other reviver cocktails to be fully listed, including one called a ''Corpse Reviver Liqueur''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Tarling |first1=W.J. |title=Cafe Royal Cocktail Book |publisher=Pall Mall Ltd. |location=London |page=preface |edition=Coronation}}</ref>

==In popular culture==

*In "The Handoff", the second episode of the seventh season of ''[[Archer (season 7)|Archer]]'', Veronica Deane orders a corpse reviver #2, but only if real absinthe is available.
*In [[Patrick deWitt]]'s novel ''[[French Exit (novel)|French Exit]]'', the main characters each drink a corpse reviver #2 prior to performing a séance.
*In [[Damien Chazelle]]'s 2022 film ''[[Babylon (2022 film)|Babylon]]'', Jack Conrad orders a corpse reviver then proceeds to give instructions on how to make one.

The '''espresso martini''', also known as a '''vodka espresso''', is a cold [[caffeinated alcoholic drink]] made with [[espresso]], [[coffee liqueur]], and [[vodka]]. It is not a true [[Martini (cocktail)|martini]] as it contains neither [[gin]] nor [[vermouth]], but is one of many [[List of drinks that that use the word martini|drinks that incorporate the term ''martini'' into their names]].

==Origin==
There are several claims for the origin of the espresso martini. One of the more common claims<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gq-magazine.co.uk/article/espresso-martini-vodka-cocktail |title=Shot in the dark: beware the espresso martini |last=Blythe |first=Thomas |date=July 23, 2012 |website=GQ UK |publisher=Condé Nast |access-date=January 27, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Parkhill |first=Chad |date=November 4, 2016 |title=Why is Australia so obsessed with the espresso martini? | url=https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2016/nov/05/why-is-australia-so-obsessed-with-the-espresso-martini |newspaper=The Guardian |location=London, England |access-date=January 27, 2017}}</ref> is that it was created by [[Dick Bradsell]] in the 1980s in [[London]] for a young woman who asked for "something to wake me up, then fuck me up".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-07-23 |title=An oral history on the espresso martini |url=https://www.gq-magazine.co.uk/article/espresso-martini-vodka-cocktail |access-date=2023-12-15 |website=British GQ |language=en-GB}}</ref> The bar where it was invented is identified as Soho Brasserie, which would date it as circa 1983, while Bradsell never identified the woman in question, only referring to her as a "top model" or an American model.<ref name="diffords">{{cite web |url=http://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/615/cocktails/vodka-espresso-espresso-martini |title=Vodka Espresso/Espresso Martini |author=Simon Difford |date=2017|website=Difford's Guide |access-date=January 27, 2017}}</ref> The woman is rumored to be [[Marie Helvin]], who was a noted American model in London at the time.<ref name="diffords" /> Later claims that the woman was [[Naomi Campbell]] or [[Kate Moss]] are implausible, as they were too young at the time.<ref name="diffords" />

Bradsell has claimed to have invented it in a widely-circulated video.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eqO-S-1PHzo |title=Dick Bradsell and his Vodka Espresso |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |date=April 24, 2011 |website=YouTube |access-date=January 27, 2017 |quote=London's Cocktail Guru Dick Bradsell has a brief interview with Kasia Olszko; Then Uncle Dick makes a Vodka Espresso, followed by a Vodka Martini.}}</ref> Bradsell has also been quoted about the circumstances of his invention of the drink, "The coffee machine at the Soho Brasseries was right next to the station where I served drinks. It was a nightmare, as there were coffee grounds everywhere, so coffee was very much on my mind. And it was all about vodka back then – it was all people were drinking."<ref name="diffords" /><ref>{{cite news |last=Hatchman  |first=John |date=August 25, 2016 |title=Spirit of the Month – Mr Black Cold Press Coffee Liqueur |url=http://www.thelondoneconomic.com/food-drink/spirit-of-the-month-mr-black-cold-press-coffee-liqueur/25/08/ |newspaper=The London Economic |location=The London Economic |access-date=January 27, 2017}}</ref>

==Recipes==
The recipes for an espresso martini vary depending on the source. Traditionally, they include [[Kahlúa]] or [[Tia Maria]].

===Difford's Guide===
Difford's Guide recommends {{convert|1.5|USoz|mL}}<!-- Difford's uses US oz --> of vodka, {{convert|1|USoz|mL}} of hot espresso coffee, and {{convert|2/3|USoz|mL}} of [[coffee liqueur]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/725/espresso-martini |title=Espresso Martini |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |website=Difford's Guide |access-date=October 11, 2021}}</ref> The ingredients are poured into a shaker filled with ice. The mixture is then shaken, fine strained and poured into a chilled [[cocktail glass|martini glass]]. The drink is garnished with coffee beans (and perhaps a twist of lemon zest) and served.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.liquor.com/recipes/espresso-martini-2/ |title=Espresso Martini |last=Newman |first=Kara |date=2016 |website=Liquor.com |access-date=January 27, 2017 |archive-date=November 27, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201127085519/https://www.liquor.com/recipes/espresso-martini-2/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Cloak |first=Felicity |date=December 28, 2016 |title=How to make the perfect espresso martini |url=https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/wordofmouth/2016/dec/28/how-to-make-the-perfect-espresso-martini |newspaper=The Guardian |location=London, England |access-date=January 27, 2017}}</ref>

==Popularity==
The drink had a surge in popularity in the early 2020s.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Sidman |first1=Jessica |title=The Espresso Martini—the Grown-Up Red Bull and Vodka—Is Back |url=https://www.washingtonian.com/2021/06/11/the-espresso-martini-the-grown-up-red-bull-and-vodka-is-back/ |access-date=13 October 2021 |work=Washingtonian |date=11 June 2021}}</ref> This popularity was met with apprehension by bartenders due to the time and effort required to prepare the drink.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Crowley |first1=Chris |title=The Espresso Martini Is the Hottest Drink on the Planet. Bartenders Hate It. |url=https://www.grubstreet.com/2021/10/why-bartenders-hate-espresso-martinis.html |access-date=13 October 2021 |work=Grub Street |date=7 October 2021 |language=en-us}}</ref>

== Variants ==
There can be slight twists made to the classic espresso martini recipe. Examples include adding [[Cointreau]] and chocolate sauce to make a Chocolate Orange Espresso Martini,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Chocolate Orange Espresso Martini |url=https://ramsbury.com/chocolate-orange-espresso-martini/ |access-date=2024-05-07 |website=Ramsbury |language=en-US |archive-date=2024-08-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240803010351/https://ramsbury.com/chocolate-orange-espresso-martini/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> or adding marshmallow syrup to make a Toasted Marshmallow Espresso Martini.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Spurr |first=Roger |date=2023-11-09 |title=Easy Toasted Marshmallow Espresso Martini Recipe |url=https://thehomecocktail.club/2023/11/09/toasted-marshmallow-espresso-martini/ |access-date=2024-05-07 |website=The Home Cocktail Club |language=en-US}}</ref>

Chris McHale (born 20th century) is an American creative enthusiast credited in popular lore with the invention of the espresso martini on the rocks in 2019 at the Smith & Wollensky steakhouse in Boston, Massachusetts. Although not formally trained as a mixologist, McHale’s improvisational request at the bar led to the widespread popularity of a variation of the classic espresso martini served over ice rather than shaken and strained.

The '''between the sheets''' is a cocktail consisting of [[white rum]] (or other [[light rum]]),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.liquor.com/recipes/between-the-sheets/|title=Classics With a Twist: Between the Sheets|first=Allen|last=Katz|website=Liquor.com}}</ref> [[cognac]], [[triple sec]], and [[lemon juice]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Between the Sheets|url=http://www.iba-world.com/index.php?option=com_content&id=190&Itemid=532|publisher=International Bartenders Association|access-date=March 25, 2015}}</ref> When made with [[gin]], instead of rum and cognac, it's called a "'''maiden's prayer'''".

==History==
The origin of the cocktail is usually credited to [[Harry MacElhone]] at [[Harry's New York Bar]] in [[Paris]] in the 1930s as a derivative of the [[sidecar (cocktail)|sidecar]].<ref name=ifood>{{cite web|title=Between the Sheets|url=http://ifood.tv/drink/between-the-sheets/about|website=ifood.tv|access-date=March 25, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Between the Sheets|url=http://www.hennessy.com/us/recipes/between-sheets/|publisher=Hennessy Cognac|access-date=March 25, 2015|archive-date=August 27, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160827132811/http://www.hennessy.com/us/recipes/between-sheets/|url-status=dead}}</ref> However, competing theories exist that claim the cocktail was created at [[The Berkeley]] in approximately 1921, or in French [[brothel]]s as an [[Apéritif and digestif|apéritif]] for consumption by the prostitutes.<ref name=ifood/><ref>{{cite web|title=Between the Sheets|url=https://www.drinkadvisor.com/en/cocktails/547-between-the-sheets.html|publisher=Drink Advisor|access-date=March 25, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150919003446/https://www.drinkadvisor.com/en/cocktails/547-between-the-sheets.html|archive-date=2015-09-19|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Variations==
The drink is similar to the [[sidecar (cocktail)|sidecar]], differing only by using less cognac and adding rum. The maiden's prayer is variously known as an alternate name for the between the sheets, and as a different drink using [[gin]] instead of rum and cognac, and adding orange juice to the lemon juice.<ref name=ifood /><ref>{{cite web|last1=Clarke|first1=Paul|title=Time for a Drink: the Maiden's Prayer|url=http://www.seriouseats.com/recipes/2010/06/time-for-a-drink-the-maidens-prayer.html|publisher=Serious Eats|access-date=March 25, 2015|date=June 4, 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Wondrich|first1=David|title=Maiden's Prayer|url=http://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/recipes/a3730/maidens-prayer-drink-recipe/|work=[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]|access-date=March 25, 2015|date=November 5, 2007}}</ref>

The '''French Martini''' is a cocktail made with [[vodka]], raspberry [[liqueur]], and pineapple juice.<ref name="Barker Puente Yancey Martini gets French twist">{{cite news |id={{ProQuest|408847507}} |title=Martini gets French twist with a splash of Chambord |first1=Olivia |last1=Barker |first2=Maria |last2=Puente |first3=Kitty Bean |last3=Yancey |newspaper=USA TODAY |date=31 August 2001 |page=D.01 }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=French Martini Cocktail Recipe |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/en-au/cocktails/recipe/798/french-martini |access-date=2025-05-28 |website=www.diffordsguide.com }}</ref> It is shaken with ice and strained into a [[Cocktail glass|martini glass]] or coupe glass, then garnished with a pineapple wedge or a raspberry.<ref name=":1" /> The drink is sweet and fruity, suitable as either a pre-dinner aperitif or a post-dinner digestif. While called a "martini," it does not contain gin or vermouth, instead belonging to the category of modern fruit-based cocktails.<ref name=":7">{{cite magazine |id={{ProQuest|2786802550}} |title=The French Martini |magazine=Esquire |date=August 2001 |page=86 }}</ref>

The French Martini is typically served in a V-shaped glass (such as a martini or coupe glass), though it bears little resemblance to a [[Martini (cocktail)|classic martini]],<ref name=":1" /> and includes [[vodka]] and raspberry liqueur. Its flavour profile is characterized by a smooth, medium-bodied balance—neither overly sweet nor excessively tart.<ref name=":1" /> Since its emergence, the cocktail has gained recognition as a popular modern creation within the new-era cocktail category.<ref name="Barker Puente Yancey Martini gets French twist"/> Numerous variations exist, with adjustments to ingredient ratios (e.g., vodka-to-liqueur proportions), alternative fruit components (such as substituting other tropical juices), or the use of different liqueurs to alter its sweetness or complexity.<ref name=":1" />

== History ==
The French Martini was created in the late 1980s by [[Keith McNally]], a New York City bar owner.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=French Martini Cocktail Recipe: How to Make a French Martini |url=https://www.barschool.net/recipes/french-martini |access-date=2025-05-28 |website=European Bartender School }}</ref> The cocktail gained traction after 1996, when bartender [[Dale DeGroff]] added it to the menu of a prominent New York bar, accelerating its popularity. By 1997–1998, the drink appeared in London establishments under the name "Fresh Fruit Martinis", reflecting its fruity profile. In the December 1998 issue of CLASS magazine, editor Simon Difford praised the French Martini in his editorial column, calling it a personal favourite. Capitalising on its rising fame, UK distributors of [[Chambord (liqueur)|Chambord]] (raspberry liqueur) and [[Absolut Vodka]] collaborated with CLASS to feature advertisements for the cocktail in CLASS starting that December,<ref name=":1" /> with campaigns running in subsequent monthly issues. This marketing effort solidified its status as a signature drink of the era.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=2018-07-21 |title=French Martini - Art of Drink |url=https://www.artofdrink.com/cocktail/french-martini |access-date=2025-05-28 }}</ref>

Despite its name, the French Martini does not have historical roots in France nor direct connections to the classic Martini. Instead, the term "French" was applied primarily due to the use of French raspberry liqueur during the 1990s,<ref name=":2" /> in which cocktails were labelled with exotic or geographic identifiers to appeal to aspirational and international sensibilities. The drink's rise was aided by a broader industry effort to market vodka and liqueur-based cocktails as modern, luxurious, and culturally sophisticated. This approach was particularly successful among younger and more diverse consumers seeking alternatives to traditional spirits and beer.<ref name=":4">{{cite journal |last1=Parkhill |first1=Chad |title=Vermouth |journal=The Lifted Brow |date=9 November 2020 |issue=12 |pages=20–23 |url=https://search.informit.org/doi/abs/10.3316/informit.791363477856227 }}</ref>

== Flavour ==
The French Martini is widely credited with sparking the flavoured martini trend, inspiring variations such as lychee, watermelon, and apple martinis. A notable example is "Liquid Love" by bartender Luis Bruce at Cruise Bar, blending fresh muddled watermelon shaken with ice, [[Frangelico]] (hazelnut liqueur), [[Tia Maria]] (coffee liqueur), and watermelon liqueur. This innovation exemplifies the creative adaptations driven by the French Martini's influence, emphasising fruit-forward flavours and unconventional liqueur pairings within the modern cocktail landscape.<ref name=":5">{{cite news |id={{ProQuest|759754544}} |title=Forbidden fruit of the martini rebels: Cocktail |last1=Connolly |first1=Ellen |newspaper=Sydney Morning Herald |date=26 October 2010 |page=26 }}</ref>

The cocktail gained international popularity in the late 1990s and early 2000s,<ref name=":1" /> it featured prominently in upscale bars and lounges. French Martini became a key symbol of the "Martini craze,"<ref name=":6">{{cite book |doi=10.4324/9781003184836 |title=Drinks in Vogue |date=2023 |last1=Inglis |first1=David |last2=Ho |first2=Hang Kei |isbn=978-1-003-18483-6 }}{{page needed|date=May 2025}}</ref> where drinks named after the classic Martini, became fashionable among urban consumers.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" /> Its popularity coincided with a period of rapid transformation in bar culture, where aesthetics, sweetness, and global branding played a role in drink selection.<ref name=":5" />

== Mixology ==
A recipe from Darcy O'Neil in 2018 is as follows:<ref name=":3" />

"Ingredients:

2 oz Vodka

½ oz Chambord

2 ½ oz Pineapple Juice

=== Instructions ===
In a [[Cocktail shaker|Boston shaker]] half full of ice, add all ingredients.

Shake vigorously for at least 20 seconds.

Strain into a martini glass.

Garnish with a lemon twist.

=== Notes ===
Vigorous shaking plays a crucial role in the French Martini’s appeal. When shaken with sufficient force, typically for around 20 seconds, the pineapple juice creates a light, frothy texture on the surface of the cocktail. This not only enhances the mouthfeel but also contributes to the drink’s signature soft pink hue, which adds to its visual allure. The extended shaking time also ensures that the drink is thoroughly chilled, achieving the ideal serving temperature.<ref name=":3" />

Additionally, while the standard recipe includes vodka, raspberry liqueur, and pineapple juice, bartenders often personalize the cocktail by adjusting the ratios of these ingredients. These modifications allow for variations in sweetness, alcohol strength, and the prominence of fruit flavors, resulting in a drink that can be tailored to individual preferences or the style of a particular venue.<ref name=":3" />

=== Other ratios ===
Some common ratios are as below (Vodka : Liqueur : Pineapple juice)

* 4:2:1<ref name=":7"/>
* 2:1:3<ref name=":5" /><ref>{{cite news |id={{ProQuest|2813065131}} |title=World Cocktail Day 2023: Easy beverage ideas & recipes including Kraken Dark 'N' Stormy & French Martini |last1=Millar |first1=Will |newspaper=The Scarborough News |date=12 May 2023 }}</ref>
* 4:1:3<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":8">{{Cite book |last=DeGroff |first=Dale |title=The Craft of the Cocktail: Everything You Need to Know to Be a Master Bartender, with 500 Recipes |date=2010 |publisher=Potter/Ten Speed/Harmony/Rodale |others=George Erml |isbn=978-0-307-76227-6 |location=Erscheinungsort nicht ermittelbar}}{{page needed|date=May 2025}}</ref>
* 3:1:3<ref name=":1" />
* 3:2:1<ref name=":1" />
* 1:1:2<ref name=":1" />
* 2:1:2<ref name=":2" />
* 8:1:4<ref>{{cite news |title=SHORT ORDERS |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/2001/07/06/short-orders/a3d21a49-6949-4d64-b7bc-cb5a663ef81d/ |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=6 July 2001 }}</ref>
* 1oz Vodka, 1/4oz Chambord, splash of pineapple juice, splash of apple cider.<ref>{{cite news |id={{ProQuest|2230124933}} |title=SHAKEN AND STIRRED; Romance in a Glass |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/01/19/style/shaken-and-stirred-romance-in-a-glass.html |work=The New York Times |date=19 January 2003 }}</ref>

The French Martini's recipe allows flexibility in ingredient selection and preparation. Vodka brands like [[Belvedere Vodka|Belvedere]],<ref name=":9">{{cite news |id={{ProQuest|2934135082}} |title=The White Horse does the French Martini |newspaper=Sydney Star Observer |date=8 November 2013 |page=25 }}</ref> Kremly,<ref name="Barker Puente Yancey Martini gets French twist"/> [[Grey Goose (vodka)|Grey Goose]],<ref name=":3" /> [[SKYY vodka|Skyy]],<ref name=":7" /> or [[Absolut Vodka|Absolut]]<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> subtly alter the drink's character. Bartenders may introduce unconventional elements, such as green apples (skin lightly dusted with fleur de sel) paired with a splash of apple cider, shaken vigorously to produce a frothy texture. Alternatively, raspberry liqueur can be swapped for watermelon liqueur or a mixed-berry infusion for varied fruit intensity. A sample iteration combines 30ml [[Belvedere Vodka|Belvedere]] Vodka, 15ml [[Chambord (liqueur)|Chambord]], 2 spoonfuls of stewed berry mix, and pineapple juice—shaken with ice and strained into a glass.<ref name=":9" /> These modifications demonstrate the cocktail's adaptability, enabling adjustments to sweetness, acidity, or herbal notes without deviating from its foundational structure.

=== Urban Oasis ===
Features dual vodkas—orange vodka.<ref name=":11" />
A detailed variation recipe:<ref name=":9" />

To prepare the cocktail syrup, combine two cups of sugar and two cups of water in a saucepan. Add summer berries—blueberries, raspberries, and strawberries are recommended for optimal flavour. Heat the mixture on high heat, stirring continuously until the sugar fully dissolves and the syrup thickens to a viscous consistency. Adjust sweetness by incorporating extra sugar if desired. Remove from heat, let the syrup cool on the stove, then refrigerate until thoroughly chilled. For serving, shake the syrup with ice and strain it into a chilled martini glass. This method ensures a balanced blend of fruit essence and sweetness, with the syrup's thickness enhancing the cocktail's texture. The recipe emphasises precision in syrup preparation to achieve a harmonious balance between tart berry notes and sugary richness.

== In popular culture ==

People always say that the drink was invented by [[Chambord (liqueur)|Chambord]],<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":5" /> a French raspberry Liqueur maker, [[Loire Valley]], and is broadly recognised as a marketing coup. Chambord is the drink's star attraction.<ref>{{cite magazine |id={{ProQuest|2047118965}} |title=Advertisement: CHAMBORD FRENCH MARTINI |magazine=Cosmopolitan |volume=233 |issue=5 |date=November 2002 |page=57 }}</ref>

=== Celebrity ===
[[Nicole Kidman]] inadvertently popularised a cocktail trend through her patronage of the Chambord French Martini. The drink gained traction as celebrities like [[Elizabeth Hurley]] and [[Cameron Diaz]] shifted preferences from the Cosmopolitan to this fruit-forward alternative.<ref name="Barker Puente Yancey Martini gets French twist"/>

[[Mark Wahlberg]], [[Joan Collins]], and [[Milla Jovovich]] publicly drank a French Martini at the opening of [[Man Ray (bar)|Man Ray]], a Parisian-themed New York restaurant co-owned by actors [[Johnny Depp]] and [[Sean Penn]]. Its popularity further surged as [[Sex and the City]] star [[Kim Cattrall]] vocalised her preference for the drink.<ref name="Barker Puente Yancey Martini gets French twist"/>

=== Controversies and identity negotiation ===
Debates over the Martini's "authenticity" revealed deeper cultural anxieties.<ref>{{Cite web |title=There Is Something about a Martini |url=https://www.americanheritage.com/there-something-about-martini |access-date=2025-05-28 |website=AMERICAN HERITAGE }}</ref> Traditionalists dismissed vodka-based variations as heretical. Purists argued that gin's botanical complexity was essential to the drink's identity. These disputes often masked class and generational tensions. Even the olive garnish sparked contention: purists rejected innovations like the "[[Martini (cocktail)|dirty Martini]]"(brine-added) as violations of the drink's "pure" modernist ethos.<ref name=":12">{{cite news |id={{ProQuest|2509185138}} |title=Real men drink Dirty Bananas… |last1=Lascelles |first1=Alice |work=FT.com |date=8 March 2021 }}</ref>

The Martini's reliance on European ingredients (French vermouth, Dutch gin) and its adoption by figures like Buñuel and Eliot underscored its transnational appeal.<ref name=":13">{{Cite book |title=The shaken and the stirred: the year's work in cocktail culture |date=2020 |publisher=Indiana University Press |isbn=978-0-253-04975-9 |editor-last=Schneider |editor-first=Stephen |series=The year's work: studies in fan culture and cultural theory |location=Bloomington, Indiana |editor-last2=Owens |editor-first2=Craig N.}}{{page needed|date=May 2025}}</ref> This duality—simultaneously American and cosmopolitan—allowed it to symbolize both national pride and elite cosmopolitanism.<ref name=":5" />

=== Cultural symbolism ===
The cocktail is the status of high art, it is called "the only American invention as perfect as a sonnet"—a comparison that framed it as both a technical achievement and a cultural export.<ref name=":13" />

== Gender and binary ==

=== Gendered aesthetics and marketing ===

[[File:Absinthe-cappiello.jpg|thumb|Advertisement poster of LIQUEUR MONT-CHRIST]]

The French Martini is often associated with femininity, a perception largely shaped by its distinct characteristics—namely, its sweet flavor, prominent fruit-forward notes, and eye-catching pink color.<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":8" /> These elements align with a long-standing marketing tradition in which cocktails that are lighter in taste, sweeter on the palate, or visually soft and delicate are classified and promoted as feminine. Such drinks are frequently framed as more appealing to women, reinforcing cultural ideas about gendered preferences in both flavor and presentation.<ref>{{cite thesis |last1=Bosco |first1=Anna |title=Diversity, Inclusion and the Cocktail Connection |date=2022 |url=https://vuir.vu.edu.au/id/eprint/44739 }}{{page needed|date=May 2025}}</ref>

=== Challenging binaries through cocktail evolution ===
By the 1980s and 1990s, beverages such as the French Martini began to challenge the prevailing binary framework that had traditionally defined gendered drinking practices.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Seaton |first1=Anthony V. |title=Cocktail Culture in the 1920s and 1930s: Prefiguring the Postmodern |journal=Hospitality Research Journal |date=February 1994 |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=35–52 |doi=10.1177/109634809401800204 }}</ref> Alcohol consumption among men—especially soldiers—was not merely tolerated but expected, symbolizing strength, camaraderie, and patriotic duty. Abstinence was sometimes seen as effeminate. Temperance advocates claimed that abstaining from alcohol was patriotic and virtuous. Yet alcohol remained pervasive in military life, and many veterans returned home believing that moderate drinking was fully compatible with patriotic masculinity.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Payne |first1=Brendan J. |title=At War with King Alcohol: Debating Drinking and Masculinity in the Civil War |journal=Civil War Book Review |date=2023 |volume=25 |issue=2 |doi=10.31390/cwbr.25.2.12 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

In this context, the French Martini became emblematic of a broader trend in which cocktails served not only as social commodities but also as instruments for expressing and reinterpreting gender identity. This development marked a departure from conventional classifications of drinks as inherently masculine or feminine, signaling an evolution in the cultural meanings attached to alcohol.<ref name=":15">{{Cite web |last=Dobson |first=Andrew |date=2024-04-26 |title=Best Gay Cocktail Recipes To Drink During Pride |url=https://dobbernationloves.com/food-drink/gay-drinks-pride-cocktails/ |access-date=2025-05-28 |website=dobbernationLOVES }}</ref>

Alcoholic beverages, particularly cocktails, continue to carry symbolic significance in contemporary societies. In recent years, cocktails have increasingly functioned as a medium for gender expression and experimentation. This shift reflects a broader cultural movement toward more fluid understandings of gender, allowing for representations that move beyond traditional masculine and feminine roles. As a result, cocktails have become part of a social landscape in which individuals may perform or explore a range of gender identities, contributing to evolving norms around consumption and self-presentation.<ref name=":16">{{Cite journal |last=Korostyshevsky |first=David |date=September 2024 |title=Megan L. Bever. At War with King Alcohol: Debating Drinking and Masculinity in the Civil War |journal=The Social History of Alcohol and Drugs |volume=38 |issue=2 |pages=371–373 |doi=10.1086/731925 }}</ref>

[[File:A French martini (2664064759).jpg|thumb|upright|"Girly drink"-French Martini]]
Post-2020 trends reveal a cultural shift: online searches for "girly drink" recipes surged, notably among male bartenders, reflecting a broader rejection of gender-binary norms in beverage preferences. The [[COVID-19 pandemic]]'s emphasis on personal exploration and comfort accelerated this change, with patrons and professionals alike embracing cocktails for flavour rather than gendered symbolism.<ref name=":5" /> The French Martini, with vodka, raspberry liqueur, and pineapple juice, now symbolises this evolving landscape, minimising divides between "masculine" austerity and "feminine" as mixology increasingly over outdated stereotypes.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":12" />

=== Shifts in cultural perception ===
Contemporary reinterpretations of the French Martini and other similarly styled cocktails have disrupted these traditional gender codes. Increasingly, these beverages are embraced in inclusive and queer spaces as playful, performative expressions of identity. This shift is evident in platforms like ''[[Queer]] Cocktails'', which celebrates cocktails not only as recipes but as symbols of gender diversity and self-expression.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Yates |first=Jonny |date=2021-07-26 |title=This Queer Cocktails book features amazing drinks inspired by LGBT+ icons – including Cider Minelli |url=https://www.thepinknews.com/2021/07/26/queer-cocktails-recipe-book-pride/ |access-date=2025-05-28 |website=PinkNews }}</ref> Similarly, lifestyle and travel platforms like ''Dobbernation Loves'' to promote flamboyant and colorful drinks, such as the French Martini, as affirmations of [[LGBTQ people|LGBTQ+]] pride.<ref name=":15" />

=== Academic reflections on gender constructs ===
Scholarship on alcohol and gender continues to highlight the limitations of binary frameworks. Misha Korostyshevsky, reviewing Megan L. Bever's work on 19th-century America, identifies how masculinity was often regulated through moral debates over alcohol use.<ref name=":16" /> While not directly focused on the French Martini, the broader cultural and social backdrop highlights the extent to which negotiating gender roles and societal expectations surrounding behavior. Over time, alcohol consumption has intersected with debates over appropriate conduct, identity performance, and the reinforcement or subversion of traditional gender norms. It positions it as a recurring arena for cultural expression and contestation. This historical context underlines how alcohol has long served as a battleground for gender and behavioral norms.<ref name=":16" />

Brian J Griffith's research shows how nationalism and masculinity were co-produced through state-sanctioned alcohol policies in France. He emphasizes that "effeminate" cocktails like the French Martini have historically been excluded from state-supported narratives of national identity and respectable masculinity.<ref name=":6" />

A '''bees knees''' (or '''bee's knees''') is a [[Prohibition in the United States|Prohibition era]] [[cocktail]] made with [[gin]], fresh [[lemon juice]],  and [[honey]]. It is served shaken and chilled, often with a [[lemon twist]]. 

The name comes from prohibition-era slang meaning "the best".<ref name="PPHL" />

==History==
The bee's knees cocktail has unclear origins. It was possibly invented by [[Frank Meier]], an Austrian-born, part Jewish bartender who was the first head bartender at the [[Hôtel Ritz Paris|Ritz in Paris]] in 1921, when its Cafe Parisian opened its doors.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Rothbaum |first1=Noah |title=Frank Meier, The Paris Ritz's Mysterious Bartender Spy |url=https://www.thedailybeast.com/frank-meier-the-paris-ritzs-mysterious-bartender-spy |website=The Daily Beast |date=2 August 2015 |publisher=The Daily Beast Company LLC |access-date=30 November 2020 }}</ref>

A 1929 news article attributes the cocktail to [[Margaret Brown]], an American socialite (the "Unsinkable" Molly Brown of [[Titanic]] fame).<ref name="Diffords">{{cite news |title=Bee's Knees Cocktail Recipe |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2144/bees-knees |access-date=6 January 2023 |work=www.diffordsguide.com |language=en}}</ref>

[[File:Bees Knees Cocktail.jpg|thumb|Bees knees cocktail with [[Barr Hill Gin]], honey, and lemon]]
In 2017, Barr Hill Gin started an annual event called Bee's Knees Week to promote their product. Bee's Knees Week is the largest sustainability event in the spirits industry, focused on pollinator protection.<ref name="HemenwayBridge2022">{{cite news |last1=Hemenway |first1=Cassandra |title=Barr Hill Expands, Pledges to Protect Pollinator Habitat |url=https://montpelierbridge.org/2022/10/barr-hill-expands-pledges-to-protect-pollinator-habitat/ |access-date=6 January 2023 |work=The [[Montpelier Bridge]] |date=4 October 2022}}</ref><ref name="Beeskneesweek">{{cite web |title=Bee's Knees Week 2022 – Caledonia Spirits |url=https://caledoniaspirits.com/bees-knees-week |access-date=6 January 2023 |archive-date=6 January 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230106185841/https://caledoniaspirits.com/bees-knees-week/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> A 2023 article published by ''[[The New York Times]]'' credited an increase in the cocktail's popularity in part to Bee's Knees Week.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Simonson |first1=Robert |title=Celebrating the Roaring 2020s With a Bee's Knees Cocktail |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/02/02/dining/drinks/bees-knees-cocktail.html |access-date=2 March 2023 |work=The New York Times |date=2 February 2023}}</ref>

==Variations==
* Several different gin brands are variously recommended, among them Barr Hill's for its honey infusion.<ref name="PPHL" />
* The honey may be diluted 1:1 with warm water to thin the consistency.<ref name="QAvenue">{{cite web|last1=Westfall|first1=JD|title=5 Prohibition Cocktails You Should Try|url=http://www.q-avenue.com/5-prohibition-cocktails-you-should-try/|website=Q Avenue|access-date=1 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160822015247/http://www.q-avenue.com/5-prohibition-cocktails-you-should-try/|archive-date=22 August 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> 
* The honey may be diluted 1:1 with simple syrup instead of water.<ref name="PPHL" />
* A sprig of basil or thyme may be used for garnish instead of lemon peel.<ref name="QAvenue" />
* Some variations contain orange juice.<ref name="Mental" />
* Add two dashes of [[absinthe]] and two dashes of orange bitters to make a variation called the "oldest living Confederate widow".<ref>{{cite web|last1=Deluna|first1=Dani|title=The Oldest Living Confederate Widow|url=https://homebargirl.com/2014/11/10/the-oldest-living-confederate-widow/|website=Home Bar Girl|access-date=20 December 2016|date=10 November 2014|archive-date=6 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210706154707/https://homebargirl.com/2014/11/10/the-oldest-living-confederate-widow/|url-status=live}}</ref>
