A '''mimosa''' [[cocktail]] consists of [[champagne]] (or other [[sparkling wine]]) and chilled citrus juice, usually [[orange juice]]. It is often served in a tall [[champagne flute]] at [[brunch]], or at festive occasions such as weddings, or as part of business or [[First class travel|first class]] service on some passenger railways and airlines.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.amtrak.com/content/dam/projects/dotcom/english/public/documents/menus/routes/Acela-Express-First-Class-Menus-0519.pdf|title=Acela Express First Class Menus.}}</ref>  The mixing ratio varies.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.southernliving.com/drinks/cocktails/champagne-cocktails|title=Creative Champagne Cocktails|website=Southern Living|language=en|access-date=2019-05-31}}</ref><ref name=EsquireClassicMimosa>{{Cite web|url=https://www.esquire.com/drinks/simple-mimosa-recipe|title=How to Make a Classic Mimosa|date=2018-03-07|website=Esquire|language=en-US|access-date=2019-05-31}}</ref>

== History ==
The cocktail is named after the bright yellow, fragrant flowers of the mimosa ''[[Acacia dealbata]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.esquire.com/drinks/mimosa-drink-recipe|title=Mimosa – Drink Recipe: How to Make the Perfect Mimosa|magazine=Esquire|first=Sylvie|last=Krekow|access-date=2012-08-02}}</ref> The origin of the cocktail is unclear, and was originally called a "champagne orange".<ref name=":15">{{Cite web |last=Moss |first=Robert |date=April 24, 2017 |title=How the Mimosa Became the Official Drink of Brunch |url=https://www.myrecipes.com/extracrispy/how-the-mimosa-became-the-official-drink-of-brunch |url-status=deviated |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180513204507/https://www.myrecipes.com/extracrispy/how-the-mimosa-became-the-official-drink-of-brunch |archive-date=May 13, 2018 |access-date=2022-04-29 |website=MyRecipes |language=en |quote=His 1934 cocktail book ''The Artistry Of Mixing Drinks'' includes the mimosa among its 300 recipes.... But Meier put a symbol—his initials inside a diamond—next to the cocktails he invented and there's no such mark next to the mimosa.}}</ref> Some credit the [[Paris Ritz]]'s bartender and cocktail writer Frank Meier for making the mimosa cocktail; however, Meier's 1934 book on mixing drinks, which has a special symbol for his inventions, does not use it for the mimosa.<ref name=":15" /> The mimosa can be considered as a variant of the cocktail [[Buck's Fizz]], or vice-versa; Buck's Fizz appears to date from 1921.<ref name=":15"/><ref name="Schuster">{{Cite book |last=Schuster |first=Amanda |url=https://londonist.com/london/drink/bucks-fizz-cocktail-created-bucks-club-mayfair |title=Signature Cocktails |publisher=Phaidon |year=2023 |access-date=25 December 2023 |via=londonist.com}}</ref> The [[International Bartenders Association]] simply says the mimosa is "Also known as Buck's Fizz".<ref name=MimosaIBA>{{cite web |url=https://iba-world.com/mimosa/ |title=Mimosa – Contemporary classics – IBA cocktail |access-date=December 12, 2022 |website=[[International Bartenders Association]]|date=29 April 2021 }}</ref> An alternate, yet less likely origin story points to San Francisco in the 1940s, crediting the legendary film director Sir Alfred Hitchcock. Known for his love of exquisite tastes, Hitchcock is thought to have either created or significantly popularized the mimosa in the United States, embedding it deeply into America's brunch culture, where it became popular in the United States in the 1960s.<ref name=":15"/> A news article published in the ''[[Sydney Morning Herald]]'' wrote about [[Queen Elizabeth II]] drinking a mimosa, introduced to her by [[Lord Mountbatten]] after his visit to the [[south of France]].<ref name=":15"/>

== Variations ==
[[Buck's Fizz]] is essentially the same cocktail,<ref name=":15"/><ref name=MimosaIBA/> said to have been invented in 1921 in London.<ref name="Schuster"/><ref name=Difford/> Some sources draw a distinction, saying the Buck's Fizz specifically uses twice as much champagne as orange juice while the mimosa should use equal proportions, that a Buck's Fizz should be served without ice and a mimosa should include ice, or that a Buck's Fizz should be served in a [[champagne flute|flute]] or [[champagne coupe|coupe]] and a mimosa should be served in an ordinary [[wine glass]].<ref name=Difford>{{Cite web|url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/1244/cocktails/bucks-fizz-and-mimosa-cocktails-history-recipes-and-tips|title=Buck's Fizz & Mimosa Cocktails – history & recipes|website=www.diffordsguide.com|language=en|access-date=2018-01-23}}</ref> However, some sources give instructions for making mimosas that clearly do not fit these characterizations.<ref name=EsquireClassicMimosa/>

Other ingredients are sometimes added, such as [[Grand Marnier]] or [[orange bitters]].<ref name=EsquireClassicMimosa/>

The ''[[Poinsettia (cocktail)|poinsettia]]'' is cranberry juice with champagne (sometimes with [[vodka]] and/or [[Cointreau]]).

The ''lemosa'' is lemonade with champagne, with a small amount of blueberry syrup.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Miyashiro|first=Lauren|date=2018-03-02|title=Lemon Blueberry Mimosas Are The Official Drink Of Spring|url=https://www.delish.com/cooking/recipe-ideas/recipes/a58461/lemosas-recipe/|access-date=2021-05-16|website=Delish|language=en-US}}</ref>

The ''Vermosa'' is [[apple cider]] with champagne, notably served in Vermont, United States.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2019-11-13|title=Apple Cider Mimosa aka Vermosa|url=https://www.dulcetscintilla.com/apple-cider-mimosa-aka-vermosa/|access-date=2021-05-16|website=Dulcet Scintilla|language=en-US}}</ref> Apple cider with champagne and brandy is called an ''apple crisp''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Apple Crisp Cocktail|url=https://www.foodnetwork.com/recipes/sandra-lee/apple-crisp-cocktail-recipe-1922628|access-date=2021-05-16|website=Food Network|language=en}}</ref>

The ''flirtini'' is made with pineapple juice, champagne and vodka.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2014-06-06|title=Flirtini – Pineapple Champagne Martini|url=https://www.willcookforsmiles.com/flirtini-pinapple-champagne-martini/|access-date=2021-05-16|website=Will Cook For Smiles|language=en-US}}</ref>

The ''megmosa''<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.epicurious.com/recipes/member/views/megmosa-589282276ad0bdd91204c551|title=Megmosa recipe {{!}} Epicurious.com|website=Epicurious|language=en-US|access-date=2018-01-23}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://food52.com/recipes/73379-megmosa|title=Megmosa Recipe on Food52|website=Food52|language=en|access-date=2018-01-23}}</ref> is a similar type of cocktail, composed of equal parts champagne and grapefruit juice.

The ''sherbet mimosa''<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |date=2019-03-05 |title=From Lychee to Lavender: Mimosa Recipes You'll Love |url=https://www.countryliving.com/food-drinks/g3073/mimosa-recipe/ |access-date=2022-05-13 |website=Country Living |language=en-US}}</ref> consists of champagne and a scoop of sherbet, instead of orange juice.

The ''lychee rose mimosa''<ref name=":2" /> consists of champagne with lychee and rosewater.

The ''Hawaiian mimosa''<ref name=":2" /> consists of rum, champagne, pineapple juice, orange juice, and cherry juice.

The ''[[Aigua de València|Valencian Water]]'' consists of cava or champagne, orange juice, vodka and gin.

== Popular culture ==
"National Mimosa Day" is an unofficial holiday observed on May 16 in the US.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date= |title=NATIONAL MIMOSA DAY – May 16 |url=https://www.nationaldaycalendar.com/national-day/national-mimosa-day-may-16 |access-date=2023-12-25 |website=National Day Calendar |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date= |title=National Mimosa Day |url=https://nationaltoday.com/national-mimosa-day/ |access-date=2023-12-25 |website=National Today |language=en-US}}</ref>

A '''lemon drop''' is a [[vodka]]-based [[cocktail]] that has a lemony, sweet and sour flavor, prepared using [[vodka]], [[triple sec]], and fresh lemon juice.<ref name="Lemon Drop Martini IBA"></ref> It has been described as a variant of, or as "a take on", the [[vodka martini]], but is in fact closer to a [[daisy (cocktail)|daisy]] or a [[White Lady (cocktail)|white lady]] variant.<ref name="Marszalek 2008" /> It is typically prepared and served [[Bartending terminology|straight up]] – chilled with ice and strained.

The drink was invented sometime in the 1970s by Norman Jay Hobday, the founder and proprietor of [[Henry Africa's]] bar in [[San Francisco]], California. Variations of the drink exist, such as blueberry and raspberry lemon drops, and some recipes that call for [[simple syrup]]. It is served at some bars and restaurants in the United States, and in such establishments in other areas of the world.<ref name="Marszalek 2008" />

==Overview==

A lemon drop is a [[cocktail]] with a lemony, sweet and sour flavor,<ref name="Saria 2013" /><ref name="Charming Bourgoin 2009" /> whereby the sweet and sour ingredients serve to contrast and balance one another.<ref name="Chirico 2015" /><ref name="Hellmich 2010" /> It is a [[vodka]]-based cocktail that is prepared with the addition of lemon juice and [[triple sec]].<ref name="Lemon Drop Martini IBA" /> Plain or citrus-[[Flavored liquor|flavored vodka]] may be used in its preparation, such as citron vodka.<ref name="Saria 2013" /><ref name="Marszalek 2008" /><ref name="San Antonio Express-News" /> Lemon-flavored vodka is also sometimes used.<ref name="Hellmich 2010" /><ref name="Gurliacci 2013" /> Lemon juice that has been freshly squeezed may be used,<ref name="San Antonio Express-News" /><ref name="Pavlides 2015" /> which can produce a superior drink compared to using commercially prepared lemon juice.<ref name="Charming Bourgoin 2009" /> Some versions are prepared using the juice from [[Meyer lemon]]s.<ref name="TheStarPress 2015" /><ref name="Aikman-Smith Lehr 2015" /><ref name="Stewart 2015" />

[[Cointreau]]-brand triple sec is used in some versions, and it may be prepared using a simple syrup that has been [[infusion|infused]] with lemon juice.<ref name="Saria 2013" /><ref name="Pavlides 2015" /><ref name="Stewart 2015" /> Some versions are prepared using [[sour mix]], a cocktail mixer.<ref name="Saria 2013" /> A garnish of a sliced lemon wheel, wedge, [[Zest (ingredient)|zest]], rind or a lemon [[Twist (cocktail garnish)|twist]] is sometimes used.<ref name="Charming Bourgoin 2009" /><ref name="Marszalek 2008" /><ref name="San Antonio Express-News" /><ref name="Marszalek 2010" /><ref name="Pavlides 2015" /> Additional ingredients may also be used in the drink's preparation, such as ginger syrup and lavender extract.<ref name="Lee 2015" />

A lemon drop is typically prepared [[Bartending terminology|straight up]], meaning that it is shaken or stirred with ice, strained, and served in a stemmed glass, such as a [[martini glass]].<ref name="San Antonio Express-News" /><ref name="Marszalek 2010" /><ref name="Sherman 2007" /> The glass may be prepared with a sugared rim, performed by dipping the rim of the glass in water or lemon juice and then dipping it into a rimmer (a shallow tray used in bartending), filled with sugar.<ref name="Charming Bourgoin 2009" /> Superfine sugar, also called bar sugar or caster sugar may be used.<ref name="Gisslen 2004" /><ref name="Algood 2013" /><ref name="Rivard 2009" />

==History==
[[File:Lemondropsinbulk.png|thumb|alt=Lemon drop candies|The inspiration]]
The lemon drop was invented sometime in the 1970s by Norman Jay Hobday, the founder and proprietor of Henry Africa's, a [[fern bar]] in the [[Russian Hill, San Francisco|Russian Hill]] neighborhood of [[San Francisco]], California that opened in 1969.<ref name="Walker 2010" /><ref name="Saekel 2005" /><ref name="McDonnell Abiol 2015" /><ref name="Whiting 2011" /><ref name="Telfer" /> It was originally served in a [[cocktail glass]].<ref name="Sherman 2007" /><ref name="McDonnell Abiol 2015" /><ref name="Abou-Ganim Faulkner Turner DeGroff 2013" /><ref name="Bloomberg.com 2015" /> The Lemon Drop was most likely named after [[lemon drop (candy)|lemon drop candy]].<ref name="Chirico 2015" /><ref name="Abou-Ganim Faulkner Turner DeGroff 2013" /> After its invention, the drink swiftly spread to many San Francisco saloons.<ref name="McDonnell Abiol 2015" /> In the early 1990s, it was often prepared as a [[shooter (drink)|shooter]] or served in a [[shot glass]].<ref name="Charming Bourgoin 2009" /><ref name="Chirico 2015" /><ref name="Solomon 2014" />  The shooter's recipe differed from the cocktail as it contained only one ingredient and a garnish.

==Variations==
Variations of the drink include lemon drops prepared with blueberries and raspberries, which may use vodkas or other liquors flavored with these respective berries.<ref name="Charming Bourgoin 2009" /><ref name="Santos 2011" /><ref name="Aikey 2012" /> These drinks may also be served or garnished with these berries,<ref name="Charming Bourgoin 2009" /> or with lemon.<ref name="Haasarud Grablewski 2014" /> A blueberry lemon drop may be prepared with [[Muddler|muddled]] blueberries,<ref name="Ellis 2013" /> and a raspberry lemon drop may be prepared with puréed or crushed raspberries.<ref name="Santos 2011" /><ref name="Pierce 2011" /> Another popular variation uses [[limoncello]] as the base spirit.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-04-29 |title=Limoncello Lemon Drop |url=https://basilandbubbly.com/limoncello-lemon-drop/ |access-date=2023-04-26 |website=Basil And Bubbly |language=en-US}}</ref>

The glass may have a sugared rim, and colored sugar may be used, prepared by adding food coloring to the sugar.<ref name="Charming Bourgoin" />

The "lemon drop shot" is a popular variant made with 2 parts vodka, 1 part lemon juice, 1/2 ounce of simple syrup, and served in a shot glass garnished with a sugar coated rim and lemon slice.

==In popular culture==
In 2006, preparation of the lemon drop was presented on ''[[The Oprah Winfrey Show]]'', prepared by [[Oprah Winfrey]] and [[Rachael Ray]].<ref name="Charming Bourgoin 2009" /><ref name="Oprah.com" /> The drink's popularity increased during this time.<ref name="Charming Bourgoin 2009" />

Singer Madonna referenced sometimes drinking Lemon Drops in the 2019 song , [[Back That Up to the Beat|Back That Up to the Beat]], released on her album, [[Madame X (album)|Madame X]].

On 18 September 2024, in an interview with journalist [[Amol Rajan]] on BBC Two, former Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, [[Sir John Major]], revealed that he was partial to the occasional Lemon Drop cocktail.{{Relevance inline|date=January 2025}}

On June 13th 2025, K-Pop group [[Ateez]] released a song entitled [[Lemon Drop (song)|"Lemon drop"]], inspired by the cocktail.

A '''Mary Pickford''' is a [[Prohibition in the United States|Prohibition Era]] [[cocktail]] made with [[white rum]], fresh [[pineapple juice]], [[grenadine]], and [[Maraschino]] liqueur. It is served shaken and chilled, often with a [[Maraschino cherry]]. 

== History ==

Named for Canadian-American film  actress [[Mary Pickford]] (1892–1979), it is said to have been created for her in the 1920s by either Eddie Woelke<ref>{{cite news|title=Mary Pickford Cocktail|url=http://imbibemagazine.com/Mary-Pickford-Cocktail-Recipe|access-date=7 July 2014|work=[[Imbibe Magazine]]|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714205719/http://imbibemagazine.com/Mary-Pickford-Cocktail-Recipe|archive-date=14 July 2014}}</ref> or Fred Kaufmann at the [[Hotel Nacional de Cuba]] on a trip she took to Havana with [[Charlie Chaplin]] and [[Douglas Fairbanks]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Thompson|first1=Kester|title=Cocktails, Cocktails, and More Cocktails|date=2011|publisher=Imagine Pub.|location=Watertown, MA|isbn=978-1-60734-423-0|page=[https://archive.org/details/cocktailscocktai0000thom/page/82 82]|url=https://archive.org/details/cocktailscocktai0000thom|url-access=registration|quote=mary pickford cocktail.}}</ref>

{{Short description|Long drink of London dry gin, lemon juice, sugar and carbonated water}} {{Other uses|John Collins (disambiguation){{!}}John Collins}} {{Use dmy dates|date=August 2022}} {{Infobox drink | name = John Collins | image = IBA Cocktail John Collins (29221732881).jpg | type = [[Mixed drink]] | base = [[Gin]] | ingredients ={{plainlist|* 45 ml [[gin]] * 30 ml fresh [[lemon juice]] * 15 ml [[simple syrup]] * 60 ml [[soda water]]}} | served = [[On the rocks]]: poured over ice | garnish = [[Lemon]] slice and [[maraschino cherry]] | prep = Pour all ingredients directly into a Collins glass filled with ice. Stir gently. | drinkware = [[Collins glass]] }} A '''John Collins''' is a [[long drink]] of [[London dry gin]], [[lemon juice]], [[sugar]] and [[carbonated water]], which was attested in 1869, but may be older. It is believed to have originated with a headwaiter of that name who worked at Limmer's Old House in [[Conduit Street]] in [[Mayfair]], which was a popular London hotel and coffee house around 1790–1817.{{cite web|last=Regan|first=Gaz|title=The Tom Collins and the John Collins: However this has been refuted by many in Ireland who claim the drink was developed in one of the first Irish pubs in New York est 1860 and named after the revolutionary Tom Collins. A Discussion|url=http://www.ardentspirits.com/ardentspirits_old/Cocktails/1B20111017.html|work=gaz's Cocktail Book|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131105024812/http://www.ardentspirits.com/ardentspirits_old/Cocktails/1B20111017.html|archive-date=5 November 2013}}{{cite book|last=Calabrese|first=Salvatore|title=Classic Cocktails|year=1997|publisher=Prion|location=London|isbn=1-85375-240-1|page=166}} It is essentially a variant of [[Tom Collins]], evidently a latter name for the same drink. ==Description== The John Collins is a Collins [[cocktail]]—that is, a [[long drink]] stirred with ice and topped with soda—made from [[London dry gin]], [[lemon juice]], [[sugar]] and [[carbonated water]]. A recipe for a John Collins is featured in the ''Steward and Barkeeper's Manual'' of 1869:
Teaspoonful of powdered sugar The juice of half a lemon A wine glass of Old Tom Gin A bottle of plain soda Shake up, or stir up with ice. Add a slice of lemon peel to finish.{{cite web|url=http://secondgoldenage.com/2012/07/21/collinses-fizzes-difference/|title=Difference between Collinses & Fizzes|website=SecondGoldenAge.com|access-date= 25 September 2015 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131105233232/http://secondgoldenage.com/2012/07/21/collinses-fizzes-difference/| archive-date= 5 November 2013| url-status= dead}}
Drinks historian David Wondrich has speculated that the original recipe that was introduced to New York in the 1850s would have been very similar to the gin punches that are known to have been served at London clubs such as [[Garrick Club|the Garrick]] during the first half of the 19th century. He states that these would have been along the lines of gin, lemon juice, chilled soda water, and [[maraschino]]. The specific call for [[Old Tom gin]] in the 1869 recipe is a likely cause for the subsequent name change to "[[Tom Collins]]" in Jerry Thomas's 1876 recipe. In contemporary parlance, the ''John Collins'' refers to a Tom Collins made with whiskey instead of gin.{{cn|date=June 2023}} Earlier versions of the gin punch are likely to have used [[Jenever|Dutch gin]] instead. ==In popular culture== The following rhyme was written by Frank and Charles Sheridan about John Collins:{{cite book|first=David|last=Solmonson|first2=Lesley Jacobs|last2=Solmonson|title=The 12 Bottle Bar|year=2014}}
My name is John Collins, head waiter at Limmer's, Corner of Conduit Street, Hanover Square, My chief occupation is filling brimmers For all the young gentlemen frequenters there.

A '''Hemingway special''' is an all day cocktail based on the [[Floridita]] [[daiquiri]]<ref name="Floridita Daiquiri">{{Cite web |url=http://www.elfloridita.net/pages/hemingway.php?language=en |title=Hemingway and the Floridita |website=El Floridita La Cuna del Daiquiri |access-date=8 April 2017 |archive-date=13 April 2013 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130413171009/http://www.elfloridita.net/pages/hemingway.php?language=en |url-status=dead }}</ref> and is recognised by the [[IBA Official Cocktail|IBA]]. It is made with [[rum]], [[lime juice]], [[maraschino]] liqueur, and [[grapefruit juice]] and served in a [[double cocktail glass]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://iba-world.com/cocktails/hemingway-special/ |title=Hemingway special |website=IBA World |access-date=8 April 2017 |archive-date=17 February 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170217052824/http://iba-world.com/cocktails/hemingway-special/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.aibmproject.it/hemingway-special/ |title=Hemingway Special |website=AIBM Project |date=30 March 2014 |access-date=8 April 2017}}</ref>

==History==
[[Ernest Hemingway]], who stayed in Cuba, tried the [[Floridita]]'s signature drink, the Floridita daiquiri, and said "That's good, but I prefer it without sugar and double rum."<ref name="Floridita Daiquiri" /> This became a cocktail now known as the Hemingway daiquiri or the Papa Doble.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.liquor.com/articles/behind-the-drink-the-hemingway-daiquiri/#gs.I2zF=Nk |title=Behind the drink: The Hemingway daiquiri |last=Curtis |first=Wayne |website=liquor.com |access-date=8 April 2017}}</ref> His recipe was later modified further, adding grapefruit juice to the mix, at which point the drink was dubbed the "Hemingway special".<ref name="Floridita Daiquiri" />

The '''Martinez''' is a classic cocktail that is widely regarded as the direct precursor to the [[Martini (cocktail)|Martini]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Calabrese |first1=Salvatore |title=Classic Cocktails |url=https://archive.org/details/classiccocktails0000cala |url-access=registration |date=1997 |publisher=Sterling Publishing Co. |location=New York |isbn=0806905077}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Martinez |url=https://punchdrink.com/recipes/martinez/ |website=punchdrink.com |accessdate=20 March 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Martinez Cocktail Recipe |url=https://www.seriouseats.com/recipes/2011/09/martinez-cocktail-gin-cocktail-recipe.html |website=seriouseats.com |accessdate=20 March 2019}}</ref> It serves as the basis for many modern cocktails, and several different versions of the original exist. These are generally distinguished by the accompaniment of either [[maraschino]] or [[Curaçao (liqueur)|curaçao]], as well as differences in gin or bitters.

==History==
The true origin of the Martinez cocktail is unclear. Two early stories attribute the making of a cocktail named the Martinez to bartender [[Jerry Thomas (bartender)|Jerry Thomas]] at the Occidental Hotel or by a bartender by the name of Richelieue who worked at a saloon in [[Martinez, California]]. Both stories are difficult to verify because records of drinks at the time are missing or incomplete, but the 1887 edition of Thomas' ''The Bar-Tender's Guide'' includes a recipe for the Martinez. It calls for a pony of [[Old Tom gin]], a glass of [[vermouth]], two dashes of [[Maraschino]], and a dash of [[Boker's Bitters]] with ice, garnished with a slice of lemon.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Calabrese |first1=Salvatore |title=Classic Cocktails |url=https://archive.org/details/classiccocktails0000cala |url-access=registration |date=1997 |publisher=Sterling Publishing Co. |location=New York |isbn=0806905077}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Martinez cocktail comeback |url=http://imbibemagazine.com/martinez-cocktail-comeback/ |website=imbibemagazine.com |date=12 September 2016 |accessdate=20 March 2019}}</ref>

An 1884 drink guide by O.H. Byron released just a few years earlier also listed a recipe for a cocktail called the Martinez by saying only: "Same as [[Manhattan (cocktail)|Manhattan]], only you substitute gin for whisky."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Byron |first1=O.H. |title=The Modern Bartenders' Guide |date=1884 |publisher=Excelsior Publishing House |location=New York}}</ref> The book contained two recipes for a Manhattan, one of which called for 2 dashes of [[Curacao (liqueur)|curaçao]], 2 dashes of [[Angostura bitters]], 1/2 a wine-glass whisky and 1/2 a wine-glass of Italian vermouth.

A later 1888 guide by Harry Johnson, the ''New and Improved Illustrated Bartender's Manual'', listed a drink that may have been incorrectly spelled as the "martine", without the letter "z". The recipes and names eventually evolved to become two different cocktails, the Martinez and the Martini.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Calabrese |first1=Salvatore |title=Classic Cocktails |url=https://archive.org/details/classiccocktails0000cala |url-access=registration |date=1997 |publisher=Sterling Publishing Co. |location=New York |isbn=0806905077}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The classic cocktail that is not a manhattan or a martini |url=https://www.saveur.com/martinez-its-not-manhattan-its-not-martini-its-classic |website=saveur.com |date=13 August 2015 |accessdate=20 March 2019}}</ref>

==Martinez ingredients==
After Jerry Thomas' recipe for the Martinez, as well as Byron's, ingredients for the drink that would retain the name Martinez began to take more firm shape, with most variations based on differences between the use of maraschino or curaçao. The ''Old Mr. Boston Official Bartender's Guide'' called for 1 oz dry gin, 1 oz French vermouth, 1/4 tsp curaçao, and a dash of orange bitters.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cotton |first1=Leo |title=Old Mr. Boston Official Bartender's Guide |date=1946 |publisher=Berke Brothers |location=Boston |edition=sixth}}</ref> In the 1940 ''The Official Mixers Manual'' by Patrick Gavin Duffy the drink calls for gin, dry vermouth, orange bitters, and "4 teaspoons Curaçao or Maraschino". In 1947 [[Trader Vic's]] called for 3/4 oz gin, 3/4 oz French vermouth, 1/2 tsp orange bitters, and 1/2 tsp curaçao.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bergeron |first1=Vic |title=Bartender's Guide |publisher=Garden City |location=New York|date=1947}}</ref>

[[Difford's Guide]] lists several versions, including an "Old Tom" version with Old Tom gin, maraschino, and angostura bitters,<ref>{{cite web |title=Martinez made with Old Tom gin |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2489/martinez-made-with-old-tom |website=diffordsguide.com |accessdate=20 March 2019}}</ref> a "London Dry" version with dry gin, maraschino, and angostura bitters,<ref>{{cite web |title=Martinez with London Dry Gin |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2490/martinez-with-london-dry-gin |website=diffordsguide.com |accessdate=20 March 2019}}</ref>  and an "Orange" version with dry gin, curaçao, and orange bitters.<ref>{{cite web |title=Martinez (Orange) |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2491/martinez-orange |website=diffordsguide.com |accessdate=20 March 2019}}</ref>

The '''Illegal''' is an [[IBA official cocktail]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Illeagal |url=https://iba-world.com/new-era-drinks/illegal/ |website=IBA Official Cocktails |access-date=May 29, 2020}}</ref> This cocktail is named after the mezcal brand [[Ilegal Mezcal]], which is one of its key ingredients. [[Mezcal]] is a type of Mexican distilled spirit made from agave plants, similar to tequila but with a distinct smoky flavor. It is prepared by pouring Mezcal, [[Rum|Jamaican White Rum]], [[Falernum]], [[Maraschino]] Luxardo, [[Lime juice|Lime Juice]], [[Simple syrup|Simple Syrup]], and, optionally, [[egg white]], into a [[Cocktail shaker|shaker]], before shaking the mixture vigorously and serving in a chilled [[cocktail glass]]. traditionally, the drink may also be served on the rocks in a clay or terracotta mug.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Illegal – IBA |url=https://iba-world.com/iba-cocktail/illegal/ |access-date=2026-03-18 |language=en-US}}</ref>

== History ==
Italian [[bartender]] Samuele Ambrosi invented the Illegal sometime in the late 1990s while working as a barman at the [[CastelBrando|Castel Brando]] hotel in [[Cison di Valmarino]] after an American patron, Dr. Joe Paul Shafer, shared his enjoyment of both [[Daiquiri|Daiquiris]] and the Central and Southern American countries he frequented for work. Inspired, Ambrosi created a Daiquiri variant featuring [[tequila]], falernum, Jamaican rum, maraschino, lime, and simple syrup, which the American patron remarked tasted "so good it must be Illegal", with said explanation birthing the idea of the name. Ambrosi would tinker with the recipe at the Dom’us in [[Oderzo]], replacing the tequila for Mezcal, eventually evolving into the cocktail known today. The Illegal was formally added to the IBA official cocktail list in 2020 with the modern recipe.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fossati |first=Stefano |date=2026-02-26 |title=Alla scoperta dell’Illegal: origini, ricetta e firma di Samuele Ambrosi |url=https://mixologyitalia.com/cocktail/alla-scoperta-dellillegal-origini-ricetta-e-firma-di-samuele-ambrosi/ |access-date=2026-03-18 |website=MixologyItalia.com |language=it-IT}}</ref>

The '''paper plane''' is a whiskey-based [[cocktail]] created in 2008. In 2020 it was added to the [[International Bartenders Association]]'s (IBA) [[IBA official cocktail|list of official cocktails]] as a new era drink.<ref name=ibaList>{{cite web |url=https://wildandwanderfultravel.com/index.php/2020/04/16/2020-iba-cocktail-list/ |title=The New 2020 IBA Cocktail List. The Quest (modified) |work=Wild and Wanderful Travel |author=Jacquelyn |date=April 16, 2020 |access-date=May 13, 2024 |archive-date=November 19, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231119021653/https://wildandwanderfultravel.com/index.php/2020/04/16/2020-iba-cocktail-list/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=ibaRecipe>{{cite web |title=Paper Plane |url=https://iba-world.com/new-era-drinks/paper-plane/ |website=IBA Official Cocktails |date=n.d. |access-date=May 13, 2024 |archive-date=November 24, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201124011812/https://iba-world.com/new-era-drinks/paper-plane/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Recipe==
The cocktail consists of equal parts [[bourbon whiskey]], [[Aperol]], [[Amaro (liqueur)|Amaro]], and [[lemon juice]], served in a standard cocktail glass. The IBA suggests the drink should be prepared without garnish,<ref name=ibaRecipe/> but ''Difford's Guide'' and ''[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]'' magazine both recommend a lemon twist.<ref name=diffords>{{cite web |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/3630/paper-plane |title=Paper Plane |work=Difford's Guide |date=n.d. |access-date=May 13, 2024 |archive-date=May 14, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240514041513/https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/3630/paper-plane |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=esquire>{{cite web |url=https://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/a22564455/best-paper-plane-recipe/ |title=How to Make a Paper Plane |date=October 11, 2019 |first=Sarah |last=Rense |access-date=May 13, 2024 |work=[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]] |publisher=[[Hearst Communications]] |archive-date=May 14, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240514041501/https://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/a22564455/best-paper-plane-recipe/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

==History==
The paper plane was created in 2008 by Sam Ross and [[Sasha Petraske]]. They created the drink as a favor for a former colleague, Toby Maloney, who wanted a summer drink to serve at his bar The Violet Hour. Ross describes the drink as "a riff on a [[Last Word (cocktail)|Last Word]] cocktail" and says the name was inspired by the [[M.I.A. (rapper)|M.I.A.]] track "[[Paper Planes (M.I.A. song)|Paper Planes]]," a song he and Petraske listened to often while creating the drink.<ref name=cocktailChemistry>{{cite AV media |author= Cocktail Chemistry |date= 19 February 2018 |title= Basic Cocktails – How To Make The Paper Plane |language= en-us |url= https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KetESaw8I4U |access-date= 7 July 2020 |publisher= [[YouTube]] |archive-date= 10 August 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200810200434/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KetESaw8I4U |url-status= live }}</ref><ref name=foodAndWine>{{cite web |url=https://www.foodandwine.com/recipes/paper-plane |title=Paper Plane |first=Sam |last=Ross |date=January 8, 2024 |access-date=May 13, 2024 |work=[[Food & Wine]] magazine |publisher=[[Dotdash Meredith]] |archive-date=May 14, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240514041501/https://www.foodandwine.com/recipes/paper-plane |url-status=live }}</ref>

When the drink was first served at The Violet Hour, Maloney listed it on the menu as the paper airplane, because he misheard Ross's "slightly buzzed" voicemail. Ross's original recipe called for [[Campari]] rather than [[Aperol]]. After submitting the recipe to Maloney, Ross began having second thoughts and revisited the drink, determining that it was too bitter and didn't reach his desired level of sweetness.<ref name=foodAndWine/><ref name=punch>{{cite web |url=https://punchdrink.com/articles/how-paper-plane-became-modern-classic-cocktail-recipe-milk-and-honey-nyc/ |title=How the Paper Plane Became a Modern Classic |first=Robert |last=Simonson |authorlink=Robert Simonson |date=September 30, 2020 |access-date=May 13, 2024 |work=Punch |publisher=[[Vox Media]] |archive-date=August 10, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230810163245/https://punchdrink.com/articles/how-paper-plane-became-modern-classic-cocktail-recipe-milk-and-honey-nyc/ |url-status=live }}</ref> He also says he tried several different spirits as the drink's base, including rye, applejack, and brandy, before selecting bourbon.<ref name=beautifulMess>{{cite web |url=https://abeautifulmess.com/paper-plane-cocktail/ |title=Paper Plane Cocktail |work=A Beautiful Mess |first=Elsie |last=Larson |date=April 11, 2024 |access-date=May 13, 2024 |archive-date=May 14, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240514041512/https://abeautifulmess.com/paper-plane-cocktail/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

The '''Jungle Bird''' is a [[Tiki culture|tiki]] [[cocktail]] made with [[dark rum|blackstrap rum]], [[Campari]], [[pineapple juice]], lime juice, and [[demerara syrup]]. Invented by Malaysian beverage manager Jeffrey Ong in 1973, it has been recognized by the [[International Bartenders Association]] as an [[List of IBA official cocktails|official cocktail]] since 2024.<ref>{{cite web |title=Jungle Bird |url=https://iba-world.com/iba-cocktail/jungle-bird/ |website=[[International Bartenders Association]] |access-date=19 January 2025}}</ref>

== History ==

The Jungle Bird debuted on 6 July 1973 at the Aviary Bar at the [[Hilton Hotels & Resorts|Hilton]] hotel in [[Kuala Lumpur]], where beverage manager Jeffrey Ong invented it as the welcome drink for guests.<ref name="difford">{{cite web |title=Jungle Bird Cocktail Recipe |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/1082/jungle-bird |website=Difford's Guide |access-date=19 January 2025 |language=en}}</ref> The cocktail's name was inspired by the colorful tropical birds fenced in at the namesake [[aviary]] visible from the bar.<ref name="epicurious">{{cite web |last1=Parsons |first1=Brad Thomas |title=The Jungle Bird Will Make Your Cocktail Hour Soar |url=https://www.epicurious.com/expert-advice/jungle-bird-cocktail-history |website=[[Epicurious]] |access-date=19 January 2025 |date=17 August 2022}}</ref> The drink was originally served in a bird-shaped ceramic vessel.<ref name="difford" /><ref name="epicurious" />

The cocktail gained international recognition after it was included in the 1989 book ''The New American Bartender's Guide'' by John J. Poister, with the recipe generically calling for [[dark rum]].<ref name="difford" /><ref name="second-coming" /> American mixologist and [[Tiki culture|tiki]] historian [[Jeff Berry (mixologist)|Jeff "Beachbum" Berry]] encountered the Jungle Bird in Poister's book and adapted it for his 2002 tropical beverage book ''Intoxica!'', tweaking the recipe to call for "dark Jamaican rum" specifically.<ref name="epicurious" /><ref name="second-coming">{{cite web |last1=Newman |first1=Kara |title=The Second Coming of the Jungle Bird |url=https://punchdrink.com/articles/second-coming-of-the-jungle-bird-cocktail-history-and-recipes/ |website=[[Punch (website)|Punch]] |access-date=20 January 2025 |language=en |date=16 May 2016}}</ref> On what inspired him to include the cocktail in the book, Berry recounted: "The only thing that made it interesting was that [[Campari]] was in it. A tropical drink with an [[Amaro (liqueur)|amaro]] was unusual."<ref name="second-coming" /> He remarked, "It definitely was on no one’s radar before I published it."<ref name="nyt">{{cite web |last1=Simonson |first1=Robert |title=A Bird Walks Into a Bar... |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/04/09/dining/a-bird-walks-into-a-bar.html |website=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=20 January 2025 |date=8 April 2014}}</ref>

In 2010, the Jungle Bird reached its modern form at Painkiller, a now-closed bar in New York City, where bartender Giuseppe González specified the more intense [[blackstrap molasses|blackstrap]] rum and reduced the [[pineapple juice]] from 4 US fl oz to 1.5 US fl oz.<ref name="second-coming" /> González's recipe has become widely accepted by bartenders as the canonical formula.<ref name="ultimate">{{cite web |last1=Frechette |first1=Chloe |title=In Search of the Ultimate Jungle Bird |url=https://punchdrink.com/articles/best-jungle-bird-cocktail-recipe-tiki-rum/ |website=[[Punch (website)|Punch]] |access-date=20 January 2025 |language=en |date=23 August 2024}}</ref>

The Jungle Bird's popularity in the United States increased in the 2010s. In a 2014 article in ''[[The New York Times]]'', it was called a "hitherto obscure tiki drink" that "has bloomed into a bartender favorite whose popularity goes well beyond the parameters of the resurgent tiki culture."<ref name="nyt" /> Berry suggests that the Jungle Bird's inclusion of Campari allowed it to bridge the gap between tiki culture and the [[craft cocktail movement]], explaining, "It was the one tiki drink you'd find in craft cocktail bars that wanted nothing to do with tiki."<ref name="second-coming" />

Malaysian newspaper ''[[The Star (Malaysia)|The Star]]'' named the Jungle Bird "Malaysia's only internationally recognised classic cocktail" in an obituary following the death of Jungle Bird inventor Jeffrey Ong in 2019.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Cheang |first1=Michael |title=Goodbye Jeffrey Ong, creator of Malaysia's only classic cocktail, Jungle Bird |url=https://www.thestar.com.my/lifestyle/food/2019/03/01/jeffery-ong-creator-jungle-bird-malaysian-classic-cocktail |website=[[The Star (Malaysia)|The Star]] |access-date=20 January 2025 |language=en |date=1 March 2019}}</ref>

The '''IBA Tiki''' is a [[Tiki culture|tiki]] [[cocktail]] made with a blend of [[rum]]s, [[amaretto]], [[Frangelico]], [[maraschino]], [[passion fruit]] purée, [[pineapple juice]], lime juice, and [[muddler|muddled]] [[ginger]]. Invented by Cuban bartender Diosmel Mendoza Medrano in 2022, it has been recognized by its namesake [[International Bartenders Association]] (IBA) as an [[List of IBA official cocktails|official cocktail]] since 2024.

== History ==

The IBA Tiki was invented by Cuban bartender Diosmel Mendoza Medrano in honor of the [[International Bartenders Association]]'s 69th annual World Cocktail Championship, held in the Cuban resort town of [[Varadero]] in November 2022, the first instance after a hiatus due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].<ref name="apetime">{{cite web |last1=Fossati |first1=Stefano |title=Ricetta cocktail: Iba Tiki, da Cuba il prossimo classico dell'aperitivo |url=https://www.apetimemagazine.com/ricetta-cocktail-iba-tiki-da-cuba-il-prossimo-classico-dellaperitivo/ |website=Magazine ApeTime |access-date=14 July 2025 |language=it-IT |date=2 April 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Bartenders from 65 countries come together for 69th World Cocktail Championships in Cuba |url=https://abc7ny.com/post/world-cocktail-championships-cuba-bartender-drinks/12423824/ |website=[[ABC7 New York]] |access-date=14 July 2025 |language=en |date=6 November 2022}}</ref> Medrano created the cocktail at El Polinesio, a [[tiki bar]] at the [[Habana Libre]] hotel in [[Havana]] that was formerly operated by [[Trader Vic's]].<ref name="apetime" />

The recipe was created at the request of the competition's organizers, in honor of the IBA's board.<ref name="apetime" /> It specifically calls for [[Havana Club]] brand rums and [[Girolamo Luxardo]] brand [[maraschino]], both of which were sponsors for the competition.<ref>{{cite web |title=USBG, International Bartenders Association Announce Winner of IBA World Cocktail Championship |url=https://www.usbg.org/press-release/usbg-international-bartenders-association-announce-winner-iba-world-cocktail |website=United States Bartenders' Guild |access-date=14 July 2025 |date=9 November 2022}}</ref><ref name="iba">{{cite web |title=IBA Tiki |url=https://iba-world.com/iba-cocktail/iba-tiki/ |website=[[International Bartenders Association]] |access-date=14 July 2025}}</ref>

The cocktail was added to the [[list of IBA official cocktails]] in March 2024, when it was included as the 101st cocktail in the organization's ''101 IBA Cocktails'' book.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Cavazzuti |first1=Nicole |title=Il nuovo libro dei cocktail IBA: un mastodontico viaggio nella storia e nell'arte della mixology |url=https://horecanews.it/il-nuovo-libro-dei-cocktail-iba-un-mastodontico-viaggio-nella-storia-e-nellarte-della-mixology |website=Horeca News |access-date=14 July 2025 |language=it-IT |date=27 March 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Fossati |first1=Stefano |title=La nuova lista dei cocktail Iba, ecco il libro ufficiale. Leggi l'anteprima |url=https://www.apetimemagazine.com/lista-cocktail-iba-libro-ufficiale/ |website=Magazine ApeTime |access-date=14 July 2025 |language=it-IT |date=30 March 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Cavazzuti |first1=Nicole |title=Ecco la nuova lista Iba: 101 cocktail tra storia, tips e video ricette. Tutte le novità |url=https://www.italiaatavola.net/wine/2024/3/29/enuova-lista-iba-101-cocktail-storia-tips-video-ricette-tutte-novita/104238/ |website=Italia a Tavola |access-date=16 July 2025 |language=it-IT |date=29 March 2024}}</ref>

The '''zombie''' is a [[Tiki culture|tiki]] [[cocktail]] made of fruit juices, [[liqueur]]s, and various [[rum]]s. It first appeared in late 1934, invented by [[Donn Beach]] at his Hollywood ''Don the Beachcomber'' restaurant.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.greatcocktails.co.uk/Zombie.html|title=A Zombie Cocktail Recipe - Great Cocktails (UK)|access-date=2009-06-19}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Zombie Recipe |url=http://beachbumberry.com/recipe-zombie.html |website=beachbumberry.com |access-date=13 February 2019}}</ref> It was popularized on the East coast soon afterwards at the [[1939 New York World's Fair]].

==History==
Legend has it that Donn Beach originally concocted the zombie to help a hung-over customer get through a business meeting.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bitner |first1=Arnold |title=Hawai'i Tropical Rum Drinks by Don the Beachcomber |date=2001 |publisher=Mutual Publishing |location=Honolulu}}</ref><ref name = bum>{{cite book|last1=Berry|first1=Jeff|title=Beachbum Berry's sippin' safari : in search of the great "lost" tropical drink recipes...and the people behind them|date=2007|publisher=SLG|location=San Jose, Calif.|isbn=978-1593620677|edition=2. printing|page=103}}</ref> The customer returned several days later to complain that he had been turned into a [[zombie]] for his entire trip. Its smooth, fruity taste works to conceal its extremely high [[alcoholic beverage|alcoholic]] content. ''Don the Beachcomber'' restaurants limited their customers to two zombies apiece because of their potency, which Beach said could make one "like the walking dead."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bitner |first1=Arnold |title=Hawai'i Tropical Rum Drinks by Don the Beachcomber |date=2001 |publisher=Mutual Publishing |location=Honolulu|page = 58}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.donthebeachcomber.com/drinking_menu.html |title=Drinking Menu |publisher=Don The Beachcomber |access-date=2011-06-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130711000619/http://www.donthebeachcomber.com/drinking_menu.html|archive-date=2013-07-11}}</ref>

According to the original recipe, the zombie cocktail included three different kinds of rum, lime juice, [[falernum]], [[Angostura bitters]], [[Pernod]], [[grenadine]], and "Don's Mix", a combination of [[cinnamon]] syrup and [[grapefruit]] juice.<ref>{{cite book|author=Jeff Berry|title=Sippin' Safari|publisher=SLG Publishing |year=2007|page=121}}</ref>

Beach was very cautious with the recipes of his original cocktails. His instructions for his bartenders contained coded references to ingredients, the contents of which were only known to him.<ref>{{cite news |title=Cracking the Code of the Zombie |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/11/28/dining/28tiki.html |newspaper=The New York Times |date=28 November 2007 |access-date=20 March 2019|last1=Kurutz |first1=Steven }}</ref> Beach had reason to worry; a copy of the zombie was served at the [[1939 New York World's Fair]] by a man trying to take credit for it named Monte Proser (later of the mob-tied [[Copacabana (nightclub)|Copacabana]]).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lapis |first1=Diane |last2=Peck-Davis |first2=Anne |title=Cocktails Across America |date=2018 |publisher=Countryman Press}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Zombie Punch |url=https://blog.distiller.com/zombie-punch/|website=blog.distiller.com |access-date=16 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Mystery in a tall glass |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB118798701049208213 |newspaper=Wall Street Journal |date=25 August 2007 |access-date=20 March 2019|last1=Felten |first1=Eric }}</ref>

Beach's original recipes for the zombie and other tiki drinks have been published in ''Sippin' Safari'' by [[Jeff Berry (mixologist)|Jeff "Beachbum" Berry]].  Berry researched the origins of many tiki cocktails, interviewing bartenders from Don the Beachcomber's and other original tiki places and digging up other original sources. ''Sippin' Safari'' details Beach's development of the zombie with three different recipes dating from 1934 to 1956.<ref name = bum/>

The zombie was occasionally served heated (a drink more commonly known today as the I.B.A. hot zombie), as outlined by the Catering Industry Employee (CIE) journal:  "Juice of 1 lime, unsweetened pineapple juice, bitters, 1 ounce heavily bodied rum, 2 ounces of Gold Label rum, 1 ounce of White Label rum, 1 ounce of apricot-flavored brandy, 1 ounce of papaya juice"<ref>CIE: Volumes 50-51 by Hotel & Restaurant Employees and Bartenders International Union, Hotel Employees & Restaurant Employees International Union, Hotel and Restaurant Employees' International Alliance and Bartenders' International League of America in 1941</ref>

The cocktail is named in the lyrics for the song "Haitian Divorce" on the 1976 album ''[[The Royal Scam]]'' by [[Steely Dan]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.streetdirectory.com/lyricadvisor/song/uolaaw/haitian_divorce/ |title=Haitian Divorce Lyrics by Steely Dan |website=streetdirectory.com/ |access-date=11 November 2022}} </ref>

== Preparation ==
Preparing a cocktail consists of adding a glass of ice and all ingredients to a shaker or juicer (except for Rum 151, if it's included in the recipe at all), shaking the closed shaker vigorously for five seconds, and serving in a glass. Then pour the 151 rum over the mixture so that it lies on top of the other ingredients, and finally, garnish the glass with a slice of some fruit of your choice.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Zombie Cocktail|url=https://www.thespruceeats.com/zombie-cocktail-recipe-761643|access-date=2024-10-24|work=www.thespruceeats.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=The Zombie Cocktail|url=https://www.acouplecooks.com/zombie-cocktail/|access-date=2024-10-24|work=www.acouplecooks.com|date=24 October 2020 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Zombie recipes|url=https://thelosttikilounge.com/cocktails/zombie-guide/|access-date=2024-10-24|work=thelosttikilounge.com|date=3 April 2019 }}</ref> 

== Options ==
One variation on the recipe is to keep the base of the various rum, brandy, and Bacardi varieties and substitute orange, pineapple, lemon, and grenadine juices for the pineapple and papaya juices.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Authentic Zombie Recipe|url=https://www.tasteatlas.com/zombie/recipe|access-date=2024-10-24|work=www.tasteatlas.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=A Delicious Bacardi Zombie Cocktail for a Summer Evening|url=https://cancanawards.com/bacardi-zombie/|access-date=2024-10-24|work=cancanawards.com}}</ref> Another version is based on giving up brandy and substituting juices from sweeter flavors to more citrusy ones like lemon, pineapple and papaya. 

The zombie voodoo cocktail is a variation of the classic zombie cocktail.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Zombie Drink Recipe|url=https://drinksworld.com/recipe/zombie-drink/|access-date=2024-10-24|work=drinksworld.com}}</ref> It contains unique ingredients like absinthe and blackberries that give it a distinctive flavor.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Zomie|url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2131/zombie|access-date=2024-10-24|work=www.diffordsguide.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=What Alcohol is in a Zombie Cocktail?|url=https://www.winemixture.com/archives/8207|access-date=2024-10-24|work=www.winemixture.com}}</ref> This version retains the tropical base of the original zombie, but takes on a slightly different flavor thanks to the added ingredients.

==Tiki culture influence==
Due to the popularity of the cocktail during the [[Tiki culture|tiki craze]], from the 1930s, and the fact that Beach kept his recipe secret and occasionally altered it, there are many variations of the zombie served at other restaurants and bars (some tasting nothing like the original cocktail). The word ''zombie'' also began to be used at other tiki themed establishments, such as at the [[Zombie Hut]] and ''Zombie Village''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kirsten |first1=Sven |title=The Book of Tiki |date=2000 |publisher=[[Taschen]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Berry |first1=Jeff |title=Beachbum Berry Remixed |date=2010 |publisher=Slave Labor Graphics |location=San Jose}}</ref>

[[Trader Vic]] also listed a recipe for the zombie in his 1947 ''Bartender's Guide''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bergeron |first1=Victor |title=Bartender's Guide |date=1947 |publisher=Garden City |location=New York}}</ref> Other competitors created drinks linked to the zombie. At Stephen Crane's Chicago [[Joseph Stephen Crane#Restaurant career & Kon-Tiki chain|Kon-Tiki Ports]] restaurant they featured a drink on the menu called ''The Walking Dead'': "Makes the dead walk and talk. For those who want immediate action – meet the first cousin to the famous 'zombie'. Demerara 151 rum. 90¢."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Berry |first1=Jeff |title=Sippin' Safari |date=2017 |publisher=Cocktail Kingdom |location=New York |page=221 |edition=10th Anniversary}}</ref>

'''Sazerac''' is a local variation of a [[cognac]] or [[whiskey]] cocktail originally from [[New Orleans]]. It is named for the ''Sazerac de Forge et Fils'' brand of cognac brandy that originally served as its main ingredient.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.sazerac.com/our-brands/sazerac-rye-whiskey.html | title=Sazerac Rye – The Character of New Orleans | publisher=[[Sazerac Company]]}}</ref> The drink is most traditionally a combination of
cognac or [[rye whiskey]], [[absinthe]], [[Peychaud's Bitters]], and sugar, although [[bourbon whiskey]] is sometimes substituted for the rye and [[Herbsaint]] is sometimes substituted for the absinthe.<ref>{{Cite news | url=https://www.mashed.com/2116497/anthony-bourdain-sazerac-cocktail/ | title=One Of Anthony Bourdain's Favorite Cocktails Dates Back To The 1800s | first=Sean | last=Pagnotti | work=[[Mashed.com]] | date=March 8, 2026}}</ref> Some claim it is the oldest known American [[cocktail]],<ref>{{cite book | last=Majumdar | first=Simon | title=Eat My Globe: One Year to Go Everywhere and Eat Everything | year=2009 | publisher=[[Simon & Schuster]] | isbn=978-1-4165-7602-0 | pages=[https://archive.org/details/eatmyglobeoneyea0000maju/page/192 192] | url=https://archive.org/details/eatmyglobeoneyea0000maju/page/192 }}</ref> with origins in [[History of Louisiana|antebellum]] [[New Orleans]], although drink historian David Wondrich is among those who dispute this,<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.liquor.com/articles/sazerac/ | title=The History and Secrets of the Sazerac | first=Amy | last=Zavatto | work=[[Liquor.com]] | date=March 5, 2019}}</ref> and American instances of published usage of the word ''cocktail'' to describe a mixture of spirits, [[bitters]], and sugar can be traced to the early 19th century.<ref>{{cite book |last=Felten | first=Eric | title=How's Your Drink? Cocktails, Culture, and the Art of Drinking Well | year=2007 | publisher=Surrey Books | isbn=978-1-57284-089-8 | pages=9–10}}</ref>

==Characteristics==
The defining feature of the Sazerac is its method of preparation, which commonly involves two chilled [[old-fashioned glass]]es. The first glass is swirled with a wash of [[absinthe]] for its flavor and strong scent.<ref>{{Cite book | last=Wondrich | first=David | title=Imbibe! | year=2007 | publisher=Perigee | isbn=978-0-399-53287-0 | pages=199–202}}</ref> The second glass is used to combine the remaining ingredients, which are stirred with ice, then strained into the first glass.<ref>{{Cite book | last=Axelrod | first=Alan | title=The Complete Idiot's Guide to Mixing Drinks | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6AqgJr_vqygC&pg=PA130 | edition=2nd | publisher=[[Penguin Books]] | isbn=0-02-864468-9 | page=130 | year=2003}}</ref> Various [[anisette]]s such as [[pastis]], [[Pernod Ricard|Pernod]], or [[Herbsaint]] are common substitutes when absinthe is unavailable. In New Orleans, Herbsaint is most commonly used due to the absence of absinthe in the U.S. market from 1912 until 2007.<ref name=50ways>{{Cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_6PR9Bh80zIC&pg=PA33 | last=Simon | first=Kate | title=Absinthe Cocktails: 50 Ways to Mix with the Green Fairy | publisher=[[Chronicle Books]] | isbn=978-1-4521-0030-2 | page=33 | year=2010}}</ref>

"New Orleans style" uses 100% whiskey, while "New York–style Sazerac" or "New York Sazerac" is typified by a split base of rye whiskey and brandy in equal proportion and is the standard version in Australia.<ref>{{Cite news | url=https://punchdrink.com/articles/new-york-sazerac-australia-recipe/ | title=In Australia, the "New York Sazerac" Reigns Supreme | first=Fred | last=Siggins | work=Punch Drink | date=January 2, 2023}}</ref>

==History==
Around 1850, Sewell T. Taylor sold his New Orleans bar, the Merchants Exchange Coffee House, to become an importer of spirits, and he began to import a brand of cognac named ''Sazerac-de-Forge et Fils''. Meanwhile, Aaron Bird assumed proprietorship of the Merchants Exchange and changed its name to Sazerac Coffee House.<ref>{{Cite book | first=Sarah | last=Roahen | editor-first=Susan | editor-last=Tucker | title=New Orleans Cuisine: Fourteen Signature Dishes and Their Histories | publisher=[[University Press of Mississippi]] | year=2009 | isbn=9781604731279 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JJ0WsDnnhT8C&pg=PA28 | pages=28-37}}</ref>

Bird began serving the "Sazerac Cocktail", made with Sazerac cognac imported by Taylor, and allegedly with [[bitters]] being made by the local apothecary, Antoine Amedie Peychaud. The Sazerac Coffee House was sold several times, until around 1870 Thomas Handy became its proprietor. It is around this time that the primary ingredient changed from cognac to rye whiskey, due to the [[Great French Wine Blight]].<ref>{{cite book | last=Arthur | first=Stanley | title=Famous New Orleans Drinks and How to Mix 'Em | year=1997 | publisher=[[Pelican Books]] | isbn=978-0-88289-132-3}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.mentalfloss.com/food/alcohol/whats-right-way-make-sazerac | title=What's the Right Way to Make a Sazerac? | first=Clair | last=McLafferty | work=[[Mental Floss]] | date=September 15, 2016}}</ref>

At some point before his death in 1889, Handy recorded the recipe for Sazerac, which made its first printed appearance in William T. "Cocktail Bill" Boothby's ''The World's Drinks and How to Mix Them'' (1908),<ref>
{{cite book | last=Boothby | first=William | year=1908 | title=The world's drinks and how to mix them: Standard authority | url=https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1908-The-World-s-Drinks-and-How-to-Mix-Them-by-Hon-Wm-Boothby/29 | page=29 | asin=B00088HN8Q}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/recipes/a3876/sazerac-drink-recipe/ | title=How to Make a Sazerac | first=Sarah | last=Rense | work=[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]] | date=March 8, 2019}}</ref> although his recipe calls for Selner Bitters, not Peychaud's.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://livethelive.com/2026/02/17/the-sazerac-classic-cocktail-of-new-orleans-5/ | title=THE SAZERAC: CLASSIC COCKTAIL OF NEW ORLEANS | work=Live the Live | date=February 17, 2026}}</ref> After absinthe was banned in the United States in 1912, it was replaced by various [[anise]]-flavored liqueurs, the most notable product being locally produced Herbsaint, which first appeared in 1934.<ref name=50ways/>

By the early 20th century, simple cocktails like the Sazerac had become rare, which eventually rekindled their popularity.<ref>{{cite book | last=Wondrich | first=David | title=Imbibe!: From Absinthe Cocktail to Whiskey Smash, a Salute in Stories and Drinks to "Professor" Jerry Thomas, Pioneer of the American Bar | year=2007 | publisher=Perigee | isbn=978-0-399-53287-0 | pages=199–202}}</ref>

The creation of the Sazerac has also been credited to Antoine Amédée Peychaud, a Creole [[apothecary]] who emigrated to New Orleans from the West Indies and set up shop in the [[French Quarter]] in the early 19th century. He was known to dispense a proprietary mix of aromatic bitters from an old family recipe. According to popular myth, he served his drink in the large end of an egg cup that was called a ''coquetier'' in French, and the Americanized mispronunciation resulted in the name ''cocktail''.<ref>{{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SV5YryuX3_EC&pg=PA315 | last=Difford | first=Simon | title=Diffordsguide Cocktails #7 | edition=7 | year=2007 | publisher=Diffordsguide | page=315 | isbn=978-0-9556276-0-6}}</ref> This belief was debunked when people discovered that the term "cocktail" as a type of drink first appeared in print at least as far back as 1803—and was defined in print in 1806 as, "a mixture of spirits of any kind, water, sugar and bitters, vulgarly called a bittered sling".<ref>{{cite book | last=Felten | first=Eric | title=How's Your Drink? Cocktails, Culture, and the Art of Drinking Well | year=2007 | publisher=Surrey Books | isbn=978-1-57284-089-8 | pages=9–10}}</ref>

===Official cocktail of New Orleans===
In March 2008, Louisiana state senator [[Edwin R. Murray]] (D-New Orleans) filed Senate Bill 6 designating the Sazerac as Louisiana's official state cocktail. The bill was defeated on April 8, 2008. After further debate, on June 23, 2008, the [[Louisiana Legislature]] agreed to proclaim the Sazerac as New Orleans' official cocktail.<ref>
{{cite news | url=https://www.npr.org/2008/06/26/91912549/new-orleans-declares-sazerac-its-cocktail-of-choice | title=New Orleans Declares Sazerac Its Cocktail of Choice | work=[[NPR]] | date=June 26, 2008}}</ref>

In 2011, as a writer for the [[HBO]] TV series ''[[Treme (TV series)|Treme]]'', [[Anthony Bourdain]] penned a scene in which chef Janette Desautel (played by [[Kim Dickens]]) tosses one in the face of restaurant critic and food writer [[Alan Richman]] (appearing as himself). Richman had angered many New Orleanians in 2006 with an article in ''[[GQ]]'' in which he criticized New Orleans' food culture after [[Hurricane Katrina]]. Despite reservations, he agreed to participate in the scene and called Sazerac "a good choice of weaponry, because it symbolizes the city",<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.gq.com/story/alan-richman-anthony-bourdain-treme | title=Alan Richman Returns To New Orleans | last=Richman | first=Alan | author-link=Alan Richman | work=[[GQ]] | date=May 16, 2011}}</ref> despite a running feud with Bourdain over, among other things, the review.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/06/05/arts/television/treme-on-hbo-focuses-on-food.html | title='Treme' Sharpens Its Focus on Food | first=Kathryn | last=Shattuck | work=[[The New York Times]] | date=June 3, 2011 | url-access=limited}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2017/02/13/anthony-bourdains-moveable-feast | title= Anthony Bourdain's Moveable Feast | first=Patrick Radden | last=Keefe | work=[[The New Yorker]] | date=February 6, 2017}}</ref>

==Similar cocktails==
A cocktail named the [[Zazarac]] was included in the 1910 version of ''Jack's Manual'', an early bartender's reference written by Jacob "Jack" Grohusko, the head bartender at Baracca's restaurant in New York.<ref>{{cite book | last1=Grohusko | first1=Jacob "Jack" | title=Jack's Manual | url=https://archive.org/details/jacksmanualonvin00groh | date=1910 | publisher=McClunn & Co | location=New York | page=[https://archive.org/details/jacksmanualonvin00groh/page/84 84] | edition=second}}</ref> It is essentially the same cocktail as the Sazerac, but called for bourbon (and not rye) instead of cognac.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.mashed.com/1382669/zazarac-cocktail-isnt-misspelled-version-iconic-sazerac/ | title=A Zazarac Cocktail Isn't A Misspelled Version Of The Iconic Sazerac | first=Courtney | last=Kaleal | work=[[Mashed.com]] | date=September 4, 2023}}</ref>

Later versions of the drink were spelled Zazarac and added rum, and are thought by some to be a variant of the Sazerac, although it might have originated completely independently of the more famous drink.<ref>{{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sCR7wWhM7IQC&q=Zazarac | title=Vintage Spirits and Forgotten Cocktails | first=Ted | last=Haigh | isbn=978-1616734756 | publisher=Quarry Books | pages=219–20 | date=February 27, 2014 }}</ref>

==Brands==
''Sazerac'' is also a brand of [[rye whiskey]] produced by the [[Sazerac Company]].

{{short description|Cocktail made with cognac, orange liqueur, and lemon}}
{{Other uses|Sidecar (disambiguation)}}

The '''sidecar''' is a [[cocktail]] traditionally made with [[brandy]] (usually [[cognac]]), orange liqueur ([[Cointreau]], [[Grand Marnier]], dry [[Curaçao (liqueur)|curaçao]], or a [[triple sec]]), and [[lemon juice]]. It became popular in Paris and London in the early 1920s. Common modifications of the original recipe are a sugar rim, added sugar syrup, and an orange twist or lemon twist.

==Similar drinks==
The sidecar is categorized as a [[daisy (cocktail)|daisy]]: a spirit, citrus juice, and a liqueur as sweetener. Other well-known daisies include the [[margarita]] (literally "daisy" in Spanish) and the [[White Lady (cocktail)|White Lady]]. Daisies are variants of the older [[Sour (cocktail)|sour]] formula, which use sugar for sweetening; daisies are more complex and often drier. Daisies in general and the sidecar in particular are considered more of a challenge for bartenders because the proportion of ingredients is more difficult to balance for liqueurs of variable sweetness.<ref>{{cite book |last=Fauchald |first=Nick |title=Cocktail Codex: Fundamentals, Formulas, Evolutions |date=2018 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jR1xDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA153 |page=152|publisher=Ten Speed Press |isbn=9781607749707 }}</ref>

In its ingredients, the drink is perhaps most closely related to the older [[Brandy Crusta|brandy crusta]], which differs both in presentation and in proportions of its components.

==History==
===Origin===
{{more citations needed section|date=July 2019}}
The exact origin of the sidecar is unclear, but it is thought to have been invented around the end of [[World War I]] in either London or Paris.<ref>{{cite book|last1=McCleat|first1=W. T.|title=Timeless Vintage Drinks & Cocktails: Here's to You!|date=2014|publisher=Bushie|isbn=978-1493589043|page=65|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZZfeAgAAQBAJ&q=Sidecar+(cocktail)|access-date=28 June 2017}}</ref> The drink was directly named for the [[sidecar|motorcycle attachment]], which was very commonly used at the time. 

The [[Hôtel Ritz Paris|Ritz Hotel in Paris]] claims origin of the drink. The first recipes for the sidecar appear in 1922, in Robert Vermeire's ''Cocktails and How to Mix Them'' and [[Harry MacElhone]]'s ''Harry's ABC of Mixing Cocktails''. It is one of six basic drinks listed in [[David A. Embury]]'s ''[[The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks]]'' (1948).

In early editions of MacElhone's book, he cites the inventor as Pat MacGarry, "the popular bartender at [[Buck's Club]], London", but in later editions he cites himself. While Vermiere states that the drink was "very popular in France. It was first introduced in London by MacGarry, the celebrated bartender of Buck's Club." Embury credits the invention of the drink to an American army captain in Paris during World War I and named after the motorcycle sidecar that the captain used.

The earliest recipe in MacElhone is:<ref>{{cite book |last=MacElhone |first=Harry |authorlink=Harry MacElhone |title=Harry of Ciro's ABC of Mixing Cocktails |date=1923 |publisher=Dean & Son Ltd |location=London |page=[https://euvs-vintage-cocktail-books.cld.bz/1923-Harry-of-Ciro-s-ABC-of-mixing-cocktails-second-impression/65 65]}}</ref>{{efn|Reference is to the second edition in 1923, but this is a reprint (with different ads) of the first edition of 1922.}}
: '''229. Side-Car Cocktail.'''
: ⅓ Cointreau (Triple sec), ⅓ Brandy, ⅓ Lemon Juice.
: ''(Recipe by MacGarry, the popular bar-tender at Buck's Club, London.)''

Journalist O.O. McIntyre reports in his 1937 summary of a visit to New York City that bartenders there attributed the drink to American expatriates Erskine Gywnne and [[Basil Woon]].<ref>{{Cite news|last=McIntyre|first=O.O.|year=1937|title=O.O. McIntyre|volume=43|page=24|work=San Bernardino Sun|issue=14|url=https://cdnc.ucr.edu/?a=d&d=SBS19370414.1.24&srpos=1&e=-------en--20--1--txt-txIN-erskine+gywnne-------1|access-date=July 28, 2021}}</ref>

===Ratios===
Both MacElhone and Vermiere state the recipe as equal parts cognac, [[Cointreau]], and lemon juice (1:1:1), now known as "the French school". Later, an "English school" of sidecars emerged, as found in the ''Savoy Cocktail Book'' (1930), which calls for two parts cognac and one part each of Cointreau and lemon juice (2:1:1).

According to Embury, the original sidecar had several ingredients, which were "refined away" (there is no evidence for this). Embury also states the drink is simply a daiquiri with brandy as its base rather than rum, and with Cointreau as the sweetening agent rather than sugar syrup. He recommends the same proportions (8:2:1) for both, making a much-less-sweet sidecar. However, Simon Difford, in his book ''Encyclopedia of Cocktails'', notes Harry Craddock's ratio of 2:1:1 in ''The Savoy Cocktail Book'', and then suggests a middle ground between Craddock's recipe and the "French school" equal parts recipe of 3:2:2, calling Embury's daiquiri formula "overly dry" for a sidecar.<ref>{{cite web |last=Difford |first=Simon |title=Sidecar (Difford's Formula) |url=http://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktail-results.jsp?id=1773&sortBy=name&}}</ref>

===Modifications===
The earliest known mention of sugaring the rim on a sidecar glass is in the 1932 American cocktail book ''Wet Drinks for Dry People''.<ref name="simonson">{{cite web |url=https://punchdrink.com/articles/ultimate-best-sidecar-brandy-cocktail-recipe/ |title= In Search of the Ultimate Sidecar |date=2019-10-17 |first=Robert |last=Simonson}}</ref> This was popular by 1934, when it appeared in three books: Burke's ''Complete Cocktail & Drinking Recipes'', Gordon's ''Cocktail & Food Recipes'', and ''Drinks As They Are Mixed'' (a revised reprint of Paul E. Lowe's 1904 book).

Common modifications of the original recipe are a sugar rim, added sugar syrup, and an orange twist or lemon twist. Recipes of the [[craft cocktail renaissance]] of the 2000s are closer to the British ratio of 2:1:1, but almost always add sugar syrup, as the drink is otherwise considered too dry and tart.<ref name="simonson" />

The '''Singapore sling''' is a gin-based [[sling (cocktail)|sling]] [[cocktail]] from [[Singapore]]. This [[long drink]] was reputed to have been developed in 1915 by Ngiam Tong Boon ({{zh|first=t|t=嚴崇文|s=严崇文|p=Yán Chóngwén|w=Yen Ch'ung-wen}}), a bartender at the Long Bar in [[Raffles Hotel]], Singapore.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Singapore Sling |url=https://www.nlb.gov.sg/main/article-detail?cmsuuid=a671de5e-c8f0-49a8-9569-4a71fd0d8408 |website=[[National Library Board]] |access-date=7 June 2025 |archive-date=2 March 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240302110023/https://www.nlb.gov.sg/main/article-detail?cmsuuid=a671de5e-c8f0-49a8-9569-4a71fd0d8408 |url-status=live }}</ref> It was initially called the '''gin sling'''.<ref>''[[The Daily Telegraph]]'', "Peterborough: Sling shot AVA GARDNER'S knickers are still missing", 13 April 1991</ref><ref>{{cite news |first=Colin |last=Campbell |title=Singapore Journal; Back to Somerset Maugham and Life's Seamy Side |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1982/12/12/travel/singapore-sling-is-spoken-here.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=12 December 1982 |archive-date=9 November 2019 |access-date=12 February 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191109180112/https://www.nytimes.com/1982/12/12/travel/singapore-sling-is-spoken-here.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

== History ==
The drink was created sometime between 1899 and 1915 at [[Raffles Hotel]]. Simon Difford wrote that the drink was originally Ngiam's "house" version of the gin sling.<ref name="difford">{{Cite web |last=Difford |first=Simon |title=Singapore Sling |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/446/cocktails/singapore-sling |work=Difford's Guide |access-date=March 2, 2024 |archive-date=19 September 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240919171038/https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/446/cocktails/singapore-sling |url-status=live }}</ref> It was socially unacceptable for women to drink alcohol in public at that time, so Ngiam made the cocktail look like fruit juice to enable women to drink it.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Hinson |first=Tamara |date=30 July 2019 |title=The story behind the Singapore Sling |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/travel/asia/singapore-sling-recipe-cocktail-how-to-make-raffles-hotel-history-a9025201.html |work=[[The Independent]] |archive-date=6 January 2026 |access-date=10 February 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260106011230/https://www.independent.co.uk/travel/asia/singapore-sling-recipe-cocktail-how-to-make-raffles-hotel-history-a9025201.html |url-status=live }}</ref> On the other hand, David Wondrich of ''[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]'' claimed that the drink was created in the 1890s and wasn't related to the Raffles until the 1920s.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Wondrich |first=David |date=March 25, 2011 |title=The Imposters |url=https://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/a9663/authentic-cocktail-recipes-0411/ |work=Esquire |archive-date=31 January 2026 |access-date=10 February 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260131161552/https://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/a9663/authentic-cocktail-recipes-0411/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

The original recipe of the Singapore sling is debated. This is because the original recipe was lost after the 1930s when the hotel stopped serving the drink.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Straits Sling|url=https://www.drinkboy.com/cocktails/Recipe.aspx?itemid=155|work=[[Robert Hess (cocktail enthusiast)|DrinkBoy]]|access-date=March 2, 2024|archive-date=12 August 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250812051941/https://drinkboy.com/Cocktails/Recipe.aspx?itemid=155|url-status=live}}</ref> [[D. A. Embury]] stated in the ''[[Fine Art of Mixing Drinks]]'': "Of all the recipes published for [this drink] I have never seen any two that were alike." ''[[The Times]]'' described the "original recipe" as a mixture of two measures of gin with one of [[Kirsch|cherry brandy]] and one each of orange, pineapple, and lime juice.<ref>p. iv/4 (Singapore Suppl.), The Times 19 July 1976</ref> The hotel's recipe was recreated based on a 1936 note by a visitor.<ref name="difford"/>

The Long Bar at Raffles Hotel sells 800-1200 Singapore slings every day. 70% of the total revenue of the bar comes from the sling, which earns the bar S$15 million in annual sales.<ref>{{cite news|last=Presser|first=Brandon|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2024-02-22/8-secrets-of-five-star-hotels-i-learned-as-a-butler-to-vips-celebrities|archive-url=https://archive.today/20241229090210/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2024-02-22/8-secrets-of-five-star-hotels-i-learned-as-a-butler-to-vips-celebrities|title=Eight Secrets of Fancy Hotels I Learned After Becoming a Butler|date=22 February 2024|work=[[Bloomberg News]]|accessdate=4 March 2024|archivedate=29 December 2024|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Today ==
By the 1980s, in countries such as the United States, the Singapore sling was often little more than gin, bottled [[sour mix]], and [[grenadine]], a mixture showing very little relationship to the recipe used elsewhere under the same name. By that time both in the Raffles Hotel and Hong Kong, and generally in the UK, the recipe had remained standardised as gin and cherry brandy (in various ratios between 2:1 and 1:2). By 2000, [[Bénédictine]] was introduced and pineapple juice used more. In New Orleans, sometimes [[Hurricane (cocktail)|Hurricane]] mix was used instead of pineapple.

In the 1983 film ''[[Superman III]]'', Gus Gorman ([[Richard Pryor]]) prepares a Singapore sling for Smallville security guard Brad ([[Gavan O27Herlihy|Gavan O'Herlihy]]). However, Brad tarnishes the drink by requesting that vodka be added.<ref>{{cite web |title=Superman III Singapore Sling |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0086393/goofs/?item=gf1794851 |website=IMDb.com |access-date=July 24, 2025}}</ref>

== Gin slings ==
The gin [[sling (drink)|sling]], attested from 1790, described a North American drink of gin, which was flavoured, sweetened, and served cold.<ref>[[OED]], '''gin-sling, n.'''</ref> The "Singapore sling" has been documented as early as 1930 as a recipe in the ''[[Savoy Cocktail Book]]'': Ingredients one-quarter lemon juice, one-quarter dry gin, one-half cherry brandy: "Shake well and strain into medium-sized glass, and fill with soda water. Add 1 lump of ice".<ref>[[OED]] '''Singapore sling n'''.</ref>

This recipe persisted for decades and is recalled in 1982 in ''The Sainsbury Book of Cocktails & Party Drinks'',<ref>{{cite book |last1=Turner |first1=Joe |title=The Sainsbury Book of Cocktails & Party Drinks |date=1982 |publisher=Cathay Books |location=London |isbn=0-86178-182-1 |page=68}}</ref> where it is also called the Singapore sling and was the classic recipe of the time.  A minor difference occurs in that the measures of the spirits were twice the quantity compared with the lemon and soda of the 1930 quotation and garnished with slice of lemon and a glacé cherry. These two very similar forms represent a traditional British version of the Singapore sling.

Also documented in ''The Sainsbury Book of Cocktails & Party Drinks'' is the Straits sling (also a Raffles Hotel invention named after the nearby [[Singapore Strait]]), which was even stronger, but also added Bénédictine, Angostura bitters, and orange bitters, but its garnish was both lemon and orange slices and it did not have the glacé cherry.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Turner |first1=Joe |title=The Sainsbury Book of Cocktails & Party Drinks |date=1982 |publisher=Cathay Books |location=London |isbn=0-86178-182-1 |page=69}}</ref>

''[[Brewer's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable]]'' (''Brewer's'') refers to the gin sling as "a drink mainly composed of gin and lemon" and states that it has been attributed to bartender John Collins of London, "but it dates from before his time and was found in the U.S.A. by 1800",<ref>''[[Brewer's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable]]'', 1969, p. 463.</ref> which is similar to the [[John Collins (cocktail)|John Collins]], another cocktail of gin and lemon.
