The '''tequila sunrise''' is a [[cocktail]] made of [[tequila]], [[orange juice]], and [[grenadine]] syrup. The drink is served unmixed in a tall glass. The modern drink originates from [[Sausalito, California]], in the early 1970s after an earlier iteration created in the 1930s in [[Phoenix, Arizona]]. The cocktail is named for its appearance when served—with gradations of color resembling an inverted sunrise.

==History==
The original tequila sunrise contained [[tequila]], [[crème de cassis]], [[lime juice]], and [[soda water]]. It was created at the [[Arizona Biltmore Hotel]] by Gene Sulit in the 1930s or 1940s.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.cocktailatlas.com/L2Signature/Arizona_Biltmore/Wright_Bar.htm |title=The Wright Bar at the Arizona Biltmore |access-date=2010-08-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100914025932/http://www.cocktailatlas.com/L2Signature/Arizona_Biltmore/Wright_Bar.htm |archive-date=2010-09-14 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
 
The more popular modern version of the cocktail contains [[tequila]], [[orange juice]], and [[grenadine]], and was created by Bobby Lozoff and Billy Rice in the early 1970s while they were working as young bartenders at [[The Trident (restaurant)|the Trident]] in [[Sausalito, California]] north of San Francisco. At a party at the Trident organized by [[Bill Graham (promoter)|Bill Graham]] to kick off the [[Rolling Stones]]' 1972 tour in America, [[Mick Jagger]] had one of the cocktails, liked it, and he and his entourage started drinking them.<ref name="marinlocalnews/tequila-sunrise">{{cite news |last1=Clinton |first1=Larry |title=Tequila Sunrise – a drink with big Marin history |url=https://marinlocalnews.com/tequila-sunrise-a-drink-with-big-marin-history/ |access-date=20 August 2023 |work=Marin Local News |agency=Sausalito Historical Society |date=9 August 2023 |archive-date=24 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230824170103/https://marinlocalnews.com/tequila-sunrise-a-drink-with-big-marin-history/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=MarinIJ>{{cite news |last=Burkhart |first=Jeff |date=2011-06-19 |title=Barfly: when it's not just another tequila sunrise |url=http://www.marinij.com/ci_18279560 |newspaper=Marin Independent Journal |location=Novato CA |publisher=David Rounds |editor=Doug Bunnell |issn=0891-5164 |oclc=61313188 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141021205601/http://www.marinij.com/ci_18279560 |archive-date=2014-10-21 |access-date=2014-10-21 |quote=Mick came up to the bar and asked for a margarita, I asked him if he had ever tried a tequila sunrise, he said no, I built him one and they started sucking them up. After that they took them all across the country.}}</ref> They later ordered them all across America, even dubbing the tour itself their "cocaine and tequila sunrise tour".<ref name=Richards-Life>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JuDQleqK5PYC |title=Life |last1=Richards |first1=Keith |date=Oct 26, 2010 |publisher=Little, Brown |location=New York |access-date=2014-10-21 |chapter=9 |page=326 |isbn=978-0316034418 |quote=The '72 tour was known by other names—the cocaine and Tequila Sunrise tour, or the STP, Stones Touring Party.}}</ref><ref name=RollingStone>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/pictures/exclusive-life-excerpt-20101014 |title=Exclusive 'Life' Excerpt from Keith Richards |last1=Richards |first1=Keith |date=October 14, 2010 |magazine=Rolling Stone  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140422133952/http://www.rollingstone.com/music/pictures/exclusive-life-excerpt-20101014 |archive-date=2014-04-22 |access-date=2014-10-21}}</ref>

According to Lozoff, at the time the Trident was the largest outlet for tequila in the United States, and in 1973 [[Jose Cuervo]] picked up on the new drink as a marketing opportunity and put the recipe for the new drink on the back of their bottles of tequila, and promoted it in other ways. Later that same year, the [[Eagles (band)|Eagles]] recorded a song called "[[Tequila Sunrise (Eagles song)|Tequila Sunrise]]" for their ''[[Desperado (Eagles album)|Desperado]]'' album as the drink was soaring in popularity.<ref name=nga-blog>{{cite web |url=http://ngablog.com/2012/02/17/just-another-tequila-sunrise/ |title=Just Another Tequila Sunrise |last1=Burkhart |first1=Jeff |date=February 17, 2012 |website=National Geographic Assignment Blog |publisher=National Geographic Society |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141021213612/http://ngablog.com/2012/02/17/just-another-tequila-sunrise/ |archive-date=2014-10-21 |access-date=2014-10-21 |quote=In 1973, Jose Cuervo seized on this new cocktail sensation and began marketing it in various print advertisements, eventually releasing it as one of their canned 'club cocktails.' 'Lou, (the manager of the Trident) talked to the Cuervo people,' said Lozoff. 'We were the biggest outlet in the United States, and they were talking to us – that recipe, with crème de cassis, went on the back of bottles, and at one point our recipe made it on the back of the gold bottle.'}}</ref> In 1988, a successful film titled ''[[Tequila Sunrise (film)|Tequila Sunrise]]'' was released, starring [[Michelle Pfeiffer]], [[Mel Gibson]], and [[Kurt Russell]] and directed by [[Robert Towne]].

[[File:Trident Historical Marker.jpg|thumb|Trident Tequila Sunrise Historical Marker]]
On June 25, 2023, the [[Marin History Museum]] placed a historical marker at the Trident Restaurant to commemorate the Rolling Stones party and the re-interpretation of the Tequila Sunrise there.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Burkhart |first1=Jeff |title=Celebrate National Tequila Sunrise Day where it has Bay Area roots |url=https://www.mercurynews.com/2023/06/21/celebrate-national-tequila-sunrise-day-where-it-has-important-roots/ |work=Mercury News |date=June 21, 2023 |access-date=June 28, 2023 |archive-date=August 24, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230824170032/https://www.mercurynews.com/2023/06/21/celebrate-national-tequila-sunrise-day-where-it-has-important-roots/ |url-status=live }}</ref>
On April 14, 2025, Lozoff died in Hawaii. He was 77 years old.<ref>{{cite news |title=Bartender who created tequila sunrise at Bay Area restaurant dies at 77 |author=Jeff Burkhart |date=April 30, 2025 |work=The Mercury News |url=https://www.mercurynews.com/2025/04/30/bobby-lozoff-bartender-who-created-tequila-sunrise-at-marin-restaurant-dies-at-77/}}</ref>

Other recipes with a similar appearance have been named in imitation of this: for instance the Caribbean sunrise is made with [[vodka]] and [[pineapple juice]] replacing the tequila and orange juice.<ref>{{cite web |title=Caribbean Sunrise Recipe |url=https://realfood.tesco.com/recipes/caribbean-sunrise.html |website=Tesco Real Food |access-date=24 April 2026}}</ref> A [[mocktail]] version can be made by replacing the tequila with a non-alcoholic substitute such as [[soda water]]<ref>{{cite web |last1=Polotnianko |first1=Nic |title=Sunrise Mocktail Recipe |url=https://www.cocktailwave.com/recipes/sunrise-mocktail |website=CocktailWave |access-date=24 April 2026}}</ref> or a combination of [[grape juice]] and lime juice.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Maize |first1=Joseph |title=Tequila Sunrise Mocktail (Non-Alcoholic): Vibrant Recipe |url=https://therookiecook.com/tequila-sunrise-mocktail/ |website=The Rookie Cook |access-date=24 April 2026}}</ref>

==Preparation and serving==
The tequila sunrise is considered a [[long drink]] and is usually served in a [[collins glass|collins]] or [[highball glass]]. The International Bartender Association has designated this cocktail as an [[IBA Official Cocktail]].

The drink is made by pouring in tequila, then the orange juices, and grenadine last. The drink's signature look is created by adding the grenadine without it mixing with the other ingredients. A spoon may be used to guide the syrup down the glass wall to the bottom with minimal mixing. Ice may be added before the tequila, or chilled orange juice may be used.

A '''rusty nail''' is a [[cocktail]] made by mixing [[Scotch whisky]] with [[Drambuie]] in a ratio ranging from 1:1 to 2:1. It is typically served [[on the rocks]] in an [[old-fashioned glass]] (also known as a rocks glass), though it can be served "[[Straight up|up]]" in a [[stemmed glass]]. The cocktail's origin goes back to the 1937 British Industries Fair, but it gained widespread popularity in the 1950s after being endorsed by New York's [[21 Club]]. Its prominence grew further a decade later when it became the go-to cocktail of the [[Rat Pack]].<ref>{{cite book|page=69|title=The New Single Malt Whiskey|editor=Carlo DeVito|publisher=[[HarperCollins|Cider Mill Press]]|isbn=9781604336474|year=2016}}</ref>

==Variations==
Variations of the drink can be made using any aged [[Liquor|spirit]] with the [[Drambuie]] (its one essential ingredient),<ref name= "ingrd">[https://whiskyadvocate.com/rusty-nail-cocktail-recipe/ ''Essential Whisky Cocktail: Rusty Nail'']; The Whisky Advocate online; accessed February 2023</ref> although using blended [[Scotch whisky]] in a 1 to 1 or 2 to 1 ratio is traditional.<ref name="DeGff" /><ref name="DWond" /> The addition of additional Drambuie tends to sweeten the cocktail.<ref name= "J-Hill"/><ref>{{cite journal | title =Rusty Nail recipe | journal =Drinks Mixer| url = http://www.drinksmixer.com/drink4306.html| access-date =December 3, 2013}}</ref> The cocktail can be garnished with a twist of citrus, usually orange, that will enhance the acidity and flavor.<ref name= "chrry" />

Other variations include:
* The ''rusty compass'', adds cherry liqueur to the rusty nail mix<ref name= "chrry">[https://www.liquor.com/recipes/rusty-compass/ ''Rusty Compass'']; Liquor.com article; accessed February 2023</ref>
* Another ''smoky nail'' that is known in Spanish as the ''clavo ahumado''; it uses [[mezcal]] instead of whisky<ref>{{cite episode | last =Caporale | first =Anthony| title =Tales of the Cocktail: Cocktails Made with Drambuie | series =Good Morning New Orleans| date =July 9, 2013| url =http://wgno.com/2013/07/19/clavo-ahumado/#axzz2ZVLSXrBY | access-date =December 3, 2013}}</ref>
* The [[Donald Sutherland]] substituted [[rye whiskey|Canadian rye whisky]] for the blended Scotch whisky<ref name= "J-Hill">{{cite news| last =Hillibish| first =Jim| title =Highland Fling: Drambuie isn't just for after dinner| newspaper =[[The Repository|Canton Repository]]| date =August 19, 2010| url =http://www.cantonrep.com/carousel/x179628616/Highland-fling-Drambuie-isnt-just-for-after-dinner| access-date =November 25, 2012| url-status =dead| archive-url =https://archive.today/20130119031518/http://www.cantonrep.com/carousel/x179628616/Highland-fling-Drambuie-isnt-just-for-after-dinner| archive-date =January 19, 2013| quote= "...the blending of 1 part Drambuie to 1 part Scotch counterbalances the Scotch flavor..."}}</ref>

==History==
According to cocktail historian David Wondrich, "...the Rusty Nail took a while to find its proper place in the world".  The combination of Drambuie—"the world's most distinguished Scotch-based liqueur"—and the whisky it is made from first appears in 1937 in the form of the B.I.F., credited to one F. Benniman and ostensibly named after the British Industries Fair.<ref name="DWond">{{cite journal | last =Wondrich | first =David| title =Rusty Nail | journal=[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]| url =http://www.esquire.com/drinks/rusty-nail-drink-recipe| access-date =December 3, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131105144806/http://www.esquire.com/drinks/rusty-nail-drink-recipe |archive-date=November 5, 2013| quote= "...The quantities here are a rough ratio ... Half and half is too sweet for us, but some folks swear by it..."}}</ref> Wondrich goes on to note that "it took another generation or so for the drink to assume its classic name and form, during which time it tried on several identities. Here it's a D&S...there a Little Club No. 1 (the Little Club being a rather swank sort of joint on East Fifty-fifth Street much haunted by showbiz types); at [[United States Air Force|USAF]] Officers' Clubs in Thailand and the Republic of Viet-Nam,{{sic}} it's a Mig-21, while in the upper Midwest it's a Knucklehead."<ref name="DWond" />

The cocktail authority [[Dale DeGroff]] said "the Rusty Nail is often credited to the clever bartenders at the [[21 Club]] in Manhattan sometime in the early 1960s"<ref name= "ingrd" /><ref name="DeGff">{{cite journal | last =Degroff | first =Dale| title =Behind the Bar: The Rusty Nail | website =Liquor.com| url =http://liquor.com/articles/behind-the-bar-the-rusty-nail/| access-date =December 3, 2013| quote= "...'Old Mister Boston' calls for a one-to-one ratio..."}}</ref> The cocktail's name was finally cemented in 1963, when Gina MacKinnon, the chairwoman of the Drambuie Liqueur Company, gave the rusty nail her endorsement in ''[[The New York Times]]''.<ref name="DeGff" /><ref>{{cite journal | title =Rusty Nail | journal =Liquor and Drink| url =http://www.liquoranddrink.com/drinks/199-rusty-nail| access-date =December 3, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131206185554/http://www.liquoranddrink.com/drinks/199-rusty-nail |archive-date=December 6, 2013 |url-status=usurped}}</ref> DeGroff reported that in the early 1960s "...the Rat Pack was enamored of the drink, which may have been responsible for the wide appeal in those years."<ref name="DeGff" />

'''White lady''' (also known as a '''Delilah''',<ref name="spruce">{{Cite web |last=Graham |first=Colleen |date=15 November 2016 |title=Delilah Cocktail or White Lady Cocktail Gin Recipe |url=https://www.thespruce.com/delilah-cocktail-recipe-759293 |access-date=3 March 2017 |website=the spruce |archive-date=4 March 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170304113953/https://www.thespruce.com/delilah-cocktail-recipe-759293 |url-status=dead }}</ref> or '''Chelsea sidecar'''<ref name=spruce/><!--These names deleted from the article; need a reliable source that isn't a likely copy from Wikipedia: '''Kiernander''', '''Janikedvence''' and '''Lillian Forever'''-->) is a classic cocktail that is made with [[gin]], [[Cointreau]] or [[triple sec]], fresh lemon juice and an optional [[egg white]].<ref name="diffords_white_lady">{{Cite web |title=White Lady cocktail |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/512/cocktails/white-lady-cocktail |website=Difford's}}</ref> It belongs to the [[Sidecar_(cocktail)|sidecar]] family, made with [[gin]] in place of [[brandy]]. The cocktail sometimes also includes additional ingredients, for example egg white, sugar, [[cream]], or [[creme de menthe]].<ref name="diffords_minty_white_lady">{{Cite web |title=Minty White Lady cocktail |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/3601/minty-white-lady-cocktail |website=Difford's}}</ref>

The classic concoction is most commonly served in a martini [[cocktail glass]]. When an egg white is added a [[Champagne stemware|champagne coupe]] is preferable; the silky foam clings more pleasingly to the curved glass.

==Origin==
The original recipe for the white lady was devised by [[Harry MacElhone]] in 1919 at Ciro's Club in London. He originally used [[crème de menthe]] (specifically, Giffard's Menthe Pastille), but replaced it with gin at [[Harry's New York Bar]] in Paris in 1929.<ref name="gin">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GIAwBAAAQBAJ |title=The Spirit of Gin: A Stirring Miscellany of the New Gin Revival |date=2014 |publisher=Simon & Schuster|isbn=978-1-60433-532-3 }}</ref><ref name="diffords_white_lady" />

According to the American Bar at the Savoy Hotel, the drink was created there by [[Harry Craddock]].<ref name="diffords_white_lady" />

==History==
A recipe for the white lady made with gin, Cointreau, and fresh lemon juice appears in the ''Savoy Cocktail Book'', published in 1930.<ref name="secondref">[http://www.findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_qn4158/is_20050219/ai_n9769314 101 cocktails that shook the world: #5: The White Lady | Independent, The (London) | Find Articles at BNET.com<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> [[Joe Gilmore]], former Head Barman at The Savoy, says this was one of [[Laurel and Hardy]]'s favorite drinks.<ref>The Savoy: Checking into History" [[Channel 4]] TV UK</ref> 

Early recipes like MacElhone's and Craddock's do not have egg white as one of the recorded ingredients.<ref name="diffords_white_lady" />

==Comparison with gin sour==
While [[Sour (cocktail)|sours]] are characterized by a bright acidity, [[Sidecar (cocktail)|sidecars]] are often drier, since they are made with [[liqueur]]s (in this case [[Cointreau]]) instead of sugar. Sidecars are considered more of a challenge for bartenders because the proportion of ingredients is more difficult to balance for liqueurs of variable sweetness.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fauchald |first=Nick |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jR1xDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA153 |title=Cocktail Codex: Fundamentals, Formulas, Evolutions |date=2018 |page=152|publisher=Clarkson Potter/Ten Speed |isbn=978-1-60774-970-7 }}</ref>

==In popular culture==
In [[John le Carré]]'s 1965 novel ''[[The Looking Glass War]]'', the British spy, and main protagonist, Fred Leiser's favourite drink is a white lady and he makes several attempts to get other agents to try the cocktail.

It is mentioned in the novel ''[[Islands in the Stream (novel)|Islands in the Stream]]'' by [[Ernest Hemingway]].<ref name=gin />

It is also mentioned in the films ''[[Inspector Hornleigh (film)|Inspector Hornleigh]]'' (1938) and ''[[Isle of Missing Men]]'' (1942). In [[The Intelligence Men]] (1965), [[Eric Morecambe]] orders a White Lady from hotel room service, after the arrival of a lady dressed in white; [[Ernie Wise]] delivers the drink, posing as a member of staff.

A mock version of the drink is made in the Japanese manga series ''[[Kaguya-sama: Love Is War]]''.

In [[Molly Keane]]'s 1981 novel [[Good Behaviour (Keane novel)|Good Behaviour]], Aroon St. Charles drinks white ladies with her brother Hubert and their friend Richard Massingham.

The White Lady is a favorite summer drink for lead character Phryne Fisher in multiple novels by [[Kerry Greenwood]] in her series "Phryne Fisher Mysteries," which are set in late 1920's Australia. A recipe is included in Book 16: "Murder in the Dark."

In Agatha Christie's novel "By the Pricking of My Thumbs," a White Lady drink is offered to Tuppence Beresford by her husband Tommy, in Chapter 3: A Funeral.

The '''Vesper''' is a [[cocktail]] that was originally made of [[gin]], [[vodka]], and [[Kina Lillet]]. Since that form of Lillet is no longer produced, modern bartenders need to modify the recipe to mimic the original taste, with [[Lillet Blanc]] or [[Cocchi Americano]] as a typical substitute. 

The drink was popularised by author [[Ian Fleming]] (1908–1964) in his 1953 novel ''[[Casino Royale (novel)|Casino Royale]],'' in which the character [[James Bond (character)|James Bond]] invents the recipe and names the cocktail after [[Vesper Lynd]]. Fleming's Bond calls it a "special martini", and though it lacks the [[vermouth]] that defined a [[martini (cocktail)|martini]] in Fleming's day, it is sometimes called a '''Vesper martini'''.

==History==
In [[Ian Fleming]]'s ''[[Casino Royale (novel)|Casino Royale]]'', the first of his works to feature [[James Bond (literary character)|James Bond]], Bond orders a dry martini in a "deep [[Champagne glass|champagne goblet]]" but then changes his order and gives the barman a recipe. The dialogue is:<ref name=CR>{{Cite book |last=Fleming |first=Ian |title=[[Casino Royale (novel)|Casino Royale]] |publisher=[[Thomas & Mercer]] |year=2012 |isbn= 9781612185439 |pages=43–4, 51 |author-link=Ian Fleming}}</ref>
{{bquote|Just a moment. Three measures of [[Gordon's Gin|Gordon's]], one of [[vodka]], half a measure of [[Kina Lillet]]. [[Shaken, not stirred|Shake]] it very well until it's ice-cold, then add a large thin slice of [[lemon peel]]. Got it? ... This drink's my own invention. I'm going to patent it when I think of a good name.}}

Bond deems the result "excellent" and calls it a "special martini".<ref name=CR/>{{efn|After tasting the resulting drink and watching "as the deep glass became frosted with the pale golden drink, slightly aerated by the bruising of the shaker", Bond advises the barman: "Excellent ... but if you can get a vodka made with grain instead of potatoes, you will find it still better." He then gently mocks himself for making such a fine distinction.<ref name=CR/>}} Later in the novel, after being introduced to the beautiful [[Vesper Lynd]], Bond tells Vesper that his search for a name is over if she will permit him to name the drink after her.<ref name=CR/>

The cocktail was not Fleming's creation. It was devised by his friend [[Josephine Hartford Bryce#Ivar Bryce|Ivar Bryce]] as evidenced by the words Fleming inscribed in Bryce's copy of ''Casino Royale'': "For Ivar, who mixed the first ''Vesper'' and said the good word."<ref name=bryce/> Naming a cocktail the Vesper was Fleming's idea though he drew inspiration from someone else's joke. He had encountered the term at evening drinks when a butler announced: "Vespers are served."<ref name=bryce>{{Cite book |last=Bryce |first=Ivar |title=You Only Live Once – Memories of Ian Fleming |publisher=[[Weidenfeld and Nicolson Productions]] |year=1975 |isbn=0-297-77022-5 |page=106 |author-link=Ivar Bryce}}</ref> Fleming adapted this pun on the name of the religious observance normally held about sunset, "[[Vespers]]". And Bond alludes to this by praising his cocktail's name as "very appropriate to the violet hour when my cocktail will now be drunk all over the world".<ref name=CR/>

Just as the character Vesper Lynd dies in ''Casino Royale'', the cocktail named for her makes no appearance in any of Fleming's later Bond novels. Fleming, in a letter to ''[[The Guardian]]'' in 1958, said that when he tasted a Vesper for the first time "several months" after including it in his novel, he found it "unpalatable".<ref name=niland>{{cite news |access-date = 25 November 2022 | newspaper = The Guardian | date = 1 October 2012 | title = Ian Fleming defends James Bond – from the archive | first = Lauren | last = Niland | url = https://static.guim.co.uk/sys-images/Guardian/Pix/pictures/2012/9/27/1348745314585/Ian-Fleming-writes-to-the-001.jpg }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |access-date = 25 November 2022 | newspaper = The Guardian | date =5 April 1958 | title = 'The Exclusive Bond', Mr Fleming on his hero | first = Ian | last = Fleming | url = https://static.guim.co.uk/sys-images/Guardian/Pix/pictures/2012/9/27/1348745314585/Ian-Fleming-writes-to-the-001.jpg }} An image of Fleming's letter to ''The Guardian'' in its entirety.</ref>

Although the production of Kina Lillet ceased in 1986,<ref name=rathbun>{{cite book | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=KNu0QfAO-RsC&pg=PA239 | page = 239 | title =Ginger Bliss and the Violet Fizz: A Cocktail Lover's Guide to Mixing Drinks Using New and Classic Liqueurs | access-date = 26 November 2022 | first =A.J. | last =Rathbun | date = 2011 | publisher = Houghton Mifflin Harcourt | isbn = 978-1-55832-665-1 }}</ref> in the 2006 film ''[[Casino Royale (2006 film)|Casino Royale]]'', Bond ([[Daniel Craig]]) gives the barman (Stephen Ucík) the same recipe as he does in the novel.{{efn|Two other characters promptly ask for the same, and a [[Felix Leiter|third]] for the same without the lemon garnish.<ref name=lifestyle/>}} When Vesper ([[Eva Green]]) asks Bond if he named the drink after her "because of the bitter aftertaste", Bond replies that he did so "because once you have tasted it, you won't drink anything else."<ref name=lifestyle>{{Cite web |date=3 January 2007 |title=Vesper Martini | website = James Bond Lifestyle | access-date = 23 November 2022|url=https://www.jamesbondlifestyle.com/product/vesper-martini}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=DeMichael |first1=Tom |title=James Bond FAQ: All That's Left to Know About Everyone's Favorite Superspy |date=2012 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |isbn=978-1-4803-3786-2 | access-date = 26 November 2022 | page = 238 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5s-GDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT238}}</ref>{{efn|The 1967 film also titled ''[[Casino Royale (1967 film)|Casino Royale]]'' was a spoof of the Bond franchise. Vesper Lynd makes an appearance but not the cocktail.}}

The Vesper, including its original recipe recited by a barman ([[Jake Seal]]), appeared again in the film ''[[Quantum of Solace]]'' (2008), a sequel to ''Casino Royale'' based on the Bond character but no specific work of Fleming's.<ref name=storey/>

Unlike the [[Martini (cocktail)#Vodka martini|vodka martini]] and the [[mojito]], popularised by the Bond films ''[[Dr. No (film)|Dr. No]]'' (1962) and ''[[Die Another Day]]'' (2002), respectively, the Vesper did not become a familiar cocktail, likely because the Kina Lillet and later the substitute [[Lillet Blanc]], were not widely distributed.<ref name=time>{{cite magazine | magazine = [[Time (magazine)|Time]] | access-date = 25 November 2022 | url = http://www.time.com/time/arts/article/0%2C8599%2C1858088%2C00.html | url-status = dead | archive-date = 16 November 2008 | title = Shaken and Stirred, James Bond Loves His Booze |quote= the Vesper struggled to become a fad because Lillet wine is hardly ubiquitous, available only in select bars and lounges | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20081116115740/http://www.time.com/time/arts/article/0,8599,1858088,00.html | first = S. James | last = Snyder }}</ref>

==Contemporary versions==
Because the production of Kina Lillet, a fruit-and-spice flavoured ''apéritif'' wine from Bordeaux,<ref name=storey/> ceased in 1986,<ref name=rathbun/> the original recipe can no longer be used to reproduce the Fleming-Bond cocktail faithfully. Substitute ingredients attempt to recapture the original flavor of the drink.

The [[International Bartenders Association]] (IBA) recipe calls for 45 ml gin, 15 ml vodka, and 7.5 ml Lillet Blanc in place of Kina Lillet.<ref name=IBA>{{cite web | url = https://iba-world.com/vesper/ | title = Vesper | access-date = 25 November 2022 | website = International Bartenders Association | date = 29 April 2021 }}</ref> Others find Lillet Blanc an inadequate substitute for Kina Lillet, as it lacks the latter's quinine which added a distinctive taste,<ref name=time/><ref>{{Cite book |last=Embury |first=David |title=The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks |publisher=[[Doubleday (publisher)|Doubleday]] |year=1948 |author-link=David A. Embury | page= }}</ref>{{page needed|date=December 2022}} while [[Kingsley Amis]] thought the original drink too bitter and improved by substituting Lillet Blanc.<ref name=storey/> Another alternative to Lillet is [[Cocchi Americano]], a similar aromatised wine,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Hyslop |first=Leah |date=19 June 2015 |title=How to make a James Bond martini (but limit yourself to one | access-date = 23 November 2022 |work=The Telegraph |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/foodanddrink/recipes/11273408/How-to-make-James-Bonds-martini-but-limit-yourself-to-one.html}}</ref> which results in a more bitter finish than Lillet Blanc.<ref name="serious">{{cite web | website =Serious Eats | date = 21 July 2021 | first = Paul | last = Clarke | access-date = 23 November 2022 | url = http://www.seriouseats.com/recipes/2011/02/vesper-cocktail-gin-vodka-lillet-cocchi-aperitivo-americano-cocktail-recipe.html | title = The Vesper Cocktail Recipe }}</ref> Another suggested substitute is Kina L'Aéro d'Or.<ref>{{cite book | access-date = 25 November 2022 | title = Cocktail Chemistry: The Art and Science of Drinks from Iconic TV Shows and Movies | first = Nick |last =Fisher |date=2022 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=hN9IEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Kina+Lillet%22&pg=PA21 | page = 21 | publisher = S&S/Simon Element | isbn = 978-1-9821-6745-5 }}</ref> In 2006, ''[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]'' suggested adding quinine powder to replace what Lillet Blanc lacks, or as a last resort ("in desperation") adding bitters.<ref name=esquire>{{cite news | last = Wondrich | first =David | url = http://www.esquire.com/food-drink/bars/a204/esq1106drinks-84/ | title = James Bond Walks Into A Bar... | work =[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]] | access-date = 26 November 2022 | date = 31 October 2006}}</ref>{{efn|"Shake (if you must) with plenty of cracked ice. 3 oz Tanqueray gin, 1 oz 100-proof [50%] Stolichnaya vodka, {{frac|1|2}} oz Lillet Blanc, {{frac|1|8}} teaspoon (or less) quinine powder or, in desperation, 2 dashes of [[Bitters#Cocktail_bitters|bitters]]. Strain into a chilled cocktail glass and twist a large swatch of thin-cut lemon peel over the top."<ref name=esquire/>}}  Others such as Ulysses Lisbon Speakeasy uses Suze (original recipe) as another substitute for the Original Kina Lillet.

The authors of a 2018 book Cocktail Codex recommend different proportions of the ingredients. Their "classic" Vesper recipe calls for one and a half ounces of gin, three quarters of an ounce of vodka half of an ounce of Lillet Blanc and a lemon twist for garnish. The justification for those proportions is to "stretch out the gin's botanicals ans allow the Lillet to shine". More precisely, the authors use [[Plymouth Gin|Plymouth gin]] and Aylesbury Duck vodka.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kaplan |first=David |title=Cocktail codes: fundamentals, formulas and evolutions |last2=Day |first2=Alex |last3=Fauchald |first3=Nick |publisher=Ten Speed Press |year=2018 |isbn=978-1-60774-970-7 |edition=1st |location=United States |pages=71 |language=en}}</ref> 

Less attention has focused on the other spirits and their alcohol content, but both [[Tanqueray]] and [[Stolichnaya]] are sometimes mentioned.<ref name=storey>{{cite book | access-date = 26 November 2022 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=jAfMDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT133 | title =History of Men's Accessories: A Short Guide for Men About Town | first =Nicholas |last=Storey |date= 2011 | publisher = Pen & Sword Books| isbn=978-1-84884-992-1 }} Entry for "Vesper Martini".</ref>{{pages needed|date=December 2022}}<ref name=esquire/>

Although Bond drinks the first Vesper from a "deep glass", presumably the "deep [[Champagne glass|champagne goblet]]" he specified when ordering a martini before substituting the Vesper's recipe,<ref name=CR/> [[cocktail glass]]es are commonly used in modern versions of this drink, as ''[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]''<ref name=esquire/> and the [[International Bartenders Association|IBA]]<ref name=IBA/> recommend.

The '''IBA official cocktails''' are [[cocktail]]s recognised by the [[International Bartenders Association]] (IBA) to be the most requested recipes.<ref name="iba-list">{{Cite web |title= IBA official cocktail list|url=https://iba-world.com/iba-official-cocktail-list/  |website=International Bartenders Association |access-date=2 January 2023}}</ref> The list was developed starting in 1960, and the first version was announced in 1961, comprising 50 cocktails.<ref name="iba-list" /> It has since undergone periodic revisions, and as of {{CURRENTYEAR}} comprises 102 cocktails in 3 categories; see {{slink||History}} for more.

==List of cocktails==
{{as of|2024}}, there are 102 IBA official cocktails, divided into three equal categories of 34: The Unforgettables, Contemporary Classics, and New Era Drinks.

; [[Margarita]] : Made with [[tequila]], [[Orange liqueur (disambiguation)|orange liqueur]], and [[lime juice]] often served with salt on the rim of the glass.
; [[Mimosa (cocktail)|Mimosa]] : Made with [[Champagne]] (or other [[sparkling wine]]) and chilled citrus juice, usually [[orange juice]] unless otherwise specified.
; [[Mint julep]] : Made primarily with [[Bourbon whiskey|bourbon]], sugar, water, crushed or shaved ice, and fresh [[Mentha|mint]].
; [[Mojito]] : Made with [[light rum|white rum]], sugar (traditionally [[sugar cane]] juice), [[lime juice]], [[Carbonated water|soda water]], and [[Mentha|mint]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Traditional Mojito recipe from Cuba |url=http://www.tasteofcuba.com/mojito.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110904041701/http://www.tasteofcuba.com/mojito.html |archive-date=4 September 2011 |access-date=1 September 2011 |publisher=Tasteofcuba.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Colleen Graham |last2=About.com Guide |date=11 June 2011 |title=About.com Mojito |url=http://cocktails.about.com/od/atozcocktailrecipes/r/mjto_cktl.htm |access-date=1 September 2011 |publisher=Cocktails. about.com |archive-date=8 August 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110808142629/http://cocktails.about.com/od/atozcocktailrecipes/r/mjto_cktl.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref>
; [[Moscow mule]] : Made with [[vodka]], spicy [[ginger beer]], and [[lime juice]], garnished with a slice or wedge of lime.
; [[Piña colada]] : Made with [[rum]], [[cream of coconut]] or [[coconut milk]], and [[pineapple juice]], usually served either blended or shaken with ice.
; [[Pisco sour]] : The Peruvian pisco sour uses Peruvian ''[[pisco]]'' as the base liquor and adds freshly squeezed [[lemon juice]], [[simple syrup]], ice, [[egg white]], and [[Angostura bitters]]. The Chilean version is similar, but uses Chilean ''pisco'' and [[Pica, Chile|pica]] lime, and excludes the bitters and egg white. Other variants of the cocktail include those created with fruits like [[pineapple]] or plants such as [[coca]] leaves.
; [[Rabo-de-galo|Rabo de galo]]: Made with [[cachaça]], [[sweet vermouth]], [[Cynar]], and [[Angostura bitters]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Rabo de Galo – IBA |url=https://iba-world.com/iba-cocktail/rabo-de-galo/ |access-date=2024-11-14 |language=en-US}}</ref> 
; [[Sea breeze (cocktail)|Sea breeze]] : Made with [[vodka]], [[cranberry juice]], and [[grapefruit juice]].<ref name="stillspirits">{{Cite web |title=Seabreeze – Cocktails – Flavour Essences |url=http://stillspirits.com/au/flavour-essences/cocktails/seabreeze.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110828023918/http://stillspirits.com/au/flavour-essences/cocktails/seabreeze.html |archive-date=28 August 2011 |access-date=13 June 2011 |publisher=Still Spirits }}</ref>
; [[Sex on the beach]]: Made with [[vodka]], peach [[schnapps]], orange juice, and cranberry juice.
; [[Singapore sling]] : A [[gin]]-based [[sling (cocktail)|sling]] [[cocktail]] from [[Singapore]].
; [[Tequila sunrise]] : Made with [[tequila]], [[orange juice]], and [[grenadine]] syrup.
; [[Vesper (cocktail)|Vesper]] : Originally made of [[Gordon's Gin|gin]], [[vodka]], and [[Lillet|Kina Lillet]]. The formulations of its ingredients have changed since its original publication in print, and so some modern bartenders have created new versions which attempt to more closely mimic the original taste.
; [[Zombie (cocktail)|Zombie]] : Made with fruit juices, [[liqueur]]s, and various [[rum]]s.

===New Era Drinks===

; [[Bee's knees]]: Made with [[gin]], fresh [[lemon juice]], and [[honey]]. It is served shaken and chilled, often with a [[lemon twist]].
; [[Bramble (cocktail)|Bramble]] : Made with dry [[gin]], lemon juice, sugar syrup, [[crème liqueur|crème de mûre (blackberry liqueur)]], and crushed ice.
; [[Canchanchara]] : Made with Cuban [[aguardiente]], [[honey]], and fresh lime juice.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Canchanchara |url=https://iba-world.com/cachanchara/ |access-date=18 February 2022 |website=IBA-World.com|date=29 April 2021 }}</ref>
; [[Chartreuse swizzle]]: Made with [[Chartreuse (liqueur)|Chartreuse]], [[pineapple juice]], fresh lime juice, and [[Falernum]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Chartreuse Swizzle – IBA |url=https://iba-world.com/iba-cocktail/chartreuse-swizzle/ |access-date=2024-11-14 |language=en-US}}</ref>
; [[Dark 'n' stormy]] : Made with [[Gosling's Rum|Goslings Black Seal Rum]] (the "dark") and [[ginger beer]] (the "stormy") served over ice and garnished with a slice of [[lime (fruit)|lime]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dark 'N' Stormy |url=http://iba-world.com/new-era-drinks/dark-n-stormy/ |access-date=6 July 2017 |website=iba-world.com |publisher=International Bartenders Association}}</ref>
; [[Don's special daiquiri]]: Made with gold Jamaican [[rum]], Cuban [[rum]], [[passion fruit]] juice, fresh lime juice, and honey syrup.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Don's Special Daiquiri – IBA |url=https://iba-world.com/iba-cocktail/dons-special-daiquiri/ |access-date=2024-11-14 |language=en-US}}</ref>
; [[Espresso martini]] : Made with [[vodka]], [[espresso]] coffee, [[coffee liqueur]], and sugar syrup. It is not a true [[Martini (cocktail)|martini]] as it contains neither [[gin]] nor [[vermouth]], but is one of many drinks that incorporate the term into their names.
; [[Fernet con coca|Fernandito]] : A [[long drink]] of [[Argentine]] origin consisting of the Italian [[Amaro (liqueur)|amaro]] liqueur [[fernet]] and [[cola]], served over ice.
; [[French martini]] : The key ingredient that makes a martini "French" is [[Chambord (liqueur)|Chambord]], a black raspberry [[liqueur]] that has been produced in France since 1685.<ref>{{Cite web|date=29 April 2021|title=French Martini|url=https://iba-world.com/french-martini/|access-date=15 February 2023|website=iba-world.com|language=en-US}}</ref>
; [[Gin basil smash]]: Made with [[gin]], fresh lemon juice, [[simple syrup]], and [[basil]] leaves.
; [[Grand margarita]]: Made with [[tequila]], [[Grand Marnier]], and fresh lime juice.
; [[IBA Tiki]]: Made with Ron Profundo [[Havana Club]] (a [[White Rum|white rum]]), Ron Smoky Havana Club (a [[Barrel ageing|barrel-aged]] rum), [[Amaretto|Licor Amaretto]] ([[almond]] liqueur), [[Frangelico|Licor Frangelico]] ([[hazelnut]] liqueur), [[Maraschino]], [[passion fruit]] purée, fresh pineapple juice, fresh lime juice, and a slice of [[ginger root]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=IBA Tiki – IBA |url=https://iba-world.com/iba-cocktail/iba-tiki/ |access-date=2024-11-14 |language=en-US}}</ref>
; [[Illegal (cocktail)|Illegal]]: Made with [[mezcal]], Jamaica [[Overproof rum|overproof]] white [[rum]], [[Falernum]], [[maraschino]] liqueur, [[lime juice]], [[simple syrup]], and optionally a few drops of egg white.
; [[Jungle Bird]]: Made with [[Blackstrap molasses|Blackstrap]] [[rum]], [[Campari]], pineapple juice, fresh lime juice, and [[Demerara sugar|demerara]] [[simple syrup]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jungle Bird – IBA |url=https://iba-world.com/iba-cocktail/jungle-bird/ |access-date=2024-11-14 |language=en-US}}</ref>
; [[Missionary's downfall]]: Made with white [[rum]], peach [[brandy]], fresh lime juice, honey mix, mint leaves, and pineapple chunks.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Missionary's Downfall – IBA |url=https://iba-world.com/iba-cocktail/missionarys-downfall/ |access-date=2024-11-14 |language=en-US}}</ref>
; [[Naked and famous (cocktail)|Naked and famous]] : Made with equal parts [[mezcal]], [[yellow Chartreuse]], [[Aperol]], and fresh lime juice.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Naked and Famous |url=https://iba-world.com/new-era-drinks/naked-and-famous/ |access-date=29 May 2020 |website=IBA Official Cocktails}}</ref>
; [[New York sour]] : Made with [[whisky|whiskey]] ([[rye whiskey|rye]] or [[Bourbon whiskey|bourbon]]), [[simple syrup]], [[lemon juice]], egg white, and red wine ([[Shiraz wine|Shiraz]] or [[Malbec]]).
; [[Old Cuban]] : Created in 2001 by [[mixologist]] [[Audrey Saunders]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=How the Old Cuban Became a Modern Classic |url=https://punchdrink.com/articles/old-cuban-modern-classic-champagne-mojito-cocktail-recipe/ |access-date=12 January 2021 |website=PUNCH |date=16 June 2020 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Rothbaum |first=Noah |date=7 March 2019 |title=Love Your Happy Hour Cocktail? Thank Audrey Saunders. |work=The Daily Beast |url=https://www.thedailybeast.com/love-your-happy-hour-cocktail-thank-audrey-saunders |access-date=12 January 2021}}</ref> it is made with aged [[rum]], fresh lime juice, [[simple syrup]], [[Angostura bitters]], mint leaves, and topped with [[Champagne]] [[Brut (wine)|brut]].
; [[Paloma (cocktail)|Paloma]] : Most commonly prepared by mixing [[tequila]], lime juice,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Paloma |url=https://www.liquor.com/recipes/paloma/ |website=Liquor.com}}</ref> and a [[grapefruit]]-flavored soda such as [[Fresca]], [[Squirt (soft drink)|Squirt]], or [[Jarritos]] and served [[on the rocks]] with a lime wedge. Adding salt to the rim of the glass is also an option.
; [[Paper plane (cocktail)|Paper plane]] : Made with equal parts [[Bourbon whiskey|bourbon]], [[Aperol]], [[amaro (liqueur)|amaro]] liqueur, and lemon juice.
; [[Penicillin (cocktail)|Penicillin]] : Made with [[whisky]], [[ginger]], and fresh [[lemon juice]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Penicillin |url=https://iba-world.com/new-era-drinks/penicillin/ |access-date=29 May 2020 |website=IBA Official Cocktails}}</ref>
; [[Pisco punch]]: Made with [[Pisco]], fresh pineapple juice, [[simple syrup]], fresh lemon juice, dry [[white wine]], and [[Clove|cloves]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pisco Punch – IBA |url=https://iba-world.com/iba-cocktail/pisco-punch/ |access-date=2024-11-14 |language=en-US}}</ref>
; [[Porn star martini]]: Made with vanilla [[vodka]], [[passion fruit]] liqueur, passion fruit purée, vanilla sugar, and [[Champagne]] on the side.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Porn Star Martini – IBA |url=https://iba-world.com/iba-cocktail/porn-star-martini/ |access-date=2024-11-14 |language=en-US}}</ref>
; [[Russian spring punch]] : Made with [[vodka]], [[crème de cassis]], sugar syrup, and [[lemon juice]].
; [[Sherry cobbler]]: Made with two kinds of [[sherry]] ([[Amontillado]] and [[Palo Cortado]]), sugar, orange wheel, and lemon wheel.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sherry Cobbler – IBA |url=https://iba-world.com/iba-cocktail/sherry-cobbler/ |access-date=2024-11-14 |language=en-US}}</ref>
; [[South Side (cocktail)|South Side]]: Made with [[gin]], [[lemon juice]], [[simple syrup]], and [[Mentha|mint]] (also known as "Southside").<ref name="MentalFloss">{{Cite web |last=Puchko |first=Kristy |date=23 February 2016 |title=The Origins Of 10 Popular Prohibition Cocktails |url=http://mentalfloss.com/article/57719/origins-10-popular-prohibition-cocktails |access-date=3 September 2016 |website=Mental Floss }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=South Side – IBA |url=https://iba-world.com/iba-cocktail/south-side/ |access-date=2024-11-14 |language=en-US}}</ref>
; [[Spicy Fifty]]: Made with [[vodka]], [[elderflower cordial]], honey syrup, red chili pepper, and fresh [[Lime (fruit)|lime juice]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Spicy Fifty |url=https://iba-world.com/new-era-drinks/spicy-fifty/ |access-date=29 May 2020 |website=IBA Official Cocktails}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=What is spicy rosé, social media's hottest new drinks trend? |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/food-and-drink/wine/what-spicy-rose-social-medias-hottest-new-drinks-trend/ |access-date=April 29, 2023 |work=The Telegraph |date=July 25, 2022 |quote=A longer standing cocktail is the spicy fifty – top of the list at The Donovan Bar at Brown's in Mayfair. Created in 2005 by master…}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Summer drinks: cocktail trolleys |url=https://www.ft.com/content/e9219e06-233d-11e4-a424-00144feabdc0 |access-date=April 29, 2023 |work=Financial Times |date=August 15, 2014 |quote=…there is no denying the deliciousness of its speciality cocktails, such as the Spicy Fifty with chillis, elderflower and honey syrup.}}</ref>
; [[Spritz (cocktail)|Spritz]] : Made with [[Prosecco]], [[bitters]], and [[soda water]].
; [[Suffering bastard]] : Name for two different mixed drinks, one being more of a standard cocktail associated with [[World War II]] and the other being more of an exotic drink associated with [[Tiki bars]].
; [[Three dots and a dash (cocktail)|Three dots and a dash]]: Made with [[Martinique]] [[rum]], blended aged [[rum]], [[Falernum]], [[allspice]] liqueur, honey syrup, fresh lime juice, fresh orange juice, and [[Angostura bitters]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Three Dots and a Dash – IBA |url=https://iba-world.com/iba-cocktail/three-dots-and-a-dash/ |access-date=2024-11-14 |language=en-US}}</ref>
; [[Manhattan (cocktail)#Variations|Tipperary]] : Made with [[Irish whiskey]], sweet red [[Vermouth]], [[green Chartreuse]], and [[Angostura bitters]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tipperary |url=https://iba-world.com/new-era-drinks/tipperary/ |access-date=29 May 2020 |website=IBA Official Cocktails}}</ref>
; [[Tommy's margarita]] : Made with [[tequila]], [[lime juice]], and [[agave nectar]] or [[simple syrup]], and orange bitters served in a [[cocktail glass]]. It is distinct from the [[margarita]] in its omission of [[Orange liqueur (disambiguation)|orange liqueur]] and its preferred substitution of agave nectar to highlight the natural agave notes in [[tequila]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=A Visit With Julio Bermejo, Creator of Tommy's Margarita |url=https://www.patrontequila.com/social-club/2016-03/a-visit-with-julio-bermejo.html |access-date=9 April 2017 |website=Tequila Patrón}}</ref>
; [[Trinidad sour]] : Made with [[Angostura bitters]], [[orgeat syrup]], [[lemon juice]], and [[rye whiskey]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Trinidad Sour – IBA |url=https://iba-world.com/iba-cocktail/trinidad-sour/ |access-date=2025-06-06 |language=en-US}}</ref>
; [[Ve.n.to]] : Made with white smooth [[grappa]], [[lemon juice]], honey mix (made with [[chamomile]] infusion if desired), chamomile [[Cordial (drink)|cordial]], and optionally egg white.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ve.N.To – IBA |url=https://iba-world.com/iba-cocktail/ve-n-to/ |access-date=2025-06-06 |language=en-US}}</ref>

==History==
After the initial 1961 list, there have been revisions in 1987, 1993, 2004, 2011, 2020, and 2024.<ref name="aibm2011">{{cite web |url=https://www.aibmproject.it/iba_official_cocktails/ |title=IBA Official Cocktails (2011 – 2019) |date=9 February 2020 |lang=it}}</ref>

===1961===
The 1961 list consisted of 50 drinks:<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aibmproject.it/iba-official-cocktails-1961-1987/ |title=IBA Official Cocktails (1961–1987) |work=AIBM Project |date=5 August 2019 }}</ref> Adonis, Affinity, Alaska, Alexander, Angel Face, Bacardi, Bamboo, Bentley, Between The Sheets, Block And Fall, Bloody Mary, Bobby Burns, Bombay, Bronx, Brooklyn, Caruso, Casino, Claridge, Clover Club, Czarina, Daiquiri, Derby, Diki-Diki, Duchess, Est-India, Gibson, Gin And It, Grand Slam, Grasshopper, Manhattan, Martini Dry, Martini Sweet, Mary Pickford, Mikado, Monkey Gland, Negroni, Old Fashioned, Old Pal, Orange Blossom, Oriental, Paradise, Parisian, Planters, Princeton, Rob Roy, Rose, Sidecar, Stinger, White Lady, Za-Za.

===1987===

A total of 24 drinks were removed: Adonis, Affinity, Alaska, Bamboo, Bentley, Block And Fall, Bobby Burns, Bombay, Brooklyn, Caruso, Claridge, Czarina, Diki-Diki, Duchess, Est-India, Grand Slam, Martini Sweet, Mikado, Old Pal, Orange Blossom, Oriental, Parisian, Princeton, Za-Za.

===1993===

===2020===
The IBA list was significantly updated in 2020, with 24 new drinks, 11 removed drinks, 2 movements between sections, and 1 renaming.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://wildandwanderfultravel.com/index.php/2020/04/16/2020-iba-cocktail-list/ |title=The New 2020 IBA Cocktail List. The Quest (modified) |author=Jacquelyn |date=2020-04-16 |work=Wild and Wanderful Travel}}</ref>

The following 24 drinks were added in the 2020 update:
* 6 drinks added to The Unforgettables: Boulevardier, Brandy Crusta, Hanky Panky, Last Word, Martinez, Vieux Carré.
* 2 drinks added to Contemporary Classics: Corpse Reviver #2, Zombie.
* 16 drinks added to New Era Drinks: Bee's Knees, Canchanchara, Fernandito, Illegal, Naked and Famous, New York Sour, Old Cuban, Paloma, Paper Plane, Penicillin, Southside, Spicy Fifty, Suffering Bastard, Tipperary, Trinidad Sour, Ve.n.to.
The following 11 drinks were removed in the 2020 update:
* 3 drinks removed from The Unforgettables: Bacardi, Derby, Screwdriver
* 4 drinks removed from Contemporary Classics: Godfather, Godmother, Harvey Wallbanger, Rose
* 4 drinks removed from New Era Drinks: B-52, Dirty Martini, Kamikaze, Vampiro

Other changes:
* Pisco Sour and Vesper both moved from "New Era Drinks" to "Contemporary Classics"
* "Spritz Veneziano" was renamed "Spritz", and remained in "New Era Drinks"

===2024===
The IBA list was updated in early November 2024 with 15 new drinks, 3 removed drinks, and 1 movement between sections. For the first time ever, each category is evenly split, with 34 drinks in each.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cocktails – IBA |url=https://iba-world.com/cocktails/ |access-date=2024-11-14 |language=en-US}}</ref>

The following 16 drinks were added in the 2024 update:
* 1 drink added to The Unforgettables: Remember the Maine
* 3 drinks added to Contemporary Classics: Cardinale, Garibaldi, Rabo De Galo.
* 11 drinks added to The New Era: Chartreuse Swizzle, Don's Special Daiquiri, Gin Basil Smash, Grand Margarita, IBA Tiki, Jungle Bird, Missionary's Downfall, Pisco Punch, Porn Star Martini, Sherry Cobbler, Three Dots and a Dash.
The following 3 drinks were removed in the 2024 update:
* 1 drink removed from Contemporary Classics: Golden Dream
* 2 drinks removed from The New Era: Barracuda, Yellow Bird.
Other changes:
* Lemon Drop Martini was moved from "New Era Drinks" to "Contemporary Classics"

* "Southside" was briefly removed in early 2021, but was present from mid-2021 to mid-2023. It was again removed from mid-2023, before being added in the 2024 update as "South Side".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-10-18 |title=New Era Drinks Archives - iba-world.com |url=https://iba-world.com/category/iba-cocktails/new-era-drinks/ |access-date=2024-11-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211018194117/https://iba-world.com/category/iba-cocktails/new-era-drinks/ |archive-date=18 October 2021 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-10-07 |title=The Unforgettables Archives - iba-world.com |url=https://iba-world.com/category/iba-cocktails/the-unforgettables/ |access-date=2024-11-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007105807/https://iba-world.com/category/iba-cocktails/the-unforgettables/ |archive-date=7 October 2024 }}</ref>

Whiskey sour:
{{short description|Mixed drink containing whiskey}}
{{Infobox drink
| name        = Whiskey sour
| image       = Whiskey Sour.jpg

* 3 cl (2 parts) fresh [[lemon juice]]
* 1.5 cl (1 part) [[Syrup#Simple sugar syrups|simple syrup]]}}
| served      = On the rocks or straight up
| garnish     = Maraschino cherry and half orange slice
| prep        = Shake with ice. Strain into chilled glass, garnish and serve.

A '''whiskey sour''' is a [[mixed drink]] or [[Shooter (drink)|shot]] containing [[whiskey]], [[lemon juice]], and [[Syrup#Simple sugar syrups|simple syrup]], and traditionally garnished with a cherry or sometimes a lemon wedge. It is a blend of [[Sour (cocktail)|sour]], bitter, and sweet flavors.

Sometimes, an egg white is included, which is sometimes called a '''Boston sour'''. When the whisky used is a [[Scotch whisky|Scotch]], it is called a '''Scotch sour'''. With a few [[bar spoon]]s of full-bodied red wine floated on top, it is usually referred to as a [[New York sour]]. It is [[Cocktail shaker|shaken]] and served either [[Straight up (bartending)|straight up]] or over ice.

The [[International Bartenders Association]] recipe includes a [[Cocktail garnish|garnish]] of half an [[Orange (fruit)|orange]] slice and a [[maraschino cherry]].<ref name="IBA">{{cite web
 |url=https://iba-world.com/whiskey-sour/
 |title=Whiskey Sour - iba-world.com
 |publisher=International Bartenders Association
 |access-date=2023-06-17
}}</ref>

A variant of the whiskey sour is the [[Ward 8 (cocktail)|Ward 8]], which often is based on bourbon or [[rye whiskey]], and includes both lemon juice and [[orange juice]], and [[grenadine]] syrup as the sweetener. The egg white sometimes employed in other whiskey sours is not usually included.

[[File:Whiskey Sour Served Up.jpg|thumb|right|A whiskey sour shaken and served up in a coupe glass]]

==History==
The oldest historical mention of a whiskey sour was published in the [[Wisconsin]] newspaper ''Waukesha Plain Dealer'', in 1870.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://i96.photobucket.com/albums/l179/ntnfan/Picture4.png |work=Waukesha Plaindealer |date=January 4, 1870 |title=Terence McGrant |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110723202726/http://i96.photobucket.com/albums/l179/ntnfan/Picture4.png |archive-date=July 23, 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://i96.photobucket.com/albums/l179/ntnfan/Picture3.png |work=Waukesha Plaindealer |date=January 4, 1870 |title=Photo from newspaperarchive.com. Magnified section |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110723202808/http://i96.photobucket.com/albums/l179/ntnfan/Picture3.png |archivedate=July 23, 2011 }}</ref>

In 1962, the [[Universidad del Cuyo]] published a story, citing the [[Peru]]vian [[newspaper]] ''El Comercio de Iquique'', which indicated that [[Pisco Sour|Elliott Stubb]] created the "whisky sour" in [[Iquique]] in 1872, using [[Limón de Pica]] for the citrus.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Zki1AAAAIAAJ&q=%22que+vimos+en+viejos+archivos+del+Club+Chino%22 |title=Historias de la Pampa Salitrera |author=Comité del Salitre |page= 49|quote=¿Sabía usted que el exquisito whisky sour, hoy trago de acaudalados, es de origen iquiqueño?. Cuentan las tradiciones y en algunos párrafos del periódico 'El Comercio de Iquique' que vimos en viejos archivos del Club Chino de este puerto que un buen mayordomo del velero "Sunshine" determinó anclar en este puerto...|year=1988 }}</ref><ref name=cuyo>{{cite journal|url=https://books.google.com/books?hl=es&q=En%20adelante%20dijo%20Elliot%20%E2%80%94%20%C3%A9ste%20ser%C3%A1%20mi%20trago%20de%20batalla%2C%20%E2%80%94%20mi%20trago%20favorito%20%E2%80%94%20%2C%20y%20se%20llamar%C3%A1%20Whisky%20Sour%20(sour%2C%20el%20%C3%A1cido%20del%20lim%C3%B3n)&sourceid=navclient-ff&rlz=1B5GGGL_esPE318&um=1&ie=UTF-8&sa=N&tab=wp |journal=Anales del Instituto de Lingüística|author= Universidad Nacional de Cuyo|volume= VIII|location= Mendoza, Argentina|page= 385|date= 1962|title=El vino y la chicha|quote=Cierto dia Elliot Stubb estaba haciendo algunos experimentos en la en la "coctelera" con whisky y limón de pica y su sabor alcanzó delicias superiores a todos los otros menjurjes que acostumbraba a dar a sus clientes. "Voy a ponerle un poco de dulce", se dijo. Echó azúcar a una porción de jugo de limón de Pica, un poco de hielo, whisky en proporción y batió algunos segundos Y probo el mas exquisito drink que habia preparado. En adelante dijo Elliot—éste será mi trago de batalla,—mi trago favorito—, y se llamará Whisky Sour (sour, el ácido del limón). Luego dominó las fronteras y hacía su aparición en Inglaterra, donde ya estaba cimentada la fama del limón de Pica, el que hasta ahora se continúa exportando a la capital del Reino Unido y otros puntos de las Islas Británicas.}}</ref>

Sea breeze (cocktail):
{{short description|Cocktail of vodka with cranberry and grapefruit juice}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=August 2022}}
{{Infobox drink

| image       = Cocktail_with_vodka.jpg

A '''sea breeze''' is a [[cocktail]] containing [[vodka]] with [[cranberry juice]] and [[grapefruit juice]].<ref name="stillspirits">{{Cite web | title = Seabreeze - Cocktails - Flavour Essences | url = http://stillspirits.com/au/flavour-essences/cocktails/seabreeze.html | publisher = Still Spirits | accessdate = 13 June 2011 | url-status = dead | archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20110828023918/http://stillspirits.com/au/flavour-essences/cocktails/seabreeze.html | archivedate = 28 August 2011 | df = dmy-all }}</ref> The cocktail is usually consumed during summer months. The drink may be shaken in order to create a foamy surface.<ref name="stillspirits"/> It is considered an [[IBA Official Cocktail]].<ref name="stillspirits"/>

The drink follows the classic cocktail principle of balancing strong ([[alcohol (drug)|alcohol]]) with weak ([[fruit juice]]) and sweet and sour.<ref name="stillspirits"/><ref name="eatoutzone">{{cite web | author=Eatoutzone | title=Cocktails with Vodka | url=http://www.eatoutzone.com/Cocktail_with_Vodka.htm#Sea_Breeze | accessdate=8 November 2007 | url-status=dead | archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20080704065346/http://www.eatoutzone.com/Cocktail_with_Vodka.htm#Sea_Breeze | archivedate=4 July 2008 | df=dmy-all }}</ref>

A [[bay breeze (cocktail)|bay breeze]], or a Hawaiian sea breeze, is similar to a sea breeze except for the substitution of [[Pineapple|pineapple juice]] for grapefruit juice.<ref name="eatoutzone"/><ref name="Agencies2000">{{cite book|author=Harvard Student Agencies|title=The official Harvard Student Agencies bartending course|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4iY21z80I0QC&pg=PA47|year=2000|publisher=Macmillan|isbn=978-0-312-25286-1|page=47}}</ref> It is also closely related to the [[Cape Codder (cocktail)|Cape Codder]] (which lacks the grapefruit juice) and the [[Salty Dog (cocktail)|Salty Dog]] (which lacks the cranberry juice and is made with a salted rim).<ref name="DeGroff2008">{{cite book|author=Dale DeGroff|title=The Essential Cocktail: The Art of Mixing Perfect Drinks|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QQPQnCwBdJ8C&pg=PT332|year=2008|publisher=Random House Digital, Inc.|isbn=978-0-307-40573-9|page=332}}</ref>

==History==
The cocktail was born in the late 1920s, but the recipe was different from the one used today, as [[gin]] and [[grenadine]] were used in the original sea breeze.<ref>{{cite web | author=Cocktail Idea | title=Sea breeze cocktail recipe | url=http://cocktail.idea.hu/sea-breeze | accessdate=8 November 2007 | url-status=dead | archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20071021010919/http://cocktail.idea.hu/sea-breeze | archivedate=21 October 2007 | df=dmy-all }}</ref> This was near the end of the [[Prohibition in the United States|Prohibition era]]. In the 1930s, a sea breeze had gin, [[apricot brandy]], grenadine, and lemon juice.<ref name="Calabrese2006">{{cite book|author=Salvatore Calabrese|title=Classic Cocktails|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ec7-H6oHpe4C&pg=PA158|year=2006|publisher=Sterling Publishing Company, Inc.|isbn=978-1-4027-3910-1|pages=158–}}</ref> Later, a Sea Breeze recipe would contain vodka, dry [[vermouth]], [[Galliano (liqueur)|Galliano]], and [[blue Curaçao]].<ref name="Calabrese2006"/>

In the 1930s, a cranberry growers' cooperative evolved into [[Ocean Spray (cooperative)|Ocean Spray]], which promoted cranberry juice as a mixer with alcohol, first with gin and later with vodka.<ref name="DeGroff2008"/> Ocean Spray created the Red Devil, later called the harpoon or Cape Codder, in 1945,<ref>"With cranberry juice he adds vodka and a dash of fresh lime and comes up with a "Red Devil Cocktail."" (Ocean Spray's Cranberry Cooperative News: Volumes 6-10 by Cranberry Canners, Inc., 1945)</ref> and its descendants such as the greyhound, the salty dog, the bay breeze, and the sea breeze were later created.<ref name="DeGroff2008"/> Starting in the 1960s, the breeze drinks were sporadically in the top ten most popular mixed drinks.<ref name="DeGroff2008"/>

According to some, the sea breeze, along with the Cape Codder and bay breeze, did not become very popular until the 1970s.<ref name="CharmingBourgoin2009">{{cite book|author1=Cheryl Charming|author2=Susan Bourgoin|title=Knack Bartending Basics: More Than 400 Classic and Contemporary Cocktails for Any Occasion|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AJKr67ceXpMC&pg=PA123|year=2009|publisher=Globe Pequot|isbn=978-1-59921-504-4|pages=123}}</ref> This was because in 1959, the [[United States Department of Health and Human Services|U.S. Department of Health]] stated that cranberry crops were tainted with toxic herbicides, collapsing the cranberry industry.<ref name="CharmingBourgoin2009"/>

A '''South Side''' or '''Southside''' is an alcoholic beverage made with [[gin]], [[lemon juice]], [[simple syrup]] and [[Mentha|mint]]. A variant, the '''Southside Fizz''', adds soda water.

==History==
Its origins are subject to speculation. It has been proposed that it gets its name from either the [[South Side, Chicago|South Side]] district of the city of [[Chicago]], Illinois, or from the [[Southside Sportsmen's Club]] on [[Long Island]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://online.wsj.com/news/articles/SB118738373350801279|title=A Privilege of the Privileged|newspaper=Wall Street Journal|date=18 August 2007|last1=Felten|first1=Eric}}</ref>

The drink may have been the preferred beverage of [[Al Capone]], whose gang dominated Chicago's South Side.<ref name="MentalFloss" /> The gin imported by Capone's rivals on the North Side of Chicago was smooth, and usually consumed with ginger ale.<ref name="MentalFloss" /> However, the gin consumed by Al Capone's gang had a rougher finish, and required more sweeteners to make it palatable.<ref name="MentalFloss" /> Thus the '''South Side''' was born.<ref name="MentalFloss" />

==21 Club recipe==
The following list of ingredients for a south side is used by the famed [[21 Club]] in [[New York City]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mensjournal.com/food-drink/the-21-clubs-mysterious-cocktail-20140123/|title=New York's Most Mysterious Cocktail|author=Christopher Osburn|date=4 December 2017 |access-date=23 December 2022}}</ref>

* {{convert|2|USoz}} [[Tanqueray gin]]
* {{convert|1|USoz}} mint simple syrup
* 4–5 fresh mint leaves
* juice of one lemon
* splash of soda

==South Side Fizz==
[[File:clover club southside fizz (3285775440).jpg|thumb|South Side Fizz]]
A '''South Side Fizz''' adds soda water:<ref name="fizz" />
* {{convert|1.25|USoz}} gin
* {{convert|1/2|USoz}} lime juice
* {{convert|1/2|USoz}} simple syrup
* 1 sprig mint (and one for garnish)
* [[club soda]]

In a shaker, muddle the mint, lime juice and simple syrup. Add the gin and fill with ice. Shake, and strain into a highball glass filled with crushed ice. Stir until frost appears on the outside of the glass. Fill with club soda and garnish with another mint sprig.<ref name="fizz" />

==Related drinks==
The [[Tom Collins]] does not include mint, and is [[carbonation|carbonated]].

The '''tuxedo''' is an [[IBA Official Cocktail]] composed of [[gin]], dry [[vermouth]], [[Bitters|orange bitters]], [[maraschino]] and [[absinthe]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Tuxedo|url=http://iba-world.com/iba-official-cocktails/tuxedo/|website=International Bartender Association|accessdate=28 June 2017}}</ref>

Related to the martini, the tuxedo has had many variations since its inception in the 1880s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cold-glass.com/2015/12/01/the-tale-of-the-tuxedo-cocktail/|title=The Tale of the Tuxedo Cocktail|date=December 2015}}</ref> The cocktail is named after the [[Tuxedo Club]] in [[Orange County, New York]] where it was first mixed. '''Tommy's margarita''' is a variant of the [[margarita]] cocktail that uses [[Agave syrup|agave nectar]] instead of [[triple sec]] and [[simple syrup]]. It is recognized by the [[List of IBA official cocktails|IBA]] as a [[List of IBA official cocktails#New era drinks|new era drink]].<ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=Tommy's Margarita |url=https://iba-world.com/iba-cocktail/tommys-margarita/ |accessdate=1 May 2025 |website=IBA World}}</ref>

==Mixture==
It is made with [[tequila]], [[Lime (fruit)#Uses|lime juice]], and agave nectar, and served in a [[cocktail glass]] with ice.<ref name=":0" /> It is distinct from the classic [[margarita]] due to its omission of orange liqueur and its preferred substitution of agave, which accents the notes in the [[agave]]-based tequila.<ref name="Tequila Patrón">{{cite web|title=A Visit With Julio Bermejo, Creator of Tommy's Margarita|url=https://www.patrontequila.com/social-club/2016-03/a-visit-with-julio-bermejo.html|website=Tequila Patrón|accessdate=9 April 2017}}</ref>

==History==
The cocktail was conceived in 1990 by Julio Bermejo while working at ''Tommy's Mexican Restaurant'' in [[San Francisco]]. Bermejo had been recently introduced to agave nectar as an ingredient, and, although it was expensive at the time, he preferred to use it to enhance the agave flavor of the tequila instead of using [[triple sec]] to highlight the citrus flavor in the original [[margarita]] recipe.<ref name="Tequila Patrón" /><ref>{{cite web|last1=Sintumang|first1=Kevin|title=The Only Margarita Recipe You Need|url=https://www.gq.com/story/the-only-margarita-recipe-you-need|website=GQ|date=3 May 2013|accessdate=9 April 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Krieger|first1=Daniel|title=Tommy's Margarita|url=http://punchdrink.com/recipes/tommys-margarita/|website=Punch|accessdate=9 April 2017}}</ref>

In 2008, it became the first venue-specific cocktail to be added to the IBA manual.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/2667/people/julio-bermejo|title = Julio Bermejo |date=n.d. |work=Difford's Guide |access-date=May 13, 2024}}</ref>

The '''suffering bastard''' is the name for two different mixed drinks, one being more of a standard cocktail (essentially a gin-and-brandy [[Buck (cocktail)|buck]] with added Angostura bitters) associated with World War II and the other being more of an exotic drink associated with [[Tiki bars]]. As is the case with many cocktails, there are multiple recipe variations and historical origins have been argued and changed over time.<ref name="Berry">{{cite book |last1=Berry |first1=Jeff |title=Beachbum Berry Remixed |date=2010 |publisher=Club Tiki Press |location=San Jose |page=92}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Anyone who picks a fight over tiki drinks |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/food/anyone-who-picks-a-fight-over-tiki-drinks-authenticity-is-missing-the-point-of-tiki-drinks/2018/06/18/7d3b85ec-7020-11e8-bf86-a2351b5ece99_story.html?noredirect=on |website=www.washingtonpost.com |accessdate=8 February 2019}}</ref><ref name=slammie>{{cite web |title=Suffering no more, this Bastard finally gets a chance to shine |url=http://www.slammie.com/atomicgrog/blog/2013/06/03/lost-cocktails-of-the-mai-kai-the-off-menu-suffering-bastard-was-just-a-mai-tai-with-a-kick/ |website=slammie.com/ |date=3 June 2013 |accessdate=8 February 2019}}</ref> Two of the earliest recipe versions have very different ingredients.  One from bartender Joe Scialom (1942) calls for brandy and gin, while another from Tiki pioneer Victor J. Bergeron (AKA Trader Vic) primarily uses rum along with "secret ingredients" and is known for being garnished with a cucumber.

==Suffering bastard (1942)==
According to Jeff Berry and others, a suffering bastard cocktail was created at the [[Shepheard's Hotel]] in Cairo.<ref name="Berry"/><ref>{{cite web |title=Suffering Bastard |url=https://punchdrink.com/recipes/suffering-bastard/ |website=punchrink.com |accessdate=8 February 2019}}</ref> Bartender Joe Scialom was looking to make a [[corpse reviver|hangover drink]] for allied troops and according to the story made one as a "cure" for the suffering soldiers who complained about the poor quality of liquor in the area.  

Both the drink and the hotel played a role in WWII.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Suffering Bastard is the cocktail that beat the Nazis in Egypt |url=https://www.wearethemighty.com/history/suffering-bastard-drink-like-sailor|website=wearethemighty.com |accessdate=8 February 2019}}</ref> When the war was going well for the Axis, German [[Erwin_Rommel|General Rommel]] allegedly said "I'll be drinking champagne in the master suite at Shepheard's soon." The allies did well, however, and the drink was supposedly so popular with the troops that a telegram was sent asking for several gallons to be made and brought to the front lines.<ref>{{cite web |title=A Suffering Bastard |url=https://www.chambar.com/anecdotes/mixology/a-suffering-bastard |website=www.chambar.com |accessdate=8 February 2019}}</ref>

According to Berry, Scialom's original handwritten recipe as provided by his daughter called for brandy. Bourbon was frequently swapped out for the brandy where it was available however, and for a short period of time the drink was also called the ''suffering bar steward'', for those that found the use of the word ''bastard'' offensive.<ref name=alprof>{{cite web |title=History of the Suffering Bastard |url=https://www.alcoholprofessor.com/blog-posts/blog/2017/09/12/classic-cocktails-in-history-suffering-bastard |website=www.alcoholprofessor.com |date=12 September 2017 |accessdate=8 February 2019}}</ref> Berry also notes that when Scialom made other versions he had different names for them, and that the addition of bourbon made the drink a ''Dying Bastard'', and the addition of both bourbon and rum made it a ''Dead Bastard''. The VenTiki Lounge uses brandy for the suffering bastard on their classic tiki drinks menu,<ref>{{cite web |title=Drink Menu (Suffering Bastard) |url=http://www.ventikiloungeandlanai.com/classicdrinks/ |website=ventikiloungeandlanai.com |accessdate=8 February 2019}}</ref> but the recipe varies from bar to bar and is significantly different from the one created by Trader Vic.

== Suffering bastard (Trader Vic) ==
Although the suffering bastard is strongly associated with Tiki bars and [[Trader Vic's|Trader Vic]], a recipe for the cocktail was not included in his 1947 ''Bartender's Guide'' recipe book.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bergeron |first1=Victor |title=Trader Vic Bartender Guide |date=1947 |publisher=Doubleday & Co. |location=New York |page=434}}</ref> It does appear in later editions however,<ref>{{cite web |title=Suffering Bastard Trader Vic's |url=http://www.gourmet.com.s3-website-us-east-1.amazonaws.com/recipes/1970s/1971/05/suffering-bastard-trader-vics.html |website=gourmet.com |accessdate=8 February 2019}}</ref> and appeared in the 1968 ''Trader Vic's Pacific Island Cookbook''<ref>{{cite web |title=Suffering Bastard – Trader Vic's |url=https://wiki.webtender.com/wiki/Suffering_Bastard_-_Trader_Vic%27s |website=wiki.webtender.com |accessdate=8 February 2019}}</ref> and calling for both light and dark rums with lime juice and dashes of [[Curaçao (liqueur)|Curaçao]], [[orgeat syrup]], and rock candy syrup.  Other Vic recipes called for the use of his commercial Mai-Tai mix<ref name=alprof/> as a basis along with multiple rums, lime juice, and the unusual garnishment for a Tiki drink of a [[cucumber]] peel.<ref name=slammie/> A hand written note allegedly from a waiter at Trader Vic's circa 1970 listed the "key" ingredient as being the inclusion of rum from [[Barbados]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Suffering Bastard at Trader Vics |url=https://bewitchingkitchen.com/2017/06/12/suffering-bastards-at-trader-vics/ |website=bewitchingkitchen.com |date=12 June 2017 |accessdate=8 February 2019}}</ref> A 21st century cocktail menu at Trader Vic's describes the drink as "A forthright blend of rums, lime and liquors with an affinity for cucumber".<ref>{{cite web |title=Signature Cocktails and Wine |url=https://tradervicsatl.com/drink/ |website=tradervicsatl.com |accessdate=8 February 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190123010527/https://tradervicsatl.com/drink/ |archive-date=23 January 2019}}</ref>

== Suffering bastard mug ==
When ordered in Tiki bars, the suffering bastard is often served in the uniquely shaped and eponymously named "suffering bastard [[Tiki mugs|Tiki mug]]",<ref>{{cite web |title=Suffering Bastard Mug |url=http://www.ooga-mooga.com/cgi-bin/all/search.cgi?terms=%22suffering+bastard%22&des_id=any&man_id=any&img_id=any&shp_id=any&clr_id=any&details=yes&mode=search_process&x=63&y=12 |website=oogamooga.com |accessdate=8 February 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Tiki Drink: Suffering Bastard |url=http://www.killingtime.com/Pegu/2012/02/16/tiki-drink-suffering-bastard/ |website=killingtime.com |accessdate=8 February 2019}}</ref> made to look like a squat fellow with a hangover holding his hands over the top of his head in pain. According to Trader Vic's the mug originally had the name of ''Mai-Tai Joe'',<ref>{{cite web |title=Suffering Bastard Mug |url=https://shop.tradervics.com/products/suffering-bastard-mug |website=tradervics.com |accessdate=8 February 2019}}</ref> perhaps because Trader Vic is largely credited with having invented the [[Mai-Tai]] and his commercial Mai-Tai mix is sometimes used in the making of suffering bastard cocktails.

A '''sherry cobbler''' is a classic American cocktail made with [[sherry]], sugar and citrus. Its origins are not known in detail, but is believed to have originated sometime in the early 19th century. The earliest known mention is from an 1838 diary of a Canadian traveler to the United States, [[Katherine Jane Ellice]], but it did not gain international name recognition until [[Charles Dickens]] included the drink in ''[[The Life and Adventures of Martin Chuzzlewit]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://punchdrink.com/recipes/sherry-cobbler/|title=Sherry Cobbler Cocktail Recipe}}</ref> 

To make the drink, orange and lemon are muddled with simple syrup, sherry is added, and the mixture is shaken with ice in a cocktail shaker and strained into a [[highball glass]] filled with crushed ice. Garnishes include mint leaves, raspberry, and orange and lemon slices.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bonappetit.com/recipe/sherry-cobbler|title=Sherry Cobbler|first=Talia|last=Baiocchi|website=Bon Appétit|date=21 April 2015 }}</ref> It can also be garnished with pineapple wedges or any seasonal berries. Some recipes add pineapple juice.<ref>{{cite web |title=Sherry Cobbler |website=Difford's Guide |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/cocktails/recipe/2895/sherry-cobbler}}</ref>

==History==
[[File:Sherry Cobbler.jpg|thumb|"Early Victorian print" showing a couple sharing a sherry cobbler through drinking straws]]
The Sherry Cobbler emerged during the 1830s and became one of the most popular mixed drinks in the 19th century United States. The invention of the drinking straw around this time made crushed ice drinks like the Sherry Cobbler more convenient. The earliest known reference to a "Cobbler" dates the diary of Canadian traveler Katherine Jane Ellice. It was included in the first book that is known to be specifically for bartenders, that is Jerry Thomas' 1862 edition of ''The Bartender's Guide''. This original recipe is made with just three ingredients:<ref>{{cite web |title=Cobblers |website=Difford's |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/1227/cocktails/cobblers}}</ref>
*2 wine glasses sherry
*1 tbsp sugar
*2 or 3 slices of orange

The popularity of Sherry Cobbler inspired many spinoff drinks like the Champagne Cobbler, Claret Cobbler, and Whiskey Cobbler. In 1888, [[Harry Johnson (bartender)|Harry Johnson]] wrote "This drink is without doubt the most popular beverage in this country, with ladies as well as with gentlemen," but like many classic cocktails their popularity fades after [[Prohibition]].

A 19th-century recipe for [[Fourth of July]] Sherry cobbler is made with strawberries, lemon peel, powdered sugar and sherry.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.foodtimeline.org/july4th.html|title=Food Timeline--Fourth of July food history|website=www.foodtimeline.org}}</ref>

==Variations==
[[File:Course -1- Rebujito (cropped).jpg|thumb|upright|A rebujito]]

[[Rebujito]] is a similar Andalusian drink made by combining sherry and a soft drink, typically white lemonade or lemon-lime soda.

Classic cobblers didn't include muddled fruits but the popularity of the Sherry Cobbler inspired the creation of more elaborate cobblers.

The King's Cobbler was made with rhubarb [[Amaro (liqueur)|amaro]] called [[Zucca (aperitif)|Zucca rabarbaro]] instead of fortified wine. Other ingredients were muddled strawberry, fresh lemon juice and simple syrup, with a mint leaf garnish.

Champagne cobbler is made with muddled pineapple, lemon and orange with [[Maraschino]] liqueur and Champagne in a 1:4 ratio.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/clip/60067922/cobbler-variations/ Variations on the Classic Cobbler] Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, 22 Mar 2012</ref>

== History ==
The cocktail was first documented in Charles H. Baker Jr.'s ''The Gentleman's Companion'' (1939), where he describes it as a drink he enjoyed in [[Havana]], [[Cuba]], in 1933.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Remember the Maine Recipe |url=https://www.seriouseats.com/remember-the-maine-cocktail-recipe |access-date=2025-03-11 |website=Serious Eats |language=en}}</ref> The name references the phrase "[[USS Maine (1889)|Remember the Maine, to Hell with Spain!]]"—a rallying cry following the explosion of the USS ''Maine'' in [[Havana Harbor]] in 1898, an event that contributed to the start of the [[Spanish–American War]].<ref name=":1" /> In 1935, ''Old Waldorf Astoria Bar Book'' wrote about a nearly identical cocktail called McKinley’s Delight ([[William McKinley|McKinley]] was also the president during the Maine incident).<ref name=":2" />

==Preparation==
Absinthe is poured into a coupe glass and swirled to coat the inside of the glass, then discarded.<ref name=":0" /> This glass is set aside.<ref name=":0" /> In a mixing glass, the whiskey, brandy, and vermouth are added, then the glass is filled three-quarters with ice.<ref name=":0" /> It is stirred until chilled.<ref name=":0" /> The mixture is strained into the coupe glass.<ref name=":0" /> The drink is garnished with lemon zest.<ref name=":0" /> Cherries can also be used as garnish.<ref name=":2" />

== Variations ==
The Remember the Maine is similar to a [[Manhattan (cocktail)|Manhattan]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=Pietrek |first=Matt |date=2015-04-05 |title=Cocktail Obsession: Remember the Maine |url=https://cocktailwonk.com/2015/04/cocktail-obsession-remember-the-maine.html |access-date=2025-03-11 |website=Cocktail Wonk |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Pastis]] can substitute the absinthe.<ref name=":2" /> [[Bourbon whiskey|Bourbon]] can substitute the rye whiskey.<ref name=":2" /> There are endless other variations, such as substituting the whiskey with [[tequila]].<ref name=":3" />

The '''IBA official cocktails''' are [[cocktail]]s recognised by the [[International Bartenders Association]] (IBA) to be the most requested recipes.<ref name="iba-list">{{Cite web |title= IBA official cocktail list|url=https://iba-world.com/iba-official-cocktail-list/  |website=International Bartenders Association |access-date=2 January 2023}}</ref> The list was developed starting in 1960, and the first version was announced in 1961, comprising 50 cocktails.<ref name="iba-list" /> It has since undergone periodic revisions, and as of {{CURRENTYEAR}} comprises 102 cocktails in 3 categories; see {{slink||History}} for more.

==List of cocktails==
{{as of|2024}}, there are 102 IBA official cocktails, divided into three equal categories of 34: The Unforgettables, Contemporary Classics, and New Era Drinks.

It is served in a large non-tapered {{convert|12|to|14|usoz|ml|adj=on}} [[Collins glass]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.neworleansonline.com/neworleans/cuisine/drinks/ramosginfizz.html |title=Ramos Gin Fizz |website=New Orleans Online |access-date=2 January 2016}}</ref>

; [[Tuxedo (cocktail)|Tuxedo]] : Made with [[gin]], dry [[vermouth]], [[Bitters|orange bitters]], [[maraschino]], and [[absinthe]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tuxedo |url=http://iba-world.com/iba-official-cocktails/tuxedo/ |access-date=28 June 2017 |website=International Bartender Association}}</ref>
